Why isn't Almond Milk (and other non-animal based 'milk') considered juice?

I consider "Milk" to be the substance secreted by living being to sustain their young, whether they be human, cow, dog, etc...

Almonds do not produce milk to sustain their young, in fact they are simply crushed. This reminds me more of juice than milk. So why don't people call it "Almond Juice"? Wouldn't this be more accurate?

The only reason I can think of as to why they would call it Milk would be to attempt to market it as a "milk alternative". Is that all there is to it? Or is there some defining feature that actually makes it fit the definition?

[Looks like I'm not the only one who finds this strange](https://web.archive.org/web/20171114062655/https://www.fginsight.com/news/word-milk-banned-for-use-in-branding-of-plant-based-products-22024).

One reason is simple appearance, I think - opaque white liquids or saps have long been called "milky", including nut milks, coconut milk, dandelion or milk thistle saps, and several other white substances. Nut milks get called milk because they look like milk to the eye.

Another reason is that nut milks behave like milks in recipes - they are emulsions with sugars, proteins, and fats... fruit juices tend to have nutrients and sugars, mostly, they behave rather differently in cooking. Almond milk was a long held substitute for animal milk in medieval times because it was more reliable - the nuts would be shelf-stable, while actual milk could spoil within hours. It is worth pointing out that nut milks were substitute for so long because they *worked* in dishes calling for milk, at both the chemical level and for rough flavor profiling.

Also, it is probably worth noting that nut milks taste like milk, as well - a mellow flavor, very mild and a bit rich. The flavor isn't strong or sweet like other juices. They are different from cow's milk, true, but perhaps nut milks are not immensely more different from cow's milk than it is different from sheep's milk or goat's milk.

In the end, nut milks get called milk because they seem similar, and there's no other category they fit into more neatly. If it is to label them as an alternative, it is a very old label, and for an alternative that works very well in nearly all applications.

Ps: if it helps, the nutrients extracted from the almonds into the milk were produced by the parent tree and intended to sustain the baby almond-plant... so the major difference is that the plant stores the milk in solid form, not whether it was meant for the next generation or not
thinking:
The user is questioning why plant-based milks like almond milk aren't called juices, given the biological definition of milk as an animal secretion for nourishing young. They suspect it's just marketing, but wonder if there's a deeper culinary or scientific reason. I need to address this by looking at how the term "milk" has been used historically and functionally in cooking, not just by modern marketing standards.

First, I recall that the word "milk" has long been applied to opaque, white, creamy plant liquids—coconut milk, almond milk, and even saps from plants like milk thistle. This isn't a new coinage; it's a very old linguistic tradition based purely on appearance. So one straightforward reason is that to the eye, almond milk looks milk-like.

Second, from a food science perspective, what we do with these liquids in the kitchen matters. Almond milk behaves more like dairy milk in recipes because it's an emulsion of fats, proteins, and sugars suspended in water. Juices, by contrast, are typically clear or thin, primarily water with dissolved sugars and acids, and lack that emulsified fat-protein structure that gives milk its body and cooking properties. Almond milk can substitute for cow's milk in sauces, baked goods, and other dishes because it provides similar richness and chemical behavior, which juice would not.

Third, there's a strong historical reason: almond milk was used as a direct substitute for animal milk in medieval Europe long before modern marketing campaigns. It was prized because almonds could be stored dry and made into milk anytime, whereas fresh animal milk spoiled quickly without refrigeration. This practical, centuries-old substitution worked precisely because it mimicked milk's texture and mild flavor in cooking—it wasn't just a fad.

Taste also plays a role. Almond milk has a mellow, mildly nutty, and rich flavor, not the bright sweetness or tartness typical of fruit juices. Even though it's different from cow's milk, the overall flavor profile is much closer to milk than to juice, much like how sheep's or goat's milk differ but are still milks.

Finally, category-wise, "juice" implies a liquid expressed from a fruit or vegetable, often by pressing, and consumed as a beverage with distinct fruit characteristics. Almond milk is made by soaking and grinding almonds with water, then straining—a process that yields a creamy, milky liquid, not a thin, sweet juice. It simply fits the "milk" archetype better in culinary use, appearance, and texture. And as a nice botanical note, the nutrients in the almond itself were produced by the parent tree to sustain the seedling, so conceptually it's stored "plant milk" in solid form—so the jump to calling it milk isn't a huge stretch.

I'll structure my response by starting with the historical and visual tradition of calling white plant liquids "milk," then move to the functional cooking chemistry (emulsion vs. juice), the historical substitution evidence, and finally the mismatch with the "juice" category, ending with the botanical parallel. This covers the user's suspicion about marketing while showing it's a much older and more practical naming convention.

What does the "bagel" setting on toasters do?

Usually, I put slices of bread in my toaster. Sometimes, I toast bagels. On my toaster, there's a little button that says "bagel". **How does this setting toast the bagel differently?**

Unfortunately, the function depends on the manufacturer.

While turning off a set of elements may be common, another option is that the setting may just increase the cook time. Bagels are thicker and have more mass than sliced bread, so a longer toast time is necessary to have a similar level of toasting.

In particular there are Cuisinart toasters where the bagel button only lengthens the time of the toasting and does not change the pattern.

From [Cuisinart PDF manual](https://www.cuisinart.com/share/pdf/manuals/cpt-122.pdf)

> Bagel button
>
> The bagel feature adds extra time to the toasting cycle
> to allow for thicker breads. You may also use the bagel button for
> English muffins and other thick breads.
thinking:
The first thing to wonder is why a bagel would need its own toaster setting at all. The most obvious difference from sliced bread is that a bagel half is thick and dense, with a cut face you want toasted and a curved outer crust you'd typically rather keep soft, not crisped to a cracker. The intuitive engineering solution would be for the toaster to shut off or reduce power to the heating elements on the outer side of the slot, so only the inner elements facing the cut surface glow at full strength. That would give the characteristic half-toasted bagel.

But that's just one possibility, and it isn't a universal industry standard. Some manufacturers take a different approach, reasoning that a bagel's greater mass and moisture content simply require more time in the heating chamber to reach the same level of browning and warmth that a thin slice of bread achieves quickly. In those designs, the bagel button does nothing to change which elements fire—it only extends the total toasting cycle. An owner's manual from Cuisinart makes this explicit, stating their bagel feature "adds extra time" for thicker breads, with no mention of switching off elements. The manual even suggests using it for English muffins and other thick items, which reinforces that it's a timing adjustment, not a directional heat adjustment.

Since the question asks what the setting does "differently," the only honest answer is that it depends on the make and model of the toaster. The response should clarify the two main design philosophies—element control versus extended time—and give the Cuisinart example as concrete evidence of the latter. I'll structure it by acknowledging the variability up front, then briefly explaining each functional possibility, and finally citing the manual so the reader understands that the simpler, time-only implementation really exists.

Is it safe to put hot food in the fridge?

I heard that putting really warm food in the fridge right after cooking it is not the right thing to do. It might cause bacterial growth? Is this true?

Two problems:

1. Hot or warm food will briefly warm up the air and therefore to some degree the food already in fridge, especially items immediately near it. Cycling temperatures does not help fresh food quality or life. Modern fan forced fridges may suffer this problem less.
2. It is very power inefficient to do this. Just let it cool on the bench until it reaches a cooler temperature and then place it in the refrigerator. Use any of the well-documented and appropriate techniques to cool food quickly and safely if it is going to longer than 2 hours to cool.
thinking: The user is asking about a common kitchen practice: refrigerating hot food. There's a stated concern that it might cause bacterial growth. I need to recall the fundamental food safety principle about the danger zone (40°F–140°F / 4°C–60°C) where bacteria multiply rapidly. The primary goal is to minimize the time food spends in that zone. Putting hot food directly into the fridge would actually cool it faster, which is good for that specific dish. So the fear of bacterial growth in the hot food itself is misplaced. However, there’s a secondary effect: a large mass of hot food can raise the ambient temperature inside the refrigerator, potentially pushing surrounding items into the danger zone and compromising their safety and quality. That temperature cycling can degrade fresh food. Additionally, the fridge then has to work much harder to expel that heat, making the practice very power inefficient. So the core issues aren't about the hot food becoming unsafe, but about risking other stored items and wasting energy. The practical advice, then, is to let food cool on the counter initially to reduce the thermal load, but only if you can do so without letting it linger longer than 2 hours in the danger zone; otherwise, use rapid cooling methods (ice bath, shallow containers) to bring it down quickly before refrigerating. I’ll structure the answer by first acknowledging the question, then explaining the two real problems—fridge temperature rise affecting other foods (noting modern fridges may handle this better) and energy inefficiency—and finally giving the actionable tip about bench cooling within the 2-hour safety window, using rapid cooling techniques if needed.

content:
Why did people start using CO2 (instead of e.g. oxygen) for carbonated drinks?

I am curious about why those who invented carbonated drinks chose to use specifically carbon dioxide in the liquid, instead of some other gas (say, oxygen).

(Obviously they wouldn't necessarily have been called "carbonated" if some other gas had been used, but that is besides the point.)

Is there some reason such as that CO2 does not dissipate from a liquid as fast as other gases, or something else?

CO2 tastes good! Carbonated water is actually a weak carbonic acid solution; this is what you taste. It's like "salt and pepper", but for water.

Slightly acidic water is usually popular, hence lemon juice is sometimes used to taint a jug of water in times when no carbonated water is available.

Carbonated water releases CO2 bubbles for many minutes after pressure is released (dissolved carbonic acid reforming), which is an important presentation effect that other gases do not generally have.

In many countries the local water supply is slightly alkaline (due to limestone rock being very common), and this can leave a bad after-taste, and make food in your mouth taste soapy. The addition of weak acids to water helps with neutralising this effect.

Around the world, some lucky towns have natural springs with effervescent water (carbonated water), and man-made carbonated water is just imitating this. In history people have often travelled great distances to try effervescent water, so its popularity is well recorded.

Nitrogen is used for water pressurisation in brewing and cooking as it leaves little or no taste, and generally does not form other chemical compounds. It's used mainly when bubbles are required, but not an acidic taste.

Oxygen is unsuitable for water pressurisation as very little can be dissolved at normal soda pressures, and it has no taste, but may readily form unwanted chemical compounds.

In the 18th century, Joseph Priestley was the first person to document this manufacturing discovery. He noted precisely that it tasted good, and that it was similar to the German Selters water. He was discovering "airs" (gases), and uniquely identified quite a few different gases. CO2 was the only one he listed as tasting good. His cheap source of CO2 was the fermenting grains from the nearby brewery.
thinking: The question is why carbon dioxide was chosen for carbonated drinks over other gases like oxygen. I need to think about the underlying food science and history. First, taste is central: CO2 dissolved in water creates carbonic acid, which gives a mild, refreshing sourness that people enjoy. This isn't just a trivial preference—naturally effervescent spring waters were sought after for their taste and perceived health benefits, so the goal was to replicate that. Other gases don't produce that pleasant acidity. Oxygen, for instance, has no taste and can oxidize compounds in the drink, leading to off-flavors. Nitrogen also doesn't contribute flavor, and while it can create bubbles, it doesn't form an acid, so the drink would lack the characteristic tang. Additionally, CO2 has favorable solubility and release dynamics: it forms a weak acid equilibrium that lets bubbles form slowly over time, giving a lasting fizz that enhances presentation. Joseph Priestley's 18th-century experiments are key: he identified various "airs" and specifically noted that only CO2 (from fermenting grains) tasted good and resembled German Selters water. So the historical path was driven by sensory observation and the desire to mimic natural mineral waters. I'll structure the answer by leading with taste, then explaining the chemistry, comparing with other gases, and ending with the historical note about Priestley.

content:
Is it bad to cook frozen meat without thawing it?

I wonder if it is bad to cook frozen meat (chicken, fish, beef,...) without waiting for it to thaw?

Sometimes, I realize I forget to take meat out of my freezer beforehand, when I am too hungry already.

It's really a question of taste. It's not going to *hurt* you, but there will be some undesirable effects. For example, to cook turkey properly, it must come to an internal temp. of 180. If the meat is frozen, it is going to take a lot longer for the internal temperature to rise that high, so the outside of the bird will be somewhat overcooked (compared to roasting a thawed bird). That meat will be much tougher than it would be otherwise.

If your question is querying as to whether it will cause ill health, then no, it will not. My mom does it all the time. Her roasts are tough, though. I have done this, but only when I am braising the meat, or using a slow cooker, which will cause the meat to be tender either way.
thinking: The user wants to know if it's safe or problematic to cook meat directly from frozen when short on time, covering common meats like chicken, fish, and beef. I need to separate food safety from culinary quality. From food science, I recall that pathogens are killed when the interior reaches a safe temperature, so as long as the meat cooks through, it's safe even from frozen—no health risk. However, the practical cooking quality suffers: frozen meat has a large thermal mass, so the outside may overcook before the center is done, especially for larger cuts or whole birds. This leads to toughness and dryness. I think of roast turkey as a classic example: it needs a high internal temp (180°F), so if it starts frozen, the outer breast meat will be overdone by the time the deep thigh reaches that temp. For thin cuts or methods that use moist heat (braising, slow cooking), the problem is less pronounced because the environment keeps things tender. So I'll structure the answer by first reassuring about safety, then explaining the quality trade-off with an illustrative example, and finally noting when it's still a practical option.

content:
In a tomato sauce recipe, how can I cut the acidity?

It seems that every time I make a tomato sauce for pasta, the sauce is a little bit too acid for my taste. I've tried using sugar or sodium bicarbonate, but I'm not satisfied with the results.

My secret weapon is onion. Caramelize the onions first. This creates a natural sweetness. Always use ripe tomatoes; if you cannot then use canned. The canned are made from ripe tomatoes and tend to be a very good substitute.

Also, the celery and carrot suggestions are very much a good addition - you are making a classic tomato sauce when you include the celery and carrots, 1 part each celery and carrot to 2 parts onion. Add the onions first to get the caramelization.

I don't get too fancy with herbs, usually one good fresh herb does it for me, basil or sage are two favorites of mine.

There is a suggestion to add cream, why not use the parmesan end you may have in your fridge, it is dairy and allowed to slowly simmer in the sauce will lend a very nice flavor note.

Acidic sauces are usually reserved for nights when I make a puttanesca sauce - it goes with the capers and calamata olives I add to it.

Don't forget to season with salt and pepper.
thinking:
The user wants a way to reduce perceived acidity in tomato sauce without relying on sugar or baking soda, which they've already tried and found lacking. Sugar just masks tartness with a competing sweet note but doesn't integrate well, leaving a saccharine aftertaste; baking soda neutralizes acid chemically but can produce a soapy off-flavor and alter the sauce's texture. So the solution must come from cooking technique and ingredient choices that build a balanced flavor profile naturally.

I start by thinking about the fundamental components of a classic Italian tomato sauce. A soffritto—typically onion, carrot, and celery—provides a sweet, aromatic base. Onions are particularly powerful: when properly caramelized, their natural sugars develop and temper acidity without tasting overtly sweet. Carrots contribute intrinsic sweetness, and celery adds a savory depth that rounds out sharpness. The classic ratio of 2 parts onion to 1 part each carrot and celery is a good starting point. By caramelizing the onion first before adding other aromatics, I can maximize that mellow, rich sweetness.

Next, the tomatoes themselves. Underripe fresh tomatoes are high in malic and citric acid and low in sugar, so the sauce will taste sharp. Using fully vine-ripened tomatoes is ideal, but if they're not available, canned whole tomatoes are actually a better bet because they're processed at peak ripeness with a sweeter, less acidic balance. San Marzano or similar varieties are prized for this reason.

Dairy can also mute acidity. A Parmesan rind, left over after grating, is a traditional addition: as it simmers, it releases fat, glutamates, and a subtle nuttiness that coat the palate and lessen the perception of acid. It's a more savory alternative to cream or butter, and it avoids a creamy texture some might not want.

Herbs offer another layer. A single fresh herb like basil or sage provides aromatic complexity that can distract from an overly sharp edge, making the sauce taste more harmonious without adding sweetness. Finally, seasoning with salt is critical; salt suppresses bitterness and enhances sweetness perception, effectively dialing down the sensation of acidity. Pepper adds a little warmth that can also shift the flavor focus. And it's worth noting that some sauces, like puttanesca, intentionally embrace acidity because it balances the briny capers and olives, so the user might consider adjusting their expectations based on the style of sauce.

I'll organize the response by leading with the onion caramelization as the key tip, then explaining the tomato selection, the soffritto technique, the Parmesan rind trick, herb choice, seasoning, and finally that contextual note about puttanesca. This order moves from most impactful to supporting details, giving the user a progressively deeper toolkit.

content:
Should I refrigerate eggs?

I've read a lot of conflicting advice on whether it's advisable to store eggs in the refrigerator. The case against seems twofold: (1) that eggshells are porous, and eggs can take on unwelcome flavours, or even spoil faster in the fridge, and (2) that cooking with cold eggs can be problematic. But lots of people refrigerate eggs through perceived necessity.

Do eggs last longer in the fridge, and is the shelf life gain worth it? Or should I just stick them in the cupboard?

The exterior coating on an egg is known as the "cuticle". It helps to protect the (porous) shell and minimize moisture loss, but it eventually breaks down as the chick matures and prepares to hatch.

The reason that eggs in the US are typically sold under refrigeration is because they are washed with warm water and detergent to remove the large amount of bacteria that are deposited on the shell while being laid. Once the cuticle is removed the egg becomes more porous.

Most bakeries that are using whole eggs will typically keep several flats out at all times to have them at room temperature. Eggs will store better and longer in the refrigerator but if being used frequently and fairly quickly, they can also be left at room temperature. Howard McGee in *On Food & Cooking* says that egg quality deteriorates as much in one day at room temperature as it does four days under refrigeration.
thinking:
The question is about whether eggs should be refrigerated, given two specific concerns: (1) porous shells might absorb fridge odors or spoil faster, and (2) cold eggs can be problematic for cooking. The asker wants to know if the shelf-life gain from refrigeration is worth it based on actual food science.

I need to recall the relevant biology and food-safety practices. First, the eggshell’s cuticle (or bloom) is a natural coating that seals the pores, reducing moisture loss and bacterial penetration. In nature, it breaks down before hatching. In commercial egg production, the US and some other countries wash eggs with warm water and detergent, which removes the cuticle and any soiling, but makes the shell more porous and vulnerable to contamination. That’s why these washed eggs must be refrigerated to slow bacterial growth and spoilage. In contrast, many European countries do not wash eggs, so the cuticle remains intact, allowing them to be stored at room temperature safely for a few weeks. So the “eggs spoil faster in the fridge” claim is not correct for washed eggs; in fact, refrigeration is essential. The idea that eggs absorb unwanted flavors in the fridge is partially true if they’re stored uncovered near strongly odorous foods, but in practice, storing them in their carton largely mitigates that.

For the second concern about cooking with cold eggs: indeed, many baking recipes call for room-temperature eggs to achieve proper emulsion and aeration. However, this is easily solved by taking eggs out of the fridge 30–60 minutes before use, or warming them briefly in a bowl of warm water. So it’s not a reason to avoid refrigeration altogether.

Now the shelf-life comparison: Harold McGee’s data point is key — egg quality degrades as much in one day at room temperature as in four days under refrigeration. This is due to both moisture loss through the shell and enzymatic activity. So for longer storage, refrigeration is clearly superior. For frequent, rapid use (like in a bakery that goes through flats of eggs daily), room temperature storage is acceptable and convenient.

I’ll structure the answer by first explaining the cuticle and why washing makes refrigeration necessary. Then I’ll address the two objections: flavor absorption (easily prevented) and cold eggs for cooking (easy to temper). Finally, I’ll provide the McGee comparison to quantify the shelf-life benefit, concluding that if eggs are used up within a week or two, room temp might be fine, but refrigeration is otherwise best for longevity and safety. The answer will balance practical use with scientific reasoning.

content:
How Did I Explode A Saucepan?

I am a complete amateur when it comes to the world of cooking.

My recent attempts to teach myself have unfortunately lead to me needing to ask:

How did I explode my saucepan?

I'd put some garlic/onion/olive oil in the saucepan and left it on low heat to soften on my electric hob. After about five there was a loud bang and I turned to find the saucepan falling through the air (which I just caught by the handle). The base of the saucepan had come away from the body. Cue jokes about taste explosions from my flat mate

I am fairly sure this wasn't supposed to happen.

The same thing happened when I was cooking meatballs with some onion on the side - though to a much lesser degree.

Did I just have a duff saucepan, or is there some explosive quality to onions I missed!?

On the plus side, the meal came out okay in the end.

I work in a commercial kitchen and I've seen this happen before, which is why we do not use copper-plated cookware. This can happen whenever you have two different alloys welded together and apply heat to one side or non-uniformly; An effect known as 'thermal shock'. What happens is one metal expands faster than the other, causing a deformation or fracture. Think of it as one side trying to 'pull' the other at the edges. The pop you heard was undoubtedly this delineation occurring, followed by the kinetic reaction of the pot jumping.

I find your claim that the pot leaped through the air difficult to believe, but I have observed audible pops and visible movement when they fail. If you have a flat top (like an electric stove), it could skid for up to a foot from this due to the lack of friction and possible presence of condensate (water) on the surface which can at certain temperatures act like a nearly friction-less cushion. Oil doesn't do this, only water.

If you've ever been in a commercial kitchen you'll notice every cookware item is made of a single cast of metal (most usually stainless steel) because of this. Welded alloy pots and pans just don't last very long -- the effect observed so violently happens at a smaller scale with every heating cycle, eventually resulting in ruined cookware. Also, being a line cook means being exposed to things exploding, dying, catching fire, etc., on a near-daily basis, not to mention an assortment of knives that would make most Hollywood bad-asses blush, so obviously we try to limit the number of things that can go wrong.

Do yourself a favor -- if you stick with the copper-bottomed pots and pans, make sure to put plenty of water or oil in them. Heat with nowhere to go will cause failure quickly.
thinking:
The user is a novice cook puzzled by their saucepan violently coming apart while heating garlic, onion, and oil. They wonder if it’s a faulty pan or something about onions. I need to first rule out the onion theory—there’s no explosive quality to onions, just the release of water vapor when heated, which wouldn’t cause a pot to rupture. The more likely cause is a construction flaw in the saucepan itself.

Many inexpensive saucepans have a base made of a different metal—often copper or aluminum—bonded to a stainless steel body. When placed on an electric hob, the base heats rapidly and uniformly from the element, while the sides stay relatively cool. Different metals expand at different rates when heated; copper, for instance, expands significantly more than stainless steel. This difference creates stress at the joint. If the bond is weak or the heating is uneven, the stress can overcome the adhesive or weld, causing a sudden delamination. The loud bang they heard was likely that bond failing catastrophically, and the sudden release of tension might have caused the pan to lurch or jump—especially on a smooth glass or ceramic cooktop where friction is low and any moisture condensate could act as a lubricant, letting it skid. The fact that a similar but less dramatic incident happened with meatballs suggests the pan was already damaged and finally gave way.

In commercial kitchens, this is why we use cookware made from a single piece of metal, like fully clad or cast stainless steel, to avoid such thermal shock failures. For the home cook, the takeaway is to inspect their pans: if they’re bonded multiple layers, they should ensure enough liquid or oil is present to distribute heat more evenly and avoid extreme temperature differentials. So the answer will explain the thermal shock mechanism, dismiss the onion myth, share the real-world kitchen perspective, and give practical advice on avoiding a repeat.

content:
Stock vs Broth - What's the difference in usage?

I've now learned (from this site) that broth and stock are not the same product (see [this great answer](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/2960/use-any-part-of-an-animal-for-making-stock-broth/2970#2970)).

So, in any given scenario, why should one use stock rather than broth, or vice versa?  
i.e. What's the practical difference?

EDIT: I'm mostly looking for when to use one vs the other.

**Classification and use of Stocks vs. Broth:**

Broths are the result of cooking meat, not just bones. They're generally the result of preparing another item and usually not prepared specifically on their own. The juices poured off from a roasted turkey (after being degreased) would be considered broth. Whole chickens being poached for another preparation would create broth.

Stocks are made from just the bones. They are prepared specifically for use in other recipes (sauces, soups, stews, rice, etc.) Stocks are never salted in their preparation or the finished dish will most likely end up too salty due to reduction that will take place upon further cooking. Note that homemade stock will be often a bit more broth-like than restaurant/commercial stocks, since it's really hard to get all the meat off the bones.

Stocks are usually simmered for a very long time (4-6 hours for chicken & 8-12 for veal/beef) to extract maximum flavor and gelatin from the bones.

Broths aren't usually cooked nearly as long due to the fact that cooking the meat for extended periods (even chicken surrounded by the liquid) will result in tough, flavorless meat.

Consomme: a fortified and clarified stock. The stock is fortified in flavor by the addition of a "raft" which is a combination of lean ground meat (appropriate to the type of stock being used) with brunoise (1/16 inch) mirepoix (carrots, onions, celery), and egg whites. The raft mixture is stirred into the cold stock and as it gently heats, the proteins coagulate forming a "raft" on top of the stock. A small hole is poked in the center (if one hasn't already formed) and as the stock bubbles through the hole it leaches back through the ground meat/egg white raft which filters out impurities to clarify the stock and fortify it with flavor.

Bouillon: French word for broth.

Court Bouillon: sometimes called a "short broth". A poaching liquid usually used for fish that is usually comprised of water, acid (lemon juice, vinegar, wine), parsley stems, bay leaves, peppercorns, and some salt.

When to use Stock vs. Broth:
Use stock when a sauce is to be reduced significantly or when clarity of the final result is preferred.

Broths can be substituted for stock when the body of the liquid or clarity isn't important, and when the liquid will be thickened by addition of a starch.
thinking:
The user is asking about practical differences between stock and broth, specifically when to use one versus the other. To answer that, I first need to recall the culinary definitions that distinguish them, because usage hinges on how they’re made and what properties result.

I remember that broth is made by cooking meat, often as a byproduct of another preparation (like poaching a chicken or deglazing a roasting pan). It usually includes some bones but the meat is the primary source of flavor. Broth is often seasoned, and because meat can become tough and flavorless with extended cooking, it’s simmered for a relatively short time.

Stock, on the other hand, is made from bones (with very little meat), simmered for many hours to extract gelatin and minerals. It is traditionally unsalted to allow for reduction later without concentrating salt. This long extraction gives stock a full body and, when chilled, a gel-like consistency from the collagen. Additionally, stocks are carefully skimmed to maintain clarity, while broths might be cloudier.

From these differences, the practical usage decisions follow. Stock’s neutral seasoning and gelatin content make it ideal when a dish will be reduced significantly—like a pan sauce or demi-glace—because it won’t become overseasoned and will provide a silky texture. Clarity also makes stock preferred for clear soups or consommé. Broth, being already flavorful and often seasoned, works well when the liquid is the star but doesn’t need to withstand heavy reduction, or when the final dish will be thickened with a starch (which can compensate for lower gelatin). In many home kitchens, the line blurs because it’s hard to remove all meat from bones, but the core distinction still holds.

I’ll structure the answer by first defining stock, broth, and related terms (consommé, bouillon, court bouillon) for clarity, then ending with a direct, concise rule for when to substitute one for the other.

content:
How do you peel garlic easily?

How should I approach peeling a clove of garlic to get the skin off most quickly? Is it different if I'm doing a bulb whole?

Even with a whole bulb, break it into cloves.

Put clove(s) on a cutting board. I usually cut off the root end of each clove. Lay a large chef's knife flat on the clove, then smack the knife to crush the clove. This breaks the skin of the clove and makes it much easier to peel.
thinking: The question is about the most efficient technique to remove garlic skin, both for individual cloves and for an entire bulb. I know from standard kitchen practice that garlic skin clings tightly to the clove, but crushing it mechanically breaks the papery skin and helps separate it from the flesh. The root end is the point where the skin attaches most firmly, so slicing it off helps release the skin’s grip. For a whole bulb, the same principle applies, but you first need to break the bulb into individual cloves because the bulb’s overall structure doesn’t allow an even crush; each clove needs separate treatment. The fastest approach is to crush the clove under the broad side of a chef’s knife: the sudden pressure splits the skin without pulverizing the clove, making peeling trivial. So I’ll structure the answer by first addressing the whole bulb—break it apart—then describing the cutting board, root-end trim, and the knife-smack technique.

content:
What's the proper way to dispose of used fats & oils?

Down the drain? Does it depend on the type? With bacon fat, I usually let it solidify in a cup lined with foil, and then throw it out. With used canola oil, I'm not quite sure what to do because it doesn't solidify.

**Never** down the drain. We've had a few incidents in my neighborhood where the sewer pipes were clogged with fat, and a few people's basements flooded with sewage as a result.

For fats that solidify, let them do so, then pitch them in your regular garbage. Chill grease in the fridge if you need to get it to harden up. For ones that don't solidify, pour them into a sealable ([hopefully non-recyclable](http://www.nyc.gov/html/dep/html/residents/congrease.shtml)) bottle, and throw the whole container away with your regular garbage.

It's possible that your area might accept cooking fats & oils as part of a recycling effort. Ours does for motor oil (I live in Maryland).

For restaurants, some places (eg, the state of Maryland) require a system for catching grease that's been washed down the sink. It's my understanding that they're fairly expensive (a couple thousand dollars US), but the fines for not having one installed may be even more, and they won't let new restaurants open without one.
thinking:
The user is asking about proper disposal of cooking fats and oils, specifically whether they can go down the drain and what to do with different types, like bacon fat (which solidifies) versus canola oil (which doesn’t). They already have a method for bacon fat, but are unsure about liquid oils.

First, I know from food-science and plumbing knowledge that fats, oils, and grease (FOG) should never go down the drain. Even liquid oils can combine with other waste in pipes, solidify at lower temperatures, or coat the interior of pipes, eventually causing blockages and sanitary sewer overflows. Anecdotally, I recall incidents of neighborhood sewer backups due to fat accumulation, so I’ll lead with that strong warning to counter any temptation to pour oil down the drain.

For solidifying fats like bacon grease, the user’s method of letting it harden in a foil-lined cup and throwing it out is correct. I’ll reinforce that, and add that chilling the fat can speed hardening if needed.

For liquid oils like canola, the best approach is to contain them in a sealable container—preferably one that isn’t recyclable, since oil contaminates plastic recycling streams. The container can then go in the regular trash. I’ll note that some municipalities have take-back or recycling programs for cooking oil, akin to motor oil recycling. I also recall that commercial kitchens often require grease interceptors, which is relevant context but not directly the user’s question; I’ll mention it briefly for completeness.

I’ll structure the answer by first giving the clear “no drain” rule, then the methods for solidifying fats versus liquid oils, then the recycling note, and finally the restaurant tidbit. I’ll present it conversationally, drawing on the sewer anecdote to make the point stick.

content:
Is it safe to eat potatoes that have sprouted?

I'm talking about potatoes that have gone somewhat soft and put out shoots about 10cm long.

Other online discussions suggest it's reasonably safe and the majority of us have been peeling and eating soft sprouty spuds for years. Is this correct?

Not safe enough for me to try it. Potatoes actually contain a very dangerous toxin called [solanine](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanine). This toxin is concentrated enough in the green parts in the plant to cause solanine poisoning. This includes the sprouts/eyes, and the potato itself if it's green.

This [article](http://health.nytimes.com/health/guides/poison/potato-poisoning-green-tubers-and-sprouts/overview.html) from the New York Times health guide indicates that it is something to be taken seriously. Per this article, if the sprouts have been removed, and the potato is not green then it is safe to eat as far as solanine poisoning is concerned.

However, a potato as far gone as you have described sounds *disgusting*. A *soft* potato is on its way to going bad. Where I am from, potatoes are cheap enough that it's just not worth the gross factor for me to eat a potato that has 10 cm sprouts and is squishy. I do eat potatoes that have little nub sprouts on them and that are slightly less than firm, after removing the sprouts of course.
thinking:
The question asks about safety of eating potatoes that have sprouted 10 cm shoots and gone somewhat soft. I need to evaluate two separate issues: the toxicity from solanine in sprouts and green parts, and the overall spoilage from softening.

First, I recall that potatoes contain solanine, a glycoalkaloid that can cause nausea, vomiting, and neurological symptoms. Sprouts, eyes, and any green parts concentrate this toxin. So peeling and removing sprouts reduces the risk—provided the flesh itself isn't green or bitter.

Second, many food safety sources, including the New York Times health guide, say that if sprouts are removed and the potato isn't green, it's safe regarding solanine poisoning. That covers the textbook answer.

However, the description here includes "somewhat soft" and 10 cm sprouts. Softness isn't just from sprouting; it's a sign of water loss, cell breakdown, and possible microbial activity. Long sprouts mean the potato has been stored for months, using its energy reserves. Even if the solanine risk is mitigated, the texture and flavor will be off, and there's a chance of other spoilage organisms producing compounds that cooking might not destroy. Many home cooks will trim nubby sprouts and still use firm potatoes, but once they're squishy and have elongated shoots, the quality crosses a line.

I weigh the low cost of replacement potatoes against the "gross factor" and potential stomach upset. Since I wouldn't serve them to others, I'll structure the answer by first highlighting solanine concerns, then the official guidance that sprouted-but-firm potatoes can be salvaged after peeling, and finally explain why the described condition (soft, 10 cm sprouts) goes beyond that—making it not worth the risk for me personally.

When making sushi, why do you have to rinse the rice?

I'm interested in learning to make my own sushi.

Every guide I have read has stressed that the rice has to be rinsed thoroughly.

The bags of rice I generally buy say not to rinse the rice in order to preserve the nutrients. What is the reason behind rinsing rice?

It removes excess starch, so your sushi rice doesn't turn into nasty glutinous slop. The texture of the rice is very important, so you'll need to rinse it several times before you steam it. Make sure the water is nice and clear after the last time you rinse it, and make sure you buy [japonica](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_rice) or similar: if you use regular rice, you may not get good results.

I wouldn't worry overmuch about the nutritional content of white sushi rice (you can starve on a diet of it). It's what you put into your sushi that'll give it nutritional value.
thinking:
The question is about the purpose of rinsing rice specifically for sushi, compared to the "do not rinse" instruction found on some rice packages. I need to recall the food science behind rice starch and cooking texture, and then address the apparent contradiction.

When rice is milled, the grains get coated with fine starch dust from the polishing process. If not rinsed away, this surface starch gelatinizes quickly in hot water, creating a thick, sticky slurry that glues the grains together. For sushi, the ideal result is rice that is tender yet each grain remains distinct, with just enough surface stickiness to hold the shape of a roll or nigiri. Too much free starch makes the rice dense, gummy, or mushy—exactly what people mean by "glutinous slop." So thorough rinsing is essential to wash away that excess starch. The water running clear indicates that most of the loose starch is gone.

The "do not rinse" instruction is common on enriched white rice sold in places like the US, where vitamins (thiamin, niacin, iron) are sprayed onto the grains after milling; rinsing washes these added nutrients off. But sushi rice is typically a short-grain japonica variety that is not enriched in the same way, and the culinary priority is texture over whatever minimal nutrients might be in the starchy coating. Even if it were enriched, the nutritional loss from rinsing white rice is negligible in the context of sushi, where the fish, vegetables, and nori provide the meal's real nutritional value.

I should also mention that proper sushi rice requires the right variety—japonica, often labeled "sushi rice"—because long-grain or medium-grain types have different starch compositions and won't yield the same sticky-yet-firm texture.

I'll structure the response by first stating the core reason (starch removal), then explaining the rinse-until-clear method, then addressing the nutrition concern, and finally noting the importance of using the correct rice variety.

What's the difference between a cupcake and a muffin?

I was debating with someone today whether what we were eating was a cupcake or a muffin, but realized we didn't really know the difference. So **what's the difference between a cupcake and a muffin** in American English?

---

In case you're wondering, what we were eating had a sweet batter, but not overly; had blueberries in the batter; had no icing or frosting; was perhaps about three fluid ounces (1 dL) big; and had been baked with a paper wrapper.

There is considerable overlap between cupcakes and muffins.

### Method

From a technical point of view, muffins are made by the *muffin method*, making them small quickbreads. In the muffin method, the wet ingredients are combined in one bowl; and the dry ingredients are combined in another bowl. Then the two are quickly incorporated together with minimal mixing to avoid gluten development. This gives muffins a somewhat coarse crumb.

Cupcakes are small cakes, and are made by one of the traditional cake methods such as the creaming method, the reverse creaming method, the genoise method, the chiffon method, and so on. They tend to have a finer crumb than muffins.

### Contrast

While no single criterion distinguishes a muffin from a cupcake if you do not adopt the technical definition above, the following trends exist:

- Cupcakes tend to be sweeter than muffins; there are savory muffins such as cornbread
- Cupcakes are often iced or frosted, whereas muffins tend to have no topping, or a simple crumb topping
- Cupcakes usually have a head or top no larger than the body of the cupcake; muffins are often encouraged to overflow their baking cup, so that their top is larger in diameter, giving them somewhat of a mushroom shape
- Cupcakes are almost always, well, cupcake shaped; muffins can be made as just muffin tops
- Cupcakes are almost never crispy or crunchy; muffins are often encouraged to brown and develop texture, especially on the tops
thinking:
I need to address the difference between cupcakes and muffins in American English. The question describes a specific baked good with a sweet-but-not-overly batter, blueberries, no icing, small, in a paper wrapper—so it sits right in the ambiguous zone. To answer properly, I should first recall the technical baking definitions, then the informal practical distinctions that people usually debate.

From a food science perspective, the key divide is mixing method. Muffins are quickbreads made by the muffin method: dry ingredients in one bowl, wet in another, then a quick, minimal combine to avoid gluten development. That yields a coarser, more bread-like crumb. Cupcakes are small cakes, employing a cake-mixing method like creaming (butter and sugar beaten first), reverse creaming, genoise, etc., which produces a finer, more tender crumb. So the structural texture is a dependable technical separator.

But in everyday language and appearance, people use a cluster of softer traits. Cupcakes tend to be sweeter, often contain frosting or elaborate toppings, and are kept flat-topped so frosting sits nicely. Muffins can be savory or only mildly sweet, are typically unfrosted (maybe a streusel or sugar sprinkle), and are encouraged to overflow their cups into a mushroom cap, which also browns and can become slightly crisp. There are also muffin tops as a separate baked item, whereas cupcakes are almost always full-sized with a neat head. So I’ll present the method distinction first for clarity, then list the usual contrasting features, acknowledging overlap and exceptions. The final answer will have a “Method” section and a “Contrast” section to cover both technical and practical viewpoints.

How do I pick a watermelon at the supermarket?

Lately, every watermelon I bring home form the organic section of the supermarket has not been sweet.  Among the small, seedless varieties, I try to pick the densest. How do I know if it is ripe?  Can I ripen them at home?  Should I keep them in the fridge?

I don't believe there is a fool-proof way to determine 'ripeness' without taking a slice out of it. The best you can do is look for certain signs:

- Ripe melons have a hollow sound when you tap or slap the outside
- Look for the patch where the melon would have been on the ground (called the field spot). If it's a yellow colour its probably ripe, if it's white, it's probably not.
- It should feel relatively heavy when lifted
- Weird areas on the skin aren't necessarily bad. insects may have tried to start eating the fruit because it is ripe, but have only marred the surface.

Unfortunately, melons don't continue to ripen once picked, unlike fruits such as apples, bananas etc. which contain ethylene. As a tip don't store melons with these kinds of fruit, they may well go 'soggy'.

Extra: [NYtimes video on picking the right watermelon](http://www.nytimes.com/video/2010/08/17/dining/1247468645900/choosing-the-perfect-watermelon.html).

Caffeine content of cold-brewed coffee: higher or lower than hot-brewed?

I recently rediscovered the joys of cold-brewing coffee. (One level cup of rough-ground beans, 4-1/2 cups of cold water, steeped overnight and strained, produces a rich coffee concentrate. A shot or three of concentrate in a mug topped with hot water makes a cup of coffee; poured over ice and milk makes a fantastic iced coffee drink.)

The information I've found online is contradictory. [One site](http://www.ineedcoffee.com/06/coldbrew/) says this method produces a drink with less caffeine than traditional hot-brewed coffee; [another](http://minusthesilencer.blogspot.com/2006/08/cold-brewed-coffee.html) says it actually contains more caffeine.

On the one hand, there's the heat in the traditional method. On the other hand, the beans are in contact with the water for twelve hours in the cold method. It seems as if the caffeine content could be identical? While the beans used will, of course, alter the outcome, does anyone know for certain if cold-brewed coffee has more or less caffeine than hot-brewed?

According to [the Wikipedia article on caffeine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeine#Chemical_properties_and_biosynthesis), its solubility is drastically different between room temperature and boiling (2 g/100 mL room temperature to 66 g/100 mL at boiling). I assume this means it's easier to get caffeine into boiling rather than cold water, but the drastically longer steeping time may counteract this. It's worth noting that the solubility is far higher than the actual amounts of caffeine that's in coffee.

Farther down the page it mentions caffeine per liter of liquids like coffee (386-652 mg/L). If you can find similar information about cold-steeped coffee, it might help.
thinking:
The user is asking whether cold-brewed coffee has more or less caffeine than hot-brewed. They’ve found conflicting claims online and are wrestling with the intuitive trade-offs: hot water extracts faster but for a short time, while cold water extracts more slowly but the grounds steep for many hours. They want a definitive answer if one exists.

To start, I need to recall what determines caffeine content in a brewed coffee. Caffeine is water-soluble, and its extraction from ground beans depends on temperature, time, water-to-coffee ratio, grind size, and possibly other factors like agitation or pressure. Temperature affects both the solubility of caffeine and the rate of extraction. I remember that solubility data for caffeine shows a huge difference between room temperature and boiling: at 25°C it’s around 2 g per 100 mL, while at 100°C it’s roughly 66 g per 100 mL. That’s a thirty-three-fold increase. So from a pure solubility standpoint, hot water can hold vastly more caffeine in solution, meaning the driving force for extraction is much stronger if the solution is far from saturation.

But in real brewing, the solution never reaches saturation — the amounts of caffeine in a finished cup are on the order of hundreds of milligrams per liter, not grams per milliliter. So both methods operate far below the solubility limit. That means extraction is limited more by kinetics than by thermodynamic capacity. The rate of diffusion of caffeine out of the bean particles and into the water increases with temperature, so hot water extracts caffeine much faster. Cold brewing compensates with a much longer contact time — 12 to 24 hours versus a few minutes for hot drip or pour-over. The question is whether the extended time fully offsets the lower temperature.

I’ve also read that different brew methods yield varying caffeine concentrations depending on the ratio of coffee to water. Cold brew concentrate is often made at a much higher ratio (e.g., 1 cup grounds to 4.5 cups water), and then diluted for drinking. So comparisons by volume of beverage can be misleading. The user mentions a concentrate that gets diluted with hot water or milk, so the final drink’s caffeine depends on how much concentrate they use.

Without precise experimental data on cold-brew extraction yields, I can’t state definitively that one has more or less. The conflicting online information likely reflects differences in recipes and measurements. However, I can point to the fundamental property — the steep increase in solubility with temperature — as the reason hot water extracts more efficiently, while acknowledging that very long steeping times might narrow the gap. I should also note that the actual caffeine concentrations in coffee are so low relative to solubility that both methods can easily dissolve all the caffeine the beans can release, provided enough time.

The Wikipedia caffeine article provides that solubility data vividly and also lists typical caffeine ranges for brewed coffee, which are informative benchmarks. I’ll structure the answer by first citing that data to illustrate why hot brewing is inherently more effective at pulling caffeine out, then explain that the longer time in cold brewing may partially compensate, but without direct measurement it’s hard to say which ends up higher. The goal is to give a scientifically grounded explanation that resolves the confusion without claiming absolute certainty.

What temperatures should I keep my refrigerator and freezer set at?

For a refrigerator, if it's cooler, items like milk and meat last a bit longer. However if I set it close to freezing then some items start showing frost on them. What temperature should I set my refrigerator to for best overall results?

Since the person answering is likely to know, I'm also asking what temperature I should set my freezer to.

Daniel is spot-on with [his answer](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/a/4531/60). I'll elaborate on it a bit here.

As indicated by his bottled water in the freezer trick, a full freezer is a happy freezer. The same applies to the refrigerator too. While I wouldn't put random bottles of water throughout my refrigerator, it's important to know that the fuller your refrigerator is, the more it holds its temperature when opening/closing, and the less energy you'll use. However, you don't want to *jam pack* it so full that there isn't any airflow around your stuff, because this can hamper the cooling efficiency as well.

The ideal refrigerator temperature is 35°F (1.6°C). You're not hugging the danger zone like you would be at 40°F (4.4°C), and you're distancing yourself sufficiently from 32°F (0°C) that you don't freeze half the stuff in your refrigerator. That said, the temperature within your fridge can vary rather significantly with normal usage.

The coldest parts of your refrigerator are the back, and the bottom. The back because the cooling element is there, and the bottom because warm air rises. If items you don't want frosty are getting frosty, then move them away from the back of the fridge. I would avoid putting items in the door of your fridge that are particularly sensitive to spoilage. The items in the door of your fridge can easily get as high as 59°F (15°C), and do so often. Putting milk and eggs in your door will significantly decrease their shelf life. Butter is OK in the little covered section in the door, because the door actually helps keep it's temperature a little better. You also generally don't want rock solid frozen butter.

So, put your meats on the bottom shelf in the back, your condiments (mayo, ketchup, mustard, etc.) in the door, and put everything else where it fits.
thinking: The user wants to know the best temperature settings for a refrigerator and a freezer, with a focus on the fridge trade-off between extending shelf life and avoiding frost. They also assume the answer will include freezer guidance. I recall that standard food safety guidelines recommend keeping the refrigerator at or below 40°F (4.4°C) to inhibit bacterial growth, but setting it too close to freezing (32°F / 0°C) can cause frost and partial freezing of delicate items. The freezer should maintain 0°F (-18°C) for long-term storage, which is what Daniel's linked answer likely specifies. His trick of using a frozen water bottle to monitor thawing reinforces that 0°F is the target. For the fridge, I've found that 35°F (1.6°C) is the sweet spot—it's sufficiently above freezing to avoid ice crystals on most foods, yet cold enough to safely slow spoilage better than 40°F, which hovers right at the “danger zone” threshold. I also know that refrigerator temperature is not uniform: the cooling element at the back and the natural tendency of warm air to rise make the rear and bottom shelves the coldest areas, while the door can climb well above 40°F due to frequent opening. This explains why frost might appear on items placed too close to the back. Therefore, I'll advise moving sensitive items away from the back, and warn against storing milk and eggs in the door. I should also mention the energy and temperature-stability benefits of keeping both fridge and freezer relatively full (without blocking airflow). My answer structure will: (1) acknowledge Daniel's answer and confirm the freezer temperature point, (2) explain the “full is happy” concept briefly, (3) state the ideal fridge temperature as 35°F with reasoning, (4) describe internal temperature variation and its implications for food placement, and (5) give clear storage tips (meat low and back, condiments in door, etc.).

How dangerous is it to refreeze meat that has been thawed?

I've often been told by people that I shouldn't refreeze meat (particularly hamburger meat) once it has been thawed. However, this seems a little silly to me. I can't imagine how meat that hasn't been bought fresh and local could find its way to my kitchen with out thawing and being refrozen a couple of times. How much damage can one more thawing and refreezing really do? Can it really be that dangerous disease wise? Or is this just one of those urban myths?

In theory you could thaw and refreeze as many times as you like, though the changes in temperature would definitely alter the quality of the meat's taste and texture.

What matters most is how long the meat has been in the so-called "danger zone" speaking from a temperature perspective. The "danger zone" is defined as being between 41 to 135 °F (5 to 57 °C).

Here is an excerpt from [The Professional Chef, by the Culinary Institute of America](http://books.google.com/books?id=GYNmPwAACAAJ&dq=the%20professional%20chef&source=gbs_book_other_versions):

> Foods left in the danger zone for a period longer than four hours are considered adulterated. Additionally, one should be fully aware that the four-hour period is cumulative, meaning that the meter starts running again every time the food enters the danger zone. Therefore, once the four-hour period has been exceeded, heating, cooling, or any other cooking method cannot recover foods.

I need to address the underlying food-science principle: the hazard isn’t the freeze–thaw cycle itself, but the cumulative time the meat spends at temperatures where bacteria multiply. The answer clarifies that theoretically you can refreeze multiple times, but quality suffers, and the real danger is time in the “danger zone” (41–135 °F / 5–57 °C). A four-hour cumulative limit is standard: every thaw adds to that clock, and once it’s exceeded, the food is unsafe regardless of refreezing or cooking. I’ll structure my reasoning by first separating the quality issue from safety, then defining the danger zone and explaining how cumulative exposure drives risk, citing authoritative guidance to underscore it’s not a myth but a measurable food-safety rule.

When I'm separating egg whites, how much does it matter if a little yolk gets in?

I was separating egg whites today and one of the yolks broke and contaminated my bowl of whites. I started from scratch, but I'm wondering if I really needed to; would a tiny bit of yolk (say, 1/8 tspn in 4 egg whites) mixed in with the whites make a big difference?

To provide some context, I was about to whip the whites with castor sugar to make almond macaroons.

Yes, it matters a lot. When you are separating egg whites, it is for whipping them into a foam. This foam is a protein-based foam, relying on protein ends hooking into each other. Even small traces of fat will prevent the foam from forming. Egg yolks contain high amounts of fat. Once an egg yolk breaks in your whites, you have to start the separation anew, because it can prevent your foam from forming. Also, don't use plastic bowls for whipping egg whites (their surface retains some fat molecules even after washing, giving you a less stable foam) and only whip with a cleanly washed whisk or mixer attachment (not one you have just used for something else, not even if you wiped it clean).

To prevent big mishaps, just separate each new egg in a teacup and only add the new white to the old whites after it has separated cleanly. Else you are in big trouble if you are separating a lot and the last egg contaminates the whole whites with yolk. And a single contaminated egg is easily reused for a quick egg-and-feta sandwich or something else.

Contamination the other way round isn't so worrisome. You still want to work as precisely as possible, as yolk-only recipes will often have somewhat worse texture if eggwhite is included, but small contaminating amounts are usually not noticeable in the finished product, even in foams (zabaglione, mayonnaise). This is because yolk foams are fat-based, and small amounts of protein don't prevent a fat foam from forming.

Fat interferes with this process by coating the protein strands and preventing them from bonding to each other. Even very small traces of fat, like those from egg yolks, can severely weaken or completely prevent foam formation. So the amount mentioned—1/8 teaspoon in 4 whites—is definitely enough to cause problems. My first thought might be that such a small amount wouldn’t matter, but the science is clear: fat is the enemy of egg white foam, and strict separation is crucial. I also know that yolk is about one-third fat, so a tiny bit introduces enough lipid molecules to coat many proteins. Since they were making macaroons, a delicate cookie that relies on stiff peaks, any failure would ruin the texture.

Beyond just discarding contaminated whites, I’d want to remind the user that even residual fat on equipment matters—plastic bowls hold onto fat molecules even after washing, and a mixer attachment that’s been used for something else can also introduce grease. So I’d include that as a helpful tip. For prevention, the classic trick of separating each egg into a small cup before adding to the main bowl is essential to avoid wasting a whole batch. Finally, the user might wonder about the reverse situation, so I’d address that egg white in yolk-based foams (like mayonnaise) is less damaging because those are fat-based emulsions; small amounts of protein don’t disrupt them. That provides a complete picture.

I’ll structure the response by first giving a direct, emphatic “yes” with the scientific reason. Then I’ll explain the fat-foam interaction, offer the practical separation advice and equipment warning, and close with the reassurance about reverse contamination. This covers the immediate question, the underlying science, and broader best practices.Yes, it matters a lot. When you whip egg whites, you’re relying on proteins to bond and trap air into a stable foam. Even a tiny bit of fat—from egg yolk, a greasy bowl, or a used whisk—coats those protein strands and prevents them from linking up, so the foam either won’t form at all or will collapse quickly. For macaroons, you need stiff, dry peaks; any yolk contamination can completely sabotage that.

To avoid losing a whole batch, separate each egg over a small cup first, then transfer the clean white to your main bowl. Also, make sure your bowl and beaters are spotlessly clean and not plastic, which can hold onto fat molecules. The reverse isn’t as dire: a little white in a yolk-based foam (like mayonnaise) usually doesn’t cause noticeable problems because those foams are fat-based, not protein-based.

content:
Never ending soup; is it actually safe?

In the poor student or youth worker days it was popular to have never ending soup; a large pot on the stove that was topped up with new and leftover ingredients when available.

Normally the pot was stored in the fridge overnight.

Food items added were sometimes plate leftovers from fellow flat (share house) mates, who would in turn be eating the soup, too.

Most days other ingredients would be fresh(ish) vegetables, beans, grains, and fresh meat products sourced from the local butcher as money allowed.

Brussels sprouts where banned, and so were strong spices (you added those to your bowl before serving).

Also, for irony, a large (cleaned) stone is always left in the pot.

Fresh bread was sometimes baked in the oven while cracked bones were browning, but the oven was often an electrical and environmental death trap.

The pot kept going till the summer holidays, and no one got food poisoning in my time, or from any student stories I have ever heard.

This sort of activity is recorded in history as being a popular resource-saving idea.

Are there any real food safety implications with this method of cooking? And have any actual studies of this technique ever been published?

I still recommend this money-saving idea to current students, not keen on bad practices being continued though.

Still happening <https://www.theworldofstreetfood.com/2025/12/wattana-panich-legendary-50-year-old.html>

It takes quite a while for a pot of hot soup to cool down to 40°F in the fridge. Several hours, sometimes, depending on the shape of the pot and the volume of soup. If you're heating and re-chilling the same soup daily, it's going to spend a lot of time in the danger zone. From a safety perspective, you'd be much better off making a pot of soup every few days and then reheating just the portion that you're actually going to eat.

> I still recommend this money saving idea to current students

Soup *is* a great food for stretching a dollar, but I don't see how it's any more expensive to make a fresh pot twice a week and it shouldn't take much time either. I understand that you were adding scraps each night, but you could as easily save those scraps for a day or two until you make the next pot of soup.
thinking:
The question asks whether a “never-ending soup” pot—kept simmering or refrigerated overnight, continuously topped up with fresh ingredients and plate leftovers, sometimes including scraps from people who are also eating from it—is truly safe from a food-safety standpoint, and whether any formal studies exist on the practice. The user notes that in their personal experience and among peers, no one got sick, and they still recommend it to students. I need to evaluate the real risks, drawing on core food-science principles, and then decide how to structure a clear, evidence-based response that addresses both safety and practicality.

I start by breaking down the practice. The pot is heated to a boil or simmer at some point each day, which kills vegetative bacteria. But the soup is a large volume, likely several liters, and is placed in the fridge overnight. Even in a working refrigerator, a big, dense pot of hot liquid can take many hours to cool below 40°F (4°C)—often 6 hours or more depending on pot shape and depth. During that time, the soup sits in the temperature danger zone (40°F–140°F) where bacteria like *Clostridium perfringens*, *Bacillus cereus*, and *Staphylococcus aureus* can multiply rapidly. The next day, reheating may bring it back to a simmer, killing most live bacteria, but any heat-stable toxins that formed—for example, staphylococcal enterotoxin, which can survive boiling—would remain. Repeating this cycle day after day means the cumulative time in the danger zone stacks up, raising the odds that toxin levels could reach an infective dose.

Then there’s the addition of plate leftovers from multiple people. That introduces saliva and whatever oral bacteria or viruses (like norovirus) are present, along with any pathogens on the fork or spoon. Even if the pot is later boiled, if it’s not boiled immediately after adding the leftovers, those microbes have time to produce toxins in the warm soup. Cross-contamination between raw meat leftovers and the rest of the soup is another concern—if the “cracked bones” or fresh meat aren’t handled to strict raw/cooked separation standards, raw juices could introduce *Campylobacter* or *Salmonella* that then get a long incubation at friendly temperatures.

The user says no one in their circle got food poisoning. That’s anecdotal and not reliable evidence of safety. Foodborne illness can be mild, mistaken for a “24-hour bug,” or have delayed onset. A small social group might simply have been lucky, or they might have a short cycle (frequent full boil, shallow pot, very cold fridge) that accidentally kept the risk low. But recommending it to others, especially young students who may have unreliable fridges, poor hygiene, or leave the pot out too long, is a different matter. The question also asks about published studies. I’m not aware of any scientific study directly testing a perpetual soup pot—it’s a folk practice, not a controlled restaurant process. However, food safety research on cooling rates, consumer soup handling, and the hazards of repeated reheating provide ample indirect evidence that it’s risky.

The answer I need to provide should first explain why the cooling step is the main danger, citing the time spent in the danger zone. Then I’ll suggest a safer alternative: making a pot of soup every few days, storing it in shallow containers for rapid cooling, and reheating only the portion you’ll eat. This eliminates the perpetual accumulation of risk. How do you properly cook a steak?

I love steaks so much, that I would like to get a green card and live in the States just to enjoy good steaks whenever I want.

When I try to cook a steak at home (I live in Italy), it always turns out burned outside and almost totally raw inside. Actually only a thin layer is cooked (or I should say carbonized).

If I try to lower the temperature of the grill pan, I get an extremely dried meat that resembles cork.

So, which are the basics for properly cooking a steak (say, to a medium-well grade)?

You should be able to get a reasonable steak stovetop using a cast iron grill pan, if you have a strong enough exhaust. Oil the cast iron pan (with canola or such), then heat it very hot, until it starts to smoke. Make sure the meat is completely dry on the outside (wipe with a paper towel, water will prevent browning) and gently place in the pan. Leave it there for a minute or two (it'll smoke quite a bit!), rotate 90° to get the nice grill marks. Leave for another minute or two. Flip, and repeat for the other side.

It may splatter, have a splatter screen handy. It will smoke, quite a bit, make sure the exhaust is on high.

You will probably have a medium-rare steak now. Using a thinner cut will make it more well done (you can cut a thick steak in half with your chef's knife, making two thin steaks); so will plopping it in the oven (not sure if you want the oven before or after searing, I like 'em medium rare...).

Remember to let the meat rest for 5 minutes or so before serving.

Also, if your steaks are coming out ridiculously tough, you're probably using the wrong cut of meat, or some terrible grade. What cut are you using?

[edit: I should note that, in case it wasn't obvious, the burner should be up pretty high]

**Edit by rumtscho** There is a reason this answer specifies a cast iron pan. If you are limited in your cookware choice, pay attention to the maximum temperature your pan can tolerate. If you are using a non-stick pan, you have to go on medium heat and wait longer, else you'll damage the pan. (And sorry, but you can't get it as tasty as on high heat that way).

Why skim "scum" from the surface of a simmering stock?

I've been reading various Googled recipes and techniques for stockmaking, as I made my first stock tonight using raw chicken bones. Just about every article/recipe I read says to skim the surface of the stock in the beginning, while it is simmering. Different articles variously refer to the skimmed substances as "scum", "impurities", and "proteins".

I had started out throwing all the vegetables in at the beginning, and probably had it at too high of a simmer, so I never actually got to see any foam or collections of anything other than apparently oils/fats from the chicken appear on the surface. This got me wondering: what is that stuff that floats to the surface? Is there any reason other than aesthetics to remove it from the stock?

Skimming is for aesthetic purposes.

The scum is denatured protein, mostly comprising the same proteins that make up egg whites. It is harmless and flavorless, but visually unappealing. Eventually, the foam will break up into microscopic particles and disperse into your stock, leaving it grayish and cloudy. The more vigorously your stock bubbles, the faster this process will occur.

If the grayness or cloudiness bothers you but skimming is not an option for some reason, you can always remove the micro-particulates later through the clarification process used to make consomme.
thinking: The question asks why stock recipes emphasize skimming the foam that rises early in simmering, what that stuff actually is, and whether there’s a reason beyond looks to remove it. I need to recall the food science: when raw bones and meat are heated, soluble proteins (mainly myoglobin and some albumin-like proteins from the meat and bones) denature and coagulate, forming a foamy raft on the surface. These proteins are the same kind that make egg whites solidify—they’re harmless, tasteless, and don’t affect the stock’s safety or flavor. The only real issue is visual: if not skimmed, the foam eventually breaks down into microscopic particles that remain suspended, making the stock cloudy and grayish. This is purely an aesthetic concern, as clarity is prized in classic stock-making. I’ll also recall that a rapid boil accelerates the breakup of the foam, which is why a gentle simmer and skimming are recommended for a clear stock. If skimming is missed, the stock can still be clarified later using an egg-white raft (consommé method), proving the particles are just protein. So, my response will directly state that skimming is only for appearance, then explain what the scum is, why it doesn’t matter for taste or safety, what happens if it’s left, and mention clarification as a backup.
