Is it safe to eat smoked bacon without grilling?

The reason I ask this is due to the fact nothing on the bacon packaging indicates it can or cannot be eaten 'raw' and in general eating raw meat is a bad idea.

In such a case, for any food item, ask yourself a question: In a 19th century household, would it have been kept in the cellar, or eaten immediately?

For bacon, it is common knowledge (or at least I think everybody knows it) that it was kept in a cellar for long time. So this is definitely not a food which perishes too quickly. You can eat it raw. (In fact, I often do when I need a quick sandwich). It can be a bit tough to tear apart with your teeth, so pre-cut it.

The reason for this is that bacon is cured meat. There are two reasons not to eat raw meat: taste and food safety. Taste is individual, some people are OK with the taste and eat raw meat as long as they can find a source of meat fresh enough (think sashimi, carpaccio, steak tartare). Food safety is not a problem with bacon. The process of turning pork to bacon includes salt and smoke. Both of these kill bacteria, create an environment which is not hospitable to new colonization (dry, salty), and give the meat a new flavor which is better than the raw meat.

If you are now asking yourself why we are bothering with the fridge for bacon and other ex-"cellar foods" at all, there is still a reason. First, most of us don't have a convenient cellar at 12° - 15°C, and not only is the bacon's life shortened if kept at usual kitchen temperatures, it also doesn't taste too good. It is just greasy. Second, you seldom get dry bacon at the supermarket; even if the curing process doesn't include brining, bacon is often aged much less than in old times, and then packed in vacuum, so it doesn't get really dry on the outside. So bacteria could very well start growing on it outside of the freezer. Inside the freezer, it keeps much longer than raw meat, and is certainly OK for consumption without frying. I guess that the popularity of fried bacon is mainly due to taste reasons.
thinking:
The user is asking about the safety of eating smoked bacon without cooking it, noting that the packaging doesn't explicitly say it's ready-to-eat and that raw meat is generally unsafe. To address this, I need to consider what makes bacon different from raw pork.

First, I recall that bacon is a cured product—pork belly that has been treated with salt, and often also smoked. Curing is a preservation method that dates back centuries, used to make meat safe for long-term storage without refrigeration. The salt draws out moisture, lowering water activity, which inhibits microbial growth. Smoking adds antimicrobial compounds like phenols and formaldehyde, and also dries the surface further. If the bacon is smoked, it has undergone both processes. So from a food safety perspective, it's not "raw" in the same sense as a fresh pork chop; the curing and smoking effectively pasteurize it and create an environment hostile to pathogens like Trichinella and bacteria.

I then think about the common rule of thumb: if a food was historically kept in a cellar rather than eaten immediately, it's a preserved food and safe to eat without further cooking. Bacon was traditionally hung in cool, dry cellars for months, making it a ready-to-eat product. That's a simple way to explain it.

However, modern supermarket bacon introduces nuance. Today's bacon is often wet-cured (injected with brine) and only lightly smoked for flavor, then vacuum-sealed. It retains more moisture and isn't dried to the same degree, so it's not shelf-stable at room temperature. Nevertheless, the salt and nitrites still make it safe to eat uncooked when properly refrigerated—the cold chain suppresses any bacterial growth that might start. The packaging may not say "ready to eat" because manufacturers expect cooking, but it's still a cured product. The risk is very low compared to truly raw meat.

I also consider that taste and texture are separate issues—some find uncooked bacon unappealing because it's flabby and greasy, while cooking renders fat and improves flavor. That's why frying is popular, not because it's necessary for safety.

I'll structure the answer by first introducing the historical cellar heuristic to immediately give a relatable benchmark for safety. Then I'll explain the scientific basis: how curing and smoking eliminate pathogens and prevent recolonization. Is there something I can do to keep ice-cream soft?

I have bought a electric ice-cream churner, I have tried so many different flavours, different recipes, used alcohols.
Have read previous questions and a don't believe that leaving ice-cream out to thaw -scoop then refreeze is the only answer.How do the commercial companies keep them soft.
I generally find the next day it is fairly reasonable to scoop, but day after day -the longer it stays the harder it becomes.

Yes, actually, there are two magic ingredients: [Guar gum](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guar_gum) and [Xanthan gum](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanthan_gum).

Guar gum is a thickener, but in small quantities can also prevent the growth of ice crystals which would cause the ice cream to harden into icicles.

Xanthan gum is a stabilizer which helps keep air (called overrun) in the mixture. Air is generally churned into ice cream by ice cream machines, but it won't stay that way without the stabilizer.
thinking:
The user is frustrated that homemade ice cream becomes progressively harder day after day, despite trying different recipes and alcohols. They suspect that simply thawing and refreezing isn't the only solution, and they want to know how commercial producers keep their ice cream consistently soft. The underlying issue is not just freezing point depression but structural integrity over time.

I recall that during the initial freezing and churning, air is whipped into the mix (overrun), and small ice crystals form. Over subsequent days, ice crystals grow through recrystallization, the air escapes, and the texture becomes dense and icy. Alcohol can lower the freezing point, making it initially softer, but it doesn't prevent crystal growth or stabilize the air cells long-term.

Commercial ice creams often include stabilizers and emulsifiers. Two common ones are guar gum and xanthan gum. Guar gum, in small amounts, acts as a thickener and coats ice crystals, inhibiting their growth and keeping them fine. Xanthan gum helps stabilize the structure of the whipped foam, trapping air and preventing it from collapsing, which maintains a softer, more scoopable texture even after prolonged freezing. These work synergistically and are used in tiny percentages.

How can I chop onions without crying?

Onions are an excellent addition to many dishes, but cutting them can be frustrating when they make you "cry" all the time.

Does anyone know any tips or tricks to help minimise the tears when chopping [onions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onion)?

The tearing of the eyes is a result of enzymes that form a sulpherous gas when the onion is cut (concentrated inside the inner core or bulb of the onion) being released into the surrounding air.

You have a few options to avoid this - one would be to not cut through the center of the onion but to extract the "core". This is kind of a pain and means you are discarding a decent chunk of onion, so I don't like it too much.

Another option is to use a fan to blow the gases away from you. A small fan next to you blowing horizontally should do the trick.

You could also wear goggles, although you'd have to leave them on for a while until the gas dissipates from the area.

Another technique is to cut a lemon in half and rub the fresh lemon against both sides of the blade. You'll have to keep "refreshing" the juice coat and your onions will have some lemon juice on them, so this is somewhat limited by that factor.

Why let dough rise twice?

I'm just wondering, what's the point of letting dough rise twice? I've seen a bunch of recipes in the form:

1. Mix dough together and knead
2. Let it rise
3. Knead again
4. Let it rise again

Why do they do this? Doesn't kneading just push the air bubbles out?

Allowing dough to rise twice results in a finer gluten structure than allowing it to rise once. It results in a smaller crumb and prevents huge gaping airholes in your bread. The reason that you have to let it re-rise is that you just pushed all the air out with the kneading you did developing that gluten structure.
thinking:
I need to understand what the user is really asking: they see that many bread recipes have two rises, with a kneading step in between that seems to deflate the dough, so why do it? They suspect it’s counterproductive because the first rise just gets knocked down.

I recall the basics of bread science: yeast produces carbon dioxide, and kneading develops gluten. The first rise is all about fermentation—yeast generates gas and flavor—while the gluten network begins to form and stretch. When you punch down and knead again after that first rise, you’re not just deflating the dough; you’re redistributing the yeast, evening out temperature and hydration, and mechanically working the gluten further. This extra kneading reorganizes the gluten strands into a tighter, more uniform matrix.

If you baked straight after the first rise without that intermediate kneading, you might get large, irregular pockets of gas trapped in a less organized gluten structure—leading to a holey, uneven crumb. The second kneading degasses the dough but leaves you with a finer, stronger gluten mesh. Then, when you let it rise again, the yeast produces gas that gets trapped in many tiny, evenly distributed pockets, yielding a smaller, more consistent crumb and preventing giant airholes. The second rise is necessary precisely because you pushed all the air out during that structure-building knead: without it, you’d bake a dense, deflated loaf.

So I’ll frame the answer around how the double rise creates a finer gluten structure, which translates to a tight, uniform crumb and no gaping holes, and I’ll clarify that the second rise reinflates the dough after the crucial gluten-developing punch-down.

content:
Why shallots over onions?

It seems that in more advanced cookbooks and when watching professional chefs that shallots are used extensively. They seem to be used in the places where onions are in cookbooks which are aimed at home cooks.

I am familiar with the genetic similarities between onions and shallots. I have not personally cooked with shallots because they cost an order of magnitude more than onions.

If it is not just my misperception that shallots are preferred- what qualities do shallots have that make them more popular than onions?  
Should I expect shallots to be much more expensive than onions or am I shopping at the wrong places?  
In short- are they worth paying more for?

Shallots certainly aren't more *popular* than onions, otherwise they'd be far more abundant and less expensive.

I do cook with shallots from time to time and would describe them as most people describe them - as somewhere between the flavour of garlic and onion, but also a good deal milder/sweeter.

I prefer to use them simply when I do not want the strong taste of onions. In fact, many of us are so accustomed to the harsh taste of onions that it's actually quite a surprise to find out how much better a certain dish might taste by substituting shallots.

They're especially common in Asian cooking, I find. Very often you're providing a lot of spice or heat from other ingredients - chilies, five spice, curry powder, etc. - and don't want the overwhelming pungency of onions mixed in. Shallots give just a *little bit* of "sharpness" without much of the sulfur taste.

Would I substitute them *everywhere?* Absolutely not. Some recipes really do call for the pungency of onions, for example almost anything involving ground beef. But try it at least once - get yourself a bag of shallots and try substituting them for onions in a few recipes. You may be pleasantly surprised.

I would say that ideal recipes to try this on, if you're unfamiliar with shallots, are stovetop recipes calling for a relatively small amount of chopped or sliced (not minced) onion; stir fries are ideal, which perhaps is why they seem to be so common in Asian cuisine.

Also, as far as pricing is concerned: Locally, where a 2 lb bag of onions might cost $1.99, a 1 lb bag of shallots would cost $1.49, which makes them roughly 50% more expensive, very far from an "order of magnitude." If you meant that literally and are finding them close to 10x more expensive than onions, then you are either shopping at the wrong stores or living in an area where they are hard to find. Try an Asian grocery store if you have one; they can usually be found for dirt cheap in those.

Why is some metal safe to use in a microwave, but others not?

This might be a more scientific question, but it relates to cooking and I thought it was interesting.

I just made my lunch which was a microwavable bowl of chunky soup.

The directions said:

> Remove metal lid, remaining metal rim is microwavable.

How can this be?

Metal on its own doesn't necessarily cause electric discharge in a microwave.

What causes the sparking that you see when you put a fork in a microwave is due to the "sharp" edges of the fork. These edges concentrate the voltage at their tips which will cause a spark when it exceeds the dielectric breakdown of air.

Things like sheet pans (with rounded edges), or rounded metal racks are used frequently in microwaves with no ill effect. The absence of any pointed edges allows this. The rim of your bowl fits this requirement.
thinking:
The question asks why some metal objects are microwave-safe while others cause sparks, using the example of a soup bowl where the metal rim is allowed but the metal lid is not. I need to explain the underlying physics in a kitchen-relevant way.

First, I recall that microwave ovens generate electromagnetic waves that induce electric currents in conductive materials like metal. Not all metal objects react the same way: a fork or foil with crinkled edges often produces dramatic sparks, while smooth metal racks or the metalized film in some packaging don't. The key difference isn't the metal itself but its shape and thickness.

I remember the phenomenon of electric discharge: when microwaves hit a metal object, they cause electrons to move. On a shape with sharp points or thin, jagged edges, the charge accumulates at those tiny tips, creating a very high electric field. If the field strength exceeds the dielectric breakdown voltage of air (about 3 million volts per meter), it ionizes the air and a spark jumps—this is arcing. A fork tine or a crumpled foil edge is essentially a lightning rod. Thick, smoothly rounded metal—like the rim of that soup bowl or a microwave-safe metal rack—doesn't concentrate the charge in the same way; currents can flow over a larger surface area without building up a dangerous field gradient. The rim likely has a continuous, blunt profile that avoids charge buildup and prevents sparking.

Additionally, if the metal is thin or loosely connected, it can act as an antenna, reflecting waves erratically and possibly overheating. But a solid rim bonded to the bowl is stable and may even shield the inner contents from direct microwave radiation, allowing the food to heat more evenly without arcing risk.

My initial thought might be that all metal is forbidden, but I correct myself: it's not the metal inherently, but the geometry that determines safety. A fork tine or a crumpled foil edge is essentially a lightning rod. Thick, smoothly rounded metal—like the rim of that soup bowl or a microwave-safe metal rack—doesn't concentrate the charge in the same way; currents can flow over a larger surface area without building up a dangerous field gradient. The rim likely has a continuous, blunt profile that avoids charge buildup and prevents sparking.

Additionally, if the metal is thin or loosely connected, it can act as an antenna, reflecting waves erratically and possibly overheating. But a solid rim bonded to the bowl is stable and may even shield the inner contents from direct microwave radiation, allowing the food to heat more evenly without arcing risk.

My initial thought might be that all metal is forbidden, but I correct myself: it's not the metal inherently, but the geometry that determines safety. So the answer will explain that sharp edges (like on a fork or torn foil) concentrate voltage and cause sparks, while rounded, continuous metal (like the bowl rim) does not.

(What Taeraresh said is also true, there are functional differences in how the different shapes hold sauces.)

content:
Why wait for water to boil?

I've always heard that you should wait for water to boil before adding pasta/perogies/vegetables/etc. What is the reason for this? Is it because it reaches boiling point faster? If so, why?

The primary reason is for accuracy and reliability in cooking times. Boiling water is guaranteed (not accounting for altitude) to be at 212 F (100 C). With a set temperature you can then say things like "boil X for 9 minutes" with a very high measure of confidence.

You certainly *can* cook things in the water as you go, but it's going to be a lot more hit-and-miss. Pasta, for example, will begin to cook *before* it reaches the boiling point. You would need to measure the temperature, and check the pasta regularly to determine when it was done. You can't give someone an accurate cooking time with this method either. The time it takes for water to boil will vary greatly with stove heat output, pot size & shape, and the amount of water.
thinking:
The question asks why recipes so often instruct to bring water to a boil before adding food like pasta or vegetables. There’s a common idea that adding food to already-hot water somehow makes the water boil faster, but that doesn’t make physical sense—adding cold mass will always lower the water’s temperature. So the real reason must be something else, probably about controlling the cooking process.

I recall that boiling water, at a given altitude, is at a fixed temperature: 212°F (100°C) at sea level. That’s a reliable benchmark. If you drop pasta into boiling water, the initial temperature drops but returns to a boil relatively quickly, and then the pasta cooks at a consistent, known temperature. This lets recipe writers give precise cooking times (“boil for 9 minutes”) that will work across different kitchens, as long as you start timing from the moment the water returns to a boil after adding the food.

If you instead put the food in cold water and then bring it to a boil, the food starts to cook from the moment the water is warm enough to begin gelatinizing starches or softening cell walls. Pasta, for instance, begins to absorb water and soften well below boiling. The time it then spends at lower temperatures is unpredictable because the rate at which the pot heats up depends on the stove’s power, the pot’s material, and the amount of water. You can’t give a reliable cooking time; the food might be overdone or unevenly cooked by the time the water finally boils. You’d have to check it constantly, which defeats the convenience of a timed recipe.

So the core reason is about precision and repeatability, not about saving time. I should also clarify that while some techniques (like starting potatoes in cold water for even cooking) intentionally use a gradual temperature rise, for most items where we want a quick, high-heat cook and a predictable result, starting with boiling water is the standard.

I’ll structure the response by stating the primary reason—boiling water gives a fixed reference temperature for accurate timing—and then explain why the alternative (starting cold) leads to unpredictable results. I’ll also briefly address the misconception about reaching the boiling point faster, just to clear it up, though that’s not the main point in the final answer snippet I’m working toward. That should make the reasoning clear and natural.

How can you reduce the heat of a chili pepper?

There are many chilis that have amazing flavors but are so hot that it is hard for most of us to appreciate them. Beyond the standard suggestion to discard the seeds and cut away the ribs, are there any other methods that can lower the capsaicin level while retaining the other flavors?

This was asked on [Dave Arnold's Cooking Issues podcast](http://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/cooking-issues-mp3-heritage/id380317598), and I'm not sure they landed on a solid answer.

EDIT: I'm looking for something that might cut the perceived heat by like 90% or even 100%, not just make it slightly milder. Something that completely neutralizes the capsaicin, not simply buffers it on your palate. (Starting a bounty).

In Indian cooking we usually add Ghee (Clarified butter) to reduce the heat of a chili pepper. Most Indian dishes, we would add a good heaping spoon of ghee before feeding little ones. This helps temper the heat but keeps the flavors alive so that the children get used to them and can gradually learn to eat hotter foods.
thinking: The user is asking for a method to reduce the heat of chili peppers that goes beyond the common seed-and-rib removal, ideally something that chemically neutralizes capsaicin rather than just masking the burn on the palate. I need to focus on capsaicin’s chemical properties: it is a lipophilic compound, meaning it dissolves in fats and oils, not in water. Dairy products, particularly those containing the protein casein (like milk), are known to bind capsaicin and help wash it away from receptors, but the user specifically wants to retain the chili’s flavor. Ghee, or clarified butter, is essentially pure butterfat with the milk solids removed, so it lacks casein but is still an excellent fat. In the context of Indian cooking, adding ghee to a dish doesn’t just mask the heat; it dissolves some of the capsaicin into the fat phase, effectively distributing it and reducing the localized burn when eaten. This tempers the overall heat perception while preserving the complex flavors of the chili, because fat is also a great carrier of flavor compounds. The method is particularly used when feeding children to introduce them to spices gradually. I’ll structure the answer by briefly explaining capsaicin’s fat-solubility and then presenting the Indian culinary practice of finishing dishes with ghee as a practical solution.

Is it possible to cook a whole fish in a dishwasher?

I heard that there is a way to cook a whole fish in a dishwasher - any techniques, tips??

Cooking in a dishwasher is related to some other non-orthodox places to cook, like on the manifold of a car on a road trip.

Basically, you're aiming to put food in an environment that's somewhere between 160F (71C) and 300F (150C) already, for non-cooking reasons. That's strange, but not entirely nuts.

The dishwasher is going to stay south of 212F (100C), but, a decent dishwasher doesn't stay *very* far below that threshold.

It's going to go through several variations of how that heat's applied, from the actual washing cycle to the drying cycle.

And, if you run a regular cycle of dishes, there's going to be a bunch of foreign substances (soap, food bits from the dishes (and in the car manifold situation, things like oil)) all around it.

So, your goal is to wrap the food in something that can both handle the heat and seal out the foreign stuff. To me, the most obvious solution to this is the vacuum sealed pouches used for sous vide.

You're not going to get anything remotely close to the consistent temps for sous vide, but for the dishwasher, you're still talking about mostly cooking in "hot water" and hot, moist air, so that's close enough to give a shot.

So, I'd fill the pouch with seasonings/marinades and let it ride and see what comes out.

I wouldn't expect it to be great, but it might be worth a shot for the shock value alone.
thinking:
The user is asking whether it’s actually possible to cook a whole fish in a dishwasher, and if so, what techniques or tips would help. This is a quirky, unconventional cooking question, so I need to assess the feasibility from a food-science perspective and then offer practical advice.

First, I recall the temperature ranges found in a typical household dishwasher. The wash and rinse cycles usually expose the interior to water between about 140 °F and 160 °F, though the drying cycle can push the air and the heating element well above 200 °F—sometimes approaching 300 °F near the element. Fish is cooked through when it reaches an internal temperature of about 145 °F, so if the dishwasher can maintain temps in that ballpark for a sufficient duration, cooking is theoretically possible. However, the heat is uneven and cycles through wet and dry phases, making it a far cry from any precisely controlled cooking method.

The bigger problem is contamination. A dishwasher running a normal load contains detergent, rinse aid, and food particles from other dishes. Exposing unwrapped fish to that environment would be unsafe and unappetizing. So, the immediate solution that comes to mind is to isolate the fish completely—similar to how we cook sous vide, where food is sealed in a vacuum pouch and submerged in a temperature-controlled water bath. A vacuum-sealed bag would shield the fish from soap and debris while allowing heat transfer through the water and steam. The moist environment inside the bag would essentially steam or poach the fish.

I need to be honest about the results though. The temperature swings mean the fish won’t have the gentle, uniform doneness of a proper sous vide; it’s more of a novelty experiment. So the tips would be: use a heavy-duty vacuum bag with seasonings and maybe a little oil or marinade, seal it meticulously, and place it on the top rack where water might not directly blast it as forcefully. I wouldn’t expect restaurant quality, but it could be a fun talking point. I’ll structure the response to first explain the unconventional cooking context, then break down the dishwasher’s thermal and contamination challenges, propose vacuum sealing as the closest viable technique, and finally set realistic expectations.

Why do we peel carrots?

So I was sitting there, looking down at my counter, realizing that I probably had a good carrot or two of shavings just going to waste. (well, I'll compost it, but it's non-food at that point).

Is there any reason we peel carrots and don't just give them a good scrubbing? I mean, the scrubbing works for potatoes (so long as they're not green under the skin), and carrots grow in dirt, too. I don't think it's a pesticide issue, as we did it growing up, and I don't think we cared about pesticides back then.

I admit that sometimes there's odd crooks that might be harder to scrub dirt out of, but is there something fundamental that I'm missing here?

I find when cooked, the skin retains a bit of bitterness and toughness, so in desserts, juices or when shaved/julienned , I'm inclined to peel them. In fast salads, quick application, I usually don't bother.
thinking: The question is about whether there's a real reason to peel carrots beyond just removing dirt—since scrubbing works for potatoes, why not carrots? I need to recall what makes carrot skin different from potato skin. Potatoes have a thicker, more starchy skin that can be pleasant when scrubbed, especially in rustic dishes, but carrot skin is much thinner and contains a higher concentration of certain compounds. Carrots store some bitterness in the outer layer, and the skin can have a slightly tougher, more fibrous texture than the tender interior. When carrots are raw, that slight bitterness and chewiness might not be very noticeable, so a good scrub is often enough for a quick salad or snack. But cooking changes things: heat can intensify bitterness and make the skin's toughness more pronounced, which is why in desserts, juices, or when the carrot is cut into fine julienne or shavings, peeling is preferred for a smoother texture and sweeter, cleaner flavor. So the "fundamental" reason isn't about dirt or safety—it's about flavor and texture, especially in cooked or refined preparations. I'll structure the response by acknowledging that the skin is edible and scrubbing works sometimes, but explain that the skin can add bitterness and toughness that become noticeable in certain dishes, so peeling is a choice based on the end use.

How to peel hard boiled eggs easily?

This is one of the most annoying duties in the kitchen, for me.

What are yours tips and tricks to peel hard boiled eggs easily?

1. Buy almost-late eggs.

   The worst-case scenario of egg-shelling is a farm-fresh egg. That annoying film that sticks to both the shell and to the egg will detach, the older the egg gets. The bubble at the fat end, too, will get bigger as the egg ages, which also makes the bottom cap pop off more easily.

   Obviously, we don't want rotten eggs. We want the almost expired *but not expired* ones.
2. Roll the egg against the countertop, cracking it along the "equator".

   This will give you lots of starting points, and it will weaken the shell in enough directions that the rest of the peeling becomes easier. Usually, the top and bottom caps come off in large and clean pieces, so don't bother cracking that part unless it sticks.
3. Start from the fat end of the egg.

   After much experimenting, I've determined that starting from the bottom of the egg (the fat end) is the best way to do it. Give the egg one good whack on the countertop, and the bottom caves in quite easily. This gives you a really nice starting point. Now peel out from there in a spiraling pattern down the rest of the egg. The top cap still comes off quite easily in one big chunk, if the egg is old enough.
thinking: The user finds peeling hard-boiled eggs frustrating. The key is to understand the food science behind why some eggs peel easily and others don’t. Freshly laid eggs have a membrane that adheres tightly to the shell and the albumen, making peeling a nightmare. As the egg ages, the membrane slowly detaches, and the air cell at the blunt end enlarges, creating a natural separation point. Common advice like cracking and rolling helps because it fractures the shell into many small pieces and provides multiple points where you can get under the membrane. Starting from the fat end takes advantage of that air pocket—one firm tap there often caves in the shell, giving a clean entry point to peel in a spiral pattern. I’ll present these as three clear, actionable tips: using eggs close to their best-by date (without spoiling), cracking along the equator by rolling, and beginning at the fat end. Each tip will be briefly explained with the scientific rationale to show why it works, so the user can apply them immediately and understand the reasoning behind each method.

content:
Frying Oil Reuse

What are some guidelines or rules with regard to filtering and reusing oil that has been used for deep frying?

Is it safe and acceptable under some circumstances to filter and keep oil? If so, does it depend on which foods were fried? How long can the filtered oil for be kept for?

Or, is it never appropriate? If not, are the reasons health or flavour related? or both?

It is absolutely OK to filter and reuse deep-fry oil.

It's not uncommon at some short-order restaurants for them to filter the oil daily and only change it once a week. Of course, it does start to taste a little "off" when you reuse it that many times.

There's also the matter of impurities lowering the smoke point; even when you filter, the result is obviously not "pure" oil; the more you reuse it, the lower the smoke point gets, and eventually it will actually start to smoke at deep-fry temperatures (i.e. become unusable).

For home use, I'd recommend no more than 3 or 4 reuses. Check the oil to see if it needs to be changed sooner than that - if the colour or smell is off, don't use it again. Best to compare it against a sample of the same "fresh" oil; sometimes it's hard to just eyeball it without a frame of reference. If it looks totally clear and smells fresh, you could probably go up to 5 or 6 reuses - but definitely not more than that.

P.S. There will be some people who tell you that you should never reuse oil for general health (not safety) reasons. My response to that tends to be that if you're eating *deep-fried food*, you're probably not all that concerned about long-term health risks. Rest assured that if you do a lot of eating out, you've eaten plenty of food fried in "leftover" oil.
thinking:
The user is asking several related questions about reusing deep-frying oil: whether filtering and keeping it is ever safe and acceptable, what the guidelines are, whether the type of food matters, how long it can be kept, and if the prohibitions are based on health or flavor. I need to address both the feasibility and the potential risks.

First, I should separate the core issues. From a culinary standpoint, reusing deep-fry oil is extremely common in both home and restaurant kitchens. The primary concerns are flavor degradation and a drop in smoke point, not immediate food-safety hazards like bacterial growth, because the oil is heated well above pathogen-killing temperatures. Filtering removes food particles that would otherwise burn, create off-flavors, and accelerate oil breakdown. So yes, it is safe and acceptable under proper conditions.

The flavor issue makes the type of food fried relevant: frying fish or heavily seasoned items can impart strong flavors that linger and transfer to later batches, so some cooks designate separate oil for delicate foods. Health-related worries usually revolve around the formation of polar compounds and free radicals with repeated high-heat exposure, but these are long-term consumption risks rather than acute poisoning. For someone who eats deep-fried food regularly, the incremental health risk of reused oil is often considered marginal compared to the food itself.

The smoke point decreases with each reuse because heating causes polymerization and breakdown of triglycerides; even filtered oil contains dissolved impurities and free fatty acids. Once the smoke point drops to the frying temperature (usually around 350–375°F / 175–190°C), the oil will smoke excessively and impart acrid flavors, so it becomes unusable well before any serious toxicity. Therefore, the practical guideline is to limit the number of reuses and to discard the oil when it darkens, smells off, or smokes prematurely.

Home cooks often wonder about storage times. Filtered oil stored cool and dark can last a couple of weeks, but rancidity from oxidation sets in eventually, so counting the number of uses is more reliable than calendar time. A common rule of thumb is 3–4 reuses for clean, light frying; extending to 5–6 only if the oil remains clear and fresh-smelling. Restaurants filter daily and can stretch oil for a week under heavy use, but they also accept a slight flavor compromise that home cooks might not.

I’ll structure the response to first give a clear “yes, it’s acceptable” and then explain the practical limits, referencing both the smoke-point issue and flavor change, give a concrete reuse count, address the food-type dependence briefly, and end with a small nod to the health debate, noting that in the context of deep-frying it’s a minor escalation. That matches the intended final answer’s blend of reassurance, practical numbers, and a touch of pragmatism about health concerns.

Does active dry yeast really expire?

I was cleaning out my spice cabinet and deep in the back I found two packages (e.g., six envelopes) of active dry Red Star yeast that expired in March 2009, 15 months ago as of writing this question.

With the thought that dry yeast is basically freeze-dried and should have a decent shelf life, I proofed one envelope in warm water with some sugar to see if it really "expires". It foamed right up, so it seems like the answer is, at least for one year after the marked date, no.

Although in this case, does "expired" really mean "less effective" or "will taste funny"?

I've used yeast that was even older than yours and although the taste of the resulting bread was fine, and it foamed up properly when tested, I found I had to use about 50% more of it to get the same density of the bread. In the end, I threw it out because it was too much trouble to experiment with it every time.
thinking:
The user is asking whether active dry yeast that is past its “expiration” date is truly unusable, or if the date just indicates a loss of potency. They’ve already proofed a very old envelope and seen it foam, so they’re wondering if “expired” means it might taste off or just be less powerful. The core of the question is about the practical consequences of using old yeast.

Active dry yeast consists of dormant yeast cells. Over time, even in a dry, sealed package, a percentage of the cells die. The expiration date is a conservative estimate of when the viability drops below what the manufacturer considers reliable. So yeast past its date usually isn’t spoiled in a safety sense—there’s no microbial contamination risk from the yeast itself—but the number of live cells per gram is lower. That means standard amounts may not produce enough carbon dioxide to leaven a dough properly. The fact that it foams in warm sugar water only shows that some cells are alive, not that the total population is still sufficient for a full rise without adjustment. It shouldn’t impart a “funny” taste unless perhaps it’s very old and the dead cells start to break down, but that’s unlikely to be perceptible; the main issue is performance.

Since I’ve dealt with this personally, the answer should reflect a real-world experience to illustrate that “expired” is about effectiveness, not spoilage. I’ll describe using yeast even older than the user’s, finding that the bread tasted fine but had poor oven spring and density unless I used roughly 50% more, which turned baking into a guessing game. In the end, it was more hassle than it was worth, so I tossed it. That directly answers whether expired yeast can work (yes, with adjustment) and whether it’s worth keeping (often not). The reply will be structured as a short anecdote that confirms both points.

Is it safe to eat moldy cheese if you slice off the edges?

Whenever my cheese gets too old and has a bit of blue/white mold on the side, I'm not sure whether I should throw it completely out or not. Is it safe to eat if I cut off the edge? Should I cut a bit off of all the sides just to be safe?

I'm particularly interested in the answer for cheddar cheese, but answers about other cheese are welcome.

I think it would depend on the cheese.

- For a reasonably hard cheese, like cheddar, I have done it, and never gotten sick (your results may vary).
- If it's pre-grated, then I would not touch it anymore.
- For a softer cheese, like a brie, I would not risk it.
thinking:
The user is asking about the safety of eating moldy cheese after cutting off the moldy parts. They specifically mention blue/white mold appearing on the edges, and they’re unsure whether to discard the whole piece or just trim it. They want to know what to do with cheddar but are open to information about other cheeses.

First, I need to recall the relevant food-science knowledge about mold growth in cheese. Mold produces thread-like roots called hyphae that can penetrate food. The depth of penetration depends heavily on the food’s moisture content and density. Hard cheeses like cheddar have low moisture and a firm structure, so mold typically stays on the surface and doesn’t easily send roots deep inside. Soft cheeses like Brie, Camembert, or cream cheese have high moisture and a looser matrix, allowing mold hyphae to spread well beyond the visible growth. Additionally, some molds produce mycotoxins that can cause illness, and harmful bacteria like Listeria can also colonize the same environments.

Government food-safety guidelines (from sources like the USDA) are clear on this: for hard or semi-hard cheeses, you can safely salvage them by cutting away at least one inch around and below the moldy spot, keeping the knife clear of the mold to avoid cross-contamination. The rest of the cheese should be fine to eat. For soft cheeses, the entire item should be discarded because invisible threads and potential toxins may have spread throughout. Pre-grated cheese is a special case: it has a huge surface area and often contains small pieces that are impossible to inspect or trim effectively, and the shredding process can introduce moisture and contaminants, so if mold appears, the whole bag should be tossed.

Now I think about the user’s situation: they see blue/white mold on the side of cheddar. Cheddar is a hard cheese, so trimming is appropriate. They also ask if they should cut a bit off all sides just to be safe—that’s a reasonable extra precaution, but the main thing is to remove the moldy spot with a generous margin. As for their personal experience, many people have done this without illness, but food safety always involves some risk, especially for immunocompromised individuals. I’ll note the “your results may vary” aspect because individual tolerance and the specific mold strain can differ.

To structure the response, I’ll break it down by cheese type: hard cheese (like cheddar), soft cheese, and pre-grated cheese. I’ll directly address cheddar first, then give the others. The tone should be practical and reassuring but with clear safety boundaries. I won’t delve into scientific detail unless needed; the answer will be concise and bullet-point-style, focusing on actionable advice.

Finally, I’ll present the answer as a short list of conditions, acknowledging the nuance, and ending with the disclaimer that it’s based on personal experience and general guidelines.For cheddar, a hard cheese, it’s generally safe to cut off the moldy part with a generous margin—aim for about an inch around and below the mold—and eat the rest, because mold struggles to penetrate deeply into firm, low-moisture cheese. Soft cheeses like Brie have high moisture, allowing mold roots and potential harmful bacteria to spread invisibly, so they should be thrown out entirely. Pre-grated cheese should also be discarded, as its large surface area and shredded shape make it impossible to trim safely and increase the risk of contamination throughout.

content:
Once a month cooking

I've heard of "once a month cooking" or "freezer cooking," where you basically spend a day cooking and fill your freezer with the next month's worth of food. This could especially come in handy when preparing for a baby. (Take-out food gets boring REALLY fast.)

What are some tips and/or resources for once a month cooking?

*Edit*: I suppose this need not be for cooking for an entire month *per se*. The idea is cooking in bulk ahead of time.

For years I did the 'once a week' cooking, which has the advantage of not requiring much freezer space (which I didn't have, with my under-counter apartment fridge). Part of the trick was cooking something that could be used multiple ways with minimal effort -- a blend of ground beef, onions and peppers could be turned into a pasta sauce, mexican food, etc.

These days, I still don't go quite to the extreme you're talking about, but I will do things like make way more than I know I'm going to use right away, and freeze the rest -- chili, black bean soup, stock, lasagna, etc. When chicken's on sale, I'll poach a large batch, shred it, then freeze it in zip top freezer bags. I can turn it into chicken tacos in a few minutes -- thaw with some water in a pan, add spices, and cook 'til the water's mostly boiled off.

Now, as in the past few months I've made a lot of meals for my brother's family while his wife was pregnant with twins, some considerations:

- **containers** : you're going to need a lot for a month, especially if you're preparing sides and such. As I had a membership to Restaurant Depot, I was able to get 2 1/4 lb rectangular aluminum containers normally used for carryout packaging. Of course, I had to get a case of 400 ... if you know a restaurant that uses 'em, you might ask if they'll sell you a few dozen. You want something that seals tightly, and you'll want to fill them so there's not much air space left in them.
- **labeling** : all containers should be marked with what's in them (if you have to open to look, it's not going to last very long), the date it was made, and possibly reheating instructions and/or ingredient lists (see below). My mom would use masking tape to label things, I just got the lids that had paper on one side, aluminum on the other.
- **variety** : my sister-in-law started getting heartburn from some ingredients (tomatoes, onions), which meant that the items I had made didn't work out so well. (She was fine after the pregnancy, though, and made use of the dinners then).

One thing I've heard about, but never done myself, is people who have a dinner exchange -- sort of like a cookie exchange for the holidays -- everyone makes up a number of casseroles, or whatever, and then people meet up, and everyone takes one of everyone else's items home. So, if you're thinking about doing this, and know of other people who might want to, also, you might be able to get some extra variety. (of course, if you don't like their cooking, it might not work out so well).

... and one last thought -- it won't help on the baby preparation front, but if I were going to do this as a regular thing, I'd consider making one or two recipes, with batches for 4-5 dinners each ... so I was staggering things, and not having to spend a whole day (or weekend) trying to make enough different things to have variety for a whole month.

What exactly is "Sushi Grade" fish?

What exactly makes some fish "Sushi Grade"?

"Sushi grade" means that it is safe to prepare and eat raw. In order to do that, it must be frozen to kill any parasites. That means it either has to be:

- Frozen at -20° C (-4° F) for 7 days; or
- Frozen at -35° C (-31° F - "flash frozen") for 15 hours.

There aren't any official regulations about the fish itself or its quality, and most sushi/sashimi distributors have much more stringent rules of their own beyond the freezing guarantee.

Italian here :) I know that the oil is a well known trick everywhere ... but Italy. The main problem about pasta is that people just tend to cook it too much. The cooking time for pasta should be between 8 and 12 minutes, above this number it will be sticky. Spaghetti is the quickest kind of pasta to get ready, so just cook it around 8-9 minutes and it won't stick.

I need to figure out why cooked pasta sticks together and what truly prevents it, beyond the common tricks that often create other problems. The user’s core issue is that timing mishaps leave spaghetti sitting and clumping, and they don’t want it mushy from staying in water. So I have to address the root cause of stickiness, not just a post-cooking workaround.

First, I recall the basic science: pasta starches gelatinize during cooking, and if overcooked, the surface becomes overly soft and sticky as excess starch is released. When that pasta is drained and starts to cool, the starches on the surface dry somewhat and act like a glue, bonding strands together. So the longer it sits, the worse the clumping gets. Adding oil to the water or rinsing afterward are often suggested, but oil can make the sauce slide off later, and rinsing washes away the starch that helps sauce cling while also cooling the pasta. Neither really solves the initial problem if the pasta is already overdone.

That makes me think the real fix starts before draining. If pasta is cooked to just al dente, the starch gelatinizes only so much, the surface remains firmer, and it releases less free starch into the water. So it naturally separates more easily even as it sits briefly. The mental note here is that many home cooks treat pasta like a boiled grain that needs to be soft, but Italian practice is precise: pull it when there’s still a slight bite. For thin strands like spaghetti, overcooking happens fast, and even an extra minute can make it limp and sticky.

The user mentions leaving it in water makes it mushy, which reinforces that overcooking is likely already happening. If the pasta were properly timed, it could be drained and left to wait a short while, and a quick toss with a little of the pasta cooking water or a drizzle of sauce later would still separate the strands because they aren’t already over-gelatinized. So instead of suggesting oil or keeping it in hot water, I’ll steer hard into cooking time: spaghetti specifically needs no more than 8–9 minutes. That one change should prevent the sticky mess, even if the sauce isn’t ready immediately.

I’ll structure my response to first dismiss the oil trick as a superficial fix, then directly name overcooking as the culprit, and finally give that concise, authoritative cooking time. Why does a brown paper bag speed ripening?

I often see this technique suggested as a way to speed ripening. Why does it?

The ripening itself is caused by ethylene gas released by the food, which is trapped by *any* kind of bag.

So the “brown paper” aspect is not about a chemical interaction but rather about the bag’s breathability. Any loosely woven bag (even a cloth or a paper bag of another color) would behave similarly, but the common household tip simply highlights brown paper because it’s cheap and readily available.

Fry onions and garlic before adding to the sauce?

I am making a tomato sauce for pasta but I am not sure whether to put the garlic and onions into the sauce raw or to sauté them first?

Sauteing onions:

- Softens them, most people prefer not to run into raw onions in their sauce. Onions will cook in a sauce, but very slowly, so frying them before makes sure they will be soft even if your sauce has a fast cooking time
- Releases sugars, making them taste sweeter
- Reduces the onion's harshness
- Browning the onions creates flavor

Sauteing garlic: garlic needs very little sauteing, far less than onion. It's very easy to overdo it, generally a minute or two is all it needs, too much and it burns and adds off flavors.

- Softens the garlic although it will cook in the sauce much faster than onion
- Releases the flavors
- Reduces harsh notes. The more you saute it the mellower the flavor but the less garlic-y it becomes. I often add garlic to my saute in 2 stages so I get both the mellowness and the edginess in my dish. It does mean adding more garlic overall, but it's worth it

So you get more depth of flavor, better flavor and texture sauteing them.

What should I look for in a good, multi-purpose chef's knife?

If I want to buy a good multi-purpose chef's knife, which characteristics should I look for?

One of the most important things is a [full tang](http://culinaryarts.about.com/od/knivescutlery/ss/anat-knife_5.htm). The tang is an extension of the metal of the blade into the handle. In knives with a full tang, it goes all the way through the handle. This improves stability, control, and durability. Cheaper knives with partial tangs will have the handle break off over time.

In a chef's knife, you want a blade from 8 to 10 inches long, whichever is more comfortable.

You can also either get a forged or stamped blade. I suggest reading [this article](http://ezinearticles.com/?Forged-Kitchen-Knives-Vs-Stamped-Kitchen-Knives&id=1509150) on the differences. To summarize, forged blades are softer, easier to sharpen, heavier, and have a bolster. Stamped blades are sharper, harder to sharpen, lighter, and have a welded on a bolster if any. With current manufacturing processes forged is *not necessarily* better than stamped. You should make your own decisions. All crap knives are stamped, but not all stamped knives are crap.

This brings me to one of the most important points: *It must feel good in your hand*. Don't buy an expensive knife just because it's expensive, or you recognize the name. Go to a store that will let you use the knife, Williams-Sonoma will do this. If you can, bring a carrot in your pocket and actually cut that in the store.

content:
What did European/American historical cooks do with the egg whites?

I do some historical cooking out of old cookbooks, like Amelia Simmons' *[American Cookery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Cookery)* or *[The Art Of Cookery Made Plain and Easy](https://archive.org/details/TheArtOfCookery)*. One thing I've noticed is that these cookbooks use *way* more egg yolks than whites. For example, I prepared an 18th century feast one night and ended up with 10 leftover egg whites in a jar.

This left me wondering, what did they do with the egg whites? Given the extreme frugality of cooks centuries ago, which included using every scrap of stale bread and every bit of a pig including the oink, I find it impossible to believe that they were wasted. They must have used them for something ... but that's not in the recipes I have. So, questions:

1. Are the cookbooks we have simply not representative of actual cookery of the 15th-18th century? That is, are they purely posh cookery and as a result did actually waste the egg whites?
2. Or were the egg whites used for some other purpose that required a lot of whites, maybe even a non-culinary purpose?

Help me solve this mystery. Thanks!

Another high-volume specialist use for egg white was mortar. Specifically, it was used very frequently in the Middle Ages, in the standard lime and sand mortar: [a 2017 study](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/320738514_Preliminary_Studies_on_the_Development_of_Lime-based_Mortar_with_Added_Egg_White) suggests that 6% egg albumen (I assume by weight) provides the strongest mortar.

It was [not the only binding agent](https://www.uh.edu/engines/epi253.htm) available to construction, but at least in the Middle East and in Europe, it was one of the [most easily procured](https://misfitsarchitecture.com/2015/01/22/its-not-rocket-science-11-keeping-the-water-out/). Its role is to aerate the mortar, which is essential in preventing thermal contraction damage (ice or heat), and [modify its hydration](https://www.physicsforums.com/threads/eggs-in-cement-making.636114/) (usually by allowing a lower water-to-cement ratio, increasing strength and water resistance while still being workable).

The use of egg white in construction persisted into the late 19th century in the colonial Philippines. According to one report, this use of egg white in the buildings transformed [native Filipino desserts](https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/filipino-desserts).

Why is a roux necessary?

A classic bechamel sauce is a roux and milk. Why can’t I just add the flour directly to the milk and cook till thickened, stirring vigorously to keep it from clumping?

You do not *need* to make a roux. While your proposed technique of adding flour directly to milk will almost certainly lead to clumps, there are other ways to incorporate flour, butter, and milk: namely, a *beurre manié*.

First, let's explore why flour clumps in hot liquid. As explained in [this Seattle Times cooking advice column](https://www.seattletimes.com/life/lifestyle/how-to-make-gravy-or-other-sauces-without-any-lumps/), flour will immediately gelatinize when added -- forming a sort of gel-like barrier that encases clumps of flour. No amount of stirring will break up these clumps. A simple fix is to use [Wondra](https://www.thekitchn.com/what-is-wondra-flour-248213) or a similar product. This flour is specially formulated to avoid clumping; I am not familiar with the details of their process, but I know that the product can be directly whisked into a sauce without clumping. It is fairly popular in America for making gravies.

But, with standard flour, the best fix is to work in fat: it works as a lubricant, keeping particles of flour separated for long enough to incorporate into the sauce. As you know, one method to accomplish this is to make a *roux*: flour is added to hot fat and stirred until incorporated. Only then is liquid slowly added. An alternative is to make a *beurre manié*: a mix of cold butter and flour that is added, uncooked, to the sauce.

Both a roux and a beurre manié provide sufficient lubrication to prevent clumps; however, many chefs prefer roux for a variety of reasons.

- Making a roux requires less mechanical action. Working cold flour and butter requires a lot of stirring or kneading. A roux, on the other hand, can be quickly whisked together with less resistance. This is ultimately a personal preferences: you may find one or the other workflow easier.
- Some people think a beurre manié tastes "floury". The hot butter in a roux lets you "cook out" the floury taste, some say. Not everyone agrees: [this cook](http://www.beyondsalmon.com/2009/11/to-cook-or-not-to-cook-roux-vs-beurre.html) tried both methods, and in a taste test, saw no discernible difference. If a sauce thickened with beurre manié tastes good to you, go for it.
- In the same vein, a roux lets you toast the flour. Dishes that use "dark roux" (like gumbos, etouffée, or Japanese curry) rely on this toasty flavor for depth, color, and balance. In this case, you cannot substitute a beurre manié without losing flavor.

The beurre manié has a bit of a bad reputation as a "shortcut" or inferior option to the roux. But, if you are struggling with roux, or just want to try a different process, I encourage you to give it a shot. If you do get some clumps, you can always just strain the sauce through a fine sieve.
thinking:
The question is why a roux is necessary for a béchamel, and whether you can just whisk flour directly into milk. The first thing to clarify is that a roux isn't strictly necessary—there are other ways to thicken the sauce. But there's a good reason direct addition doesn't work well: when raw flour hits hot liquid, the starch granules swell and gelatinize almost instantly at the surface, forming a gel barrier that traps clumps of dry flour inside. No amount of vigorous whisking can break those clumps apart because the gelatinized outer layer seals them. So the problem isn't just about mixing; it's a physical barrier issue.

I recall that fat solves this by coating the flour particles, keeping them separated so they can hydrate gradually without clumping. That's the core principle behind both a roux (flour cooked in hot fat) and a beurre manié (flour kneaded into cold butter, then added to the liquid). So a roux isn't the only fat-based method. There's also Wondra flour, which is processed to resist clumping and can be whisked straight into liquid—an option for those who want to skip the fat entirely, though it's not part of the classic béchamel.

Now, why might a chef still choose a roux over a beurre manié? I can think of a few practical and flavor reasons. First, working cold flour and butter into a paste requires a bit of elbow grease compared to quickly whisking flour into hot butter. That's a matter of personal preference. Second, raw flour can taste starchy or "floury," and cooking it in the roux can remove that taste. However, I've seen experiments where tasters couldn't tell the difference in a finished sauce, so that may be a minor point. Third, and most compelling, is that a roux allows you to toast the flour to varying degrees—blond, brown, dark—which develops deep, nutty flavors critical for dishes like gumbo or Japanese curry. A beurre manié won't deliver that because the flour remains uncooked until it hits the liquid, so no toasty notes develop. 

So, the answer will open by stating that a roux isn't necessary, then explain why direct addition fails (gelatinization clumping), mention Wondra as a quick fix, then introduce the fat-coating concept and the two methods. It will then compare roux and beurre manié on those points: ease of mixing, floury taste, and toasting capability. It will conclude that beurre manié is a perfectly valid shortcut, and if clumps do happen, straining is always an option. That covers the science, the alternatives, and the practical cooking advice in a balanced way.

Why should one pre-heat an oven?

When cooking potatoes and bellpepper in an oven, it is highly recommended to pre-heat the oven. Why would it be a problem to put them in the oven while it is heating up ?

Thank you very much ! :)

It is not a problem to put whole potatoes for roasting in the oven while it heats up. In fact, it's a good idea.

However, if you are following instructions or cooking times written for a preheated oven, you will need to add about 10 minutes to the cooking time (depending on how fast your oven heats up).

The rule of thumb I use for this is to add 1/2 of the time my oven takes to heat up to the recommended cooking time. Since my oven takes about 20 minutes to get to 400F, that's 10 minutes.

However, regarding bell peppers it depends on *why* you are putting them in the oven. If you're talking stuffed bell peppers, then it's fine to start with a cold oven. However, if you are trying to char the peppers to remove the skins, you need to start with an oven that's as hot as possible, otherwise you will cook the peppers to mush before the skins are charred (and, ideally, use the broiler).
thinking:
The user is asking why preheating is so important when roasting potatoes and bell peppers, and what problems might arise if you put them in a cold oven. At first glance, it seems like a general rule that an oven must be preheated for everything, but I need to think about what actually happens with these particular vegetables and the different cooking goals. 

I recall that preheating serves to set an immediate high temperature for browning, crisping, or rapid cooking, which is crucial for things like baking bread or roasting meats where you want a sear. But for some foods, a gradual heat-up is not harmful and can even be beneficial. For whole potatoes, many chefs actually recommend starting them in a cold oven. The gradual heating allows the starches to gelatinize more evenly and the interior to steam gently, leading to a fluffy texture, while the skin eventually crisps. So it's not a problem at all—it's often preferred. The only catch is that most recipe timings assume a preheated oven, so the user would need to account for the extra time the oven spends reaching temperature. 

For bell peppers, the situation is entirely different depending on what you're trying to achieve. If you're making stuffed peppers, the goal is to cook the filling and soften the pepper shell without burning anything. Starting cold is fine because the pepper and filling can heat through together without the outside overcooking. But if the goal is to char the skin to peel it off, you need intense, immediate heat from a preheated oven or the broiler; otherwise, the pepper will slowly cook and turn mushy before the skin has a chance to blacken and blister. So the "problem" only arises when the cooking method and desired outcome require a thermal shock.

The answer should clarify that the user's assumption—that it's always a problem to skip preheating—isn't universally true. I'll structure it by addressing potatoes first, explaining that it's actually fine and giving a practical timing adjustment, then moving to bell peppers and breaking it down by cooking purpose to show when a cold start is acceptable and when it isn't.

When a recipe asks to add spices to the oil, can you add the spices directly to the sauce for the same effect?

Many chefs add spices to the oil because the "oil brings out the flavors". But I want to experiment with different spices and quantities (which is hard because you can't taste the oil and predict the end result). My question - when a recipe clearly asks for spices in the oil, how can you add the spices to the finished sauce for the same effect?

The effect will be different for a few reasons.

1. When you add spices to hot oil, they cook at a considerably higher temperature (up to around 200°C) than in a simmering sauce (100°C as it's likely to be mostly water). Important cooking chemistry happens at this higher temperature, so the flavour is actually changed (just as with onions and garlic).
2. Whole or coarse spices sometimes pop and break up (I often add whole or lightly crushed cumin seeds to hot oil and fry, but if you add them after adding watery liquids they get stuck in your teeth). This can be mitigated by using finely crushed/ground spices.
3. Even if the oil is cold, many major flavour compounds are much more soluble in oil than water, [capsaicin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsaicin) being a significant example. The flavour extraction will be affected. Taking chilli flakes as an example, you *can* add them later, even at the table, but the heat will be concentrated in the flakes; adding them at the beginning of cooking allows the flavour to infuse the whole dish. Again finer spices can help here by dispersing in the sauce.

On the other hand it's perfectly sensible to add black pepper to a simmering sauce, to taste. Turmeric is also often added towards the end of cooking as too much cooking removes some of the best elements of the flavour. Paprika is also sometimes added late (or even to the oil *and* at the end).

Bearing this in mind, experimenting is a good thing. If you put a baseline level of spice in the oil, you can get away with topping up the flavour, with a little care.
thinking: The user is asking whether they can skip the step of adding spices to hot oil and instead toss them directly into the sauce, achieving the same flavor. To answer, I need to recall the food-science principles behind blooming spices: many flavor compounds are fat-soluble, and high heat triggers chemical transformations (like Maillard reactions or release of volatile aromatics) that don't occur in a water-based liquid limited to boiling point. I also need to address the practical concern about tasting and adjusting—why it's harder to judge the outcome from the oil stage. The answer should explain the key differences: temperature extremes (oil can reach ~200°C vs. sauce at 100°C), extraction efficiency (oil vs. water solubility), and physical behavior of whole spices. Then I can address the user's desire to experiment by noting that some spices work well added late, and a hybrid approach—infusing a baseline in oil and finishing with additional ground spices in the sauce—is a viable path. I'll structure the response by first stating the effect is different, then detailing the physical and chemical reasons, offering specific examples (chili, cumin, turmeric, paprika), and finally suggesting a practical compromise for experimentation.

Can a pizza stone be fixed after soap has been used to clean it?

We bought a pizza stone from a thrift store (so at least it was cheap). Unfortunately we cleaned it with soap before reading up on how to clean them. I know, rookie mistake.

Is there any way to fix it or should I just toss it out and consider it a lesson is researching new tools before messing with them? Obviously, I have no idea if the prior owner misused it so this might be a lesson in not buying used stoneware.

I haven't tried baking on it since using soap on it and the soap was only lightly used. I guess I should perform an experiment and find out if it makes things taste soapy.

I would rinse well with clear water. Allow to dry thoroughly, and then use as normal.

There is a small chance that your pizza stone will impart a soap flavor to your pizza, but I would say that it is worth a couple of pizza cooks to determine if there is a long term problem. It's really not that much of a risk.
thinking:
The question is about whether a porous pizza stone that was lightly washed with soap once can be salvaged. Pizza stones, typically made of cordierite or unglazed ceramic, are very absorbent because of their open-pore structure. Soap molecules, especially if they contain fragrances or surfactants, can get lodged in those pores and potentially release a soapy taste or smell when heated. The user’s concern is valid—many instructions explicitly warn against soap—but the severity depends on how much soap was used and how deeply it penetrated.

Since the soap was used only lightly and the stone was bought secondhand (so its prior condition is unknown), the first step is to try to flush out as much residue as possible. Rinsing with clear water—perhaps even soaking briefly in clean water and then rinsing thoroughly—can help draw out some of the water-soluble soap components. Then letting it dry completely is crucial because trapping moisture inside the stone can lead to steam explosions and cracking during baking. After that, the simplest test is to just use it: bake a test pizza on it. The high heat of the oven might burn off some volatile soap remnants, and if any off-flavor remains, it will become immediately apparent. Because the stone was cheap and the risk is a single ruined pizza, it makes far more sense to experiment than to discard it preemptively. I’ll explain this by advising a thorough rinse, full drying, and a practical trial, noting the small chance of failure is worth the attempt.

Mint vs Peppermint

Are mint and peppermint the same thing?
Can we substitute one for the other.
How can we differentiate between mint and peppermint?

Peppermint is a hybrid breed of two plants belonging to the mint genus, spearmint and watermint. In my experience, when 'mint' is referred to by itself without any other descriptors, it usually refers to the spearmint flavour people are used to (from things like green restaurant mint candies, toothpaste, etc). Peppermint will be denoted as peppermint. However, as mentioned in the comments, this may vary based on region.

There is a significant difference in taste between peppermint and spearmint; I find peppermint to have a much more intense flavour. Scientifically, peppermint gets its flavour from its high menthol content, whereas as spearmint owes its flavour to the compound L-carvone. Substitution will not replicate the same flavour as the original.

Source for science related parts:
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentha>
thinking:
We need to untangle a common culinary confusion: “mint” vs. “peppermint.” First, what’s being asked? Three things: whether they’re the same, whether you can swap them, and how to tell them apart. I’ll address each in order.

To answer the first, I recall that in botanical terms, “mint” is the genus *Mentha*, which includes many species and hybrids. Peppermint (*Mentha × piperita*) is a specific hybrid of spearmint and watermint. So strictly, peppermint is a kind of mint, but they are not identical. In everyday cooking and labeling, “mint” without qualification almost always means spearmint—the flavor people know from classic mint jelly, mint chocolate chip, or fresh mint leaves in salads and Middle Eastern dishes. That’s a key distinction: when a recipe calls for “mint,” it expects that sweeter, milder spearmint taste.

Now, substitution: I think about the primary aroma compounds. Peppermint gets its penetrating, cooling kick from high menthol content, while spearmint gets its gentler, slightly spicy-sweet character from L-carvone. Swapping one for the other will drastically alter the flavor profile—imagine peppermint in a tabbouleh, or spearmint in a candy cane. So while you can physically substitute, you won’t replicate the intended flavor.

Differentiation: The obvious way is taste. Peppermint has that intense, almost medicinal, cool menthol burn; spearmint is sweeter and more delicate. In stores, products are usually labeled “peppermint” explicitly—like peppermint extract or tea—whereas “mint” alone typically denotes spearmint (mint sauce, fresh mint). Regional differences exist, but this pattern holds widely. I’ll note the scientific basis to ground the explanation.

The response should concisely state the botanical relationship, clarify the “mint = spearmint” convention, explain why substitution fails, and point to the key flavor compounds. I’ll wrap it up by referencing the source for the science. That structure directly answers each part of the question.

content:
Is pad thai actually Thai?

*More like meta-cooking question, but I believe it fits here better than on travel stack.*

All around the world, one of the symbols of Thailand is Pad Thai. And multiple versions of curry.

But when I wander around Bangkok or other Thai cities, I see pad thai served mostly in tourist areas like Khao San Road and its surroundings, around the Royal Palace, etc.
When I look and most food street carts there are plenty of sticks (meat/fish/sausages/balls/seafood put on short wooden sticks and grilled over fire), soups (tom yum based, clear soup with noodles, wonton's), many kinds of meat, seafood, noodles (though not strictly pad thai I think) and so on.
Not that many curries either, but in more in-house restaurants you can find them.

So my question is - **is the pad thai really Thai**? Maybe I'm just overlooking it, or search in wrong places. Or is it a dish once found by a western traveller, made famous in the West and then its renown came back with the travellers.

It's Thai, but it's a relatively new dish as it doesn't date back when the country was called Siam, and it uses Chinese style noodles and preparation (with Thai flavors).

There was a coup against the monarchy in 1932; in 1938 Plaek Phibunsongkhram (aka Phibun) came to power as prime minister. Phibun ordered the creation of a new national dish, "Gway Teow Pad Thai" (Thai fried rice noodles). The thing was, noodles weren't popular in Thailand before that, but there are stories that as this coincided with World War II, it was a way to get people to eat less rice. (although, it's rice noodles, so I don't understand that part)

The government pushed for the dish, including subsidizing food carts (and banning non-Thai food cart vendors, so there wasn't competition from the Chinese noodle vendors)

...

But they're not the only country where foods we associate with them are relatively new -- potatoes and tomatoes are "new world" crops, not European, and untrusted (as they're part of the nightshade family along with capsicums (peppers), eggplant, and tomatillos). So Irish and Italian cuisines before 1500CE (aka 1500AD) were extremely different from what we think of as their cuisines today.
thinking:
The question raises a common suspicion: pad thai is so ubiquitous in tourist zones and internationally known as the emblematic Thai dish that it’s fair to wonder whether it’s an authentic tradition or a modern invention, perhaps even a foreign creation that was re-imported. To answer this, I need to recall what I know about the origins of pad thai.

I remember reading that pad thai is indeed a Thai creation, but it’s not ancient. It didn’t exist when the country was still called Siam. The dish’s emergence is tied to a specific political moment: after the 1932 coup that ended the absolute monarchy, a nationalist leader named Plaek Phibunsongkhram (often called Phibun) became prime minister in 1938. He launched a series of nation-building campaigns to modernize and unify Thai identity. One of his initiatives was to promote a new national noodle dish. The dish would use rice noodles, which were Chinese in origin but given a distinctly Thai flavor profile with tamarind, fish sauce, and palm sugar. The name he gave it was “Gway Teow Pad Thai” — literally “Thai-style stir-fried rice noodles” — to stamp it with a Thai identity.

I also recall that this push coincided with World War II, and there are stories that the government wanted to reduce rice consumption because rice was expensive or needed for export, and noodles used less rice? That part is a bit confusing since rice noodles are still made from rice, but possibly broken rice or using a different form was economical. More concretely, the government actively promoted the dish by distributing recipes, subsidizing food carts that sold it, and even banning foreign (mainly Chinese) food vendors from competing, so the new national dish could take hold.

So pad thai is not a foreign invention imported by tourists; it was a deliberate, top-down creation by a Thai government. The fact that it’s more visible in tourist areas today might reflect that it succeeded internationally as a symbol of Thai cuisine, so vendors in tourist hubs naturally serve it. Locals may eat it less frequently or in different contexts, but that doesn’t make it inauthentic — just a relatively young and politically motivated dish.

There’s a broader point worth making here: many cuisines we think of as timeless are actually quite recent due to the introduction of new ingredients. For example, potatoes and tomatoes are New World crops that didn’t arrive in Europe until after Columbus. So what we consider traditional Irish cuisine (potatoes) or Italian cuisine (tomatoes) didn’t exist before the 1500s. Pad thai is a similar case of a relatively modern invention that has come to define a national food identity.

I’ll structure the response by first confirming it’s Thai, then briefly explaining the historical creation under Phibun, including the name and the promotional tactics. I’ll then add the comparative note about other cuisines to put this modern origin into perspective. This directly addresses the asker’s suspicion while educating about food history.
