Why is 180 degrees C so common in recipes?

Is there any particular reason 180 degrees Celsius is so commonly called for in baking, roasting, deep frying?

Ovens are by their nature a high-heat cooking method, and thus create a temperature gradient in the food. The outside of the item is the hottest, because it is in contact with the hot air, and exposed to the radiant (infrared) heat coming from the oven walls, ceiling and floor.

Heat from the outside then conducts into the inside overtime. The effect of this is that the surface of the food will be the hottest, and the center the coolest.,

180 C (350 F) is a moderate oven. It balances:

- Cooking the food through
- Overcooking the outside

It is suitable for a wide range of baked goods and other dishes, although often within limits (especially for non-baked goods) you can trade temperature and time off.

Note that a single oven can only have one temperature, and a moderate oven is good for many cakes and cookies; for baking and heating through casseroles; for roasting root vegetables; for maintaining a braise; and for roasting many meats; and many other tasks. If you want to have multiple items in the oven at the same time, it is a good temperature to choose that will give good results for a wide variety of items, even if it is not ideal for every item.

Still, it is not ideal for every cooking technique and food item. Low and slow roasting (for tremendously succulent pulled pork, brisket, and so on) is done as low as 200 F (93 C); some people favor high temperature roasting of certain meats to get a crispy exterior while maintaining a rare interior with temperatures of 450 F (232 C), or even higher.

Many breads are baked at higher temperatures--and of course, pizza infamously is ideally done at temperatures home ovens cannot even achieve, so at home they are often baked at the maximum oven setting around 550 F (280 C).

---

Deep frying is a separate matter, and it is a complete coincidence that the ideal temperature for deep frying matches that of roasting.

The way deep frying works is that the heat of the oil heats the outside of the food, but it is hot enough to nearly instantly vaporize the water at the surface of the food. This water creates a small pocket of vapor around the food, preventing the oil from entering and making the item completely oily. In order for this effect to happen, the oil must be sufficiently hot which starts around 180 C / 350 F.

On the other hand, again, you don't want the food to burn on the outside before it cooks through, but more importantly, you don't want the oil smoking, and developing off flavors (many culinary fats have a smoke point starting not too far above these temperatures). For these reasons, frying much above this temperature is generally not a good idea. Most ideal frying temperatures are somewhere in the 350 F - 365 F (180 C 0 185 C) range.

I suspect many recipes indicate 350 F simply because it has become common and conventional.
thinking:
The question asks why 180°C is so common in recipes, and specifically whether there's a reason it appears in baking, roasting, and deep frying. I need to unpack what's happening at that temperature across these different methods.

First, I recall that ovens cook by surrounding food with hot air and radiant heat from the walls. This creates a temperature gradient from the outside in. If the oven is too hot, the surface can burn or dry out before the interior is done. If it's too cool, cooking takes very long and might not produce desirable browning or texture. 180°C (roughly 350°F) is considered a moderate oven. I think about what happens at that temperature: it's hot enough to drive browning reactions—like Maillard and caramelization—at the surface within a reasonable timeframe, but not so hot that the outside scorches before the heat can penetrate to the center. So it's a sweet spot for many baked goods like cakes, cookies, and for roasting vegetables and meats to doneness without excessive charring.

I also consider the practical utility: many cooks have only one oven, and they might want to bake multiple things at once. A moderate temperature like 180°C works adequately for a range of dishes—casseroles, roasted roots, a simple cake—even if it's not the absolute optimal for each. So part of its prevalence could be sheer convenience and versatility.

Now, deep frying is a completely different heat-transfer medium, but it's also often cited at 180°C. I need to connect the dots. In frying, the food is submerged in hot oil, which transfers heat much faster than air. The key dynamic there is moisture. When food hits oil at around 180°C, the surface water instantly vaporizes, creating a steam barrier that prevents oil from soaking in and making the food greasy. That's the threshold where the steam cushion is sustained. Below that, the food absorbs oil and becomes soggy. On the other end, if the oil is much hotter, it risks burning the exterior before the inside cooks, and more critically, many cooking oils have smoke points just above 180°C (e.g., peanut oil around 230°C, but butter much lower; standard vegetable oils around 200–220°C). Frying above 190°C often leads to off-flavors from oil breakdown and potentially hazardous smoking. So 180°C is also an ideal balance for frying—hot enough for a crisp crust and no oil ingress, but below smoke points of common fats.

I realize there's a coincidence: the same numeric temperature works for both oven cooking and deep frying, but for different reasons. In oven cooking, the balance is about heat penetration and browning; in frying, it's about vapor barrier and oil stability. The commonality has likely become self-perpetuating: recipes standardize to 180°C because it works, and home cooks' ovens and fryers are calibrated to it, reinforcing its use.

My response should clarify these distinct reasons, then note that convention plays a role. I'll structure it by first addressing oven cooking: the gradient, balance, versatility. Then pivot to deep frying, explaining the steam barrier and smoke points. Finally, I'll remark on how the overlap is partly coincidental and partly cultural reinforcement. I'll avoid making it sound like a definitive scientific law, but rather a practical convergence.I need to work out why 180°C is so recurring, and the question separates baking/roasting from deep frying. I’ll start by thinking about what ovens actually do: they heat food from the outside in via hot air and infrared radiation. The outside inevitably gets hotter than the inside, so there’s a constant trade‑off between cooking the centre thoroughly and overcooking the surface. That trade‑off depends on temperature. A very high temperature will brown or even burn the exterior long before the middle is done, unless the item is very thin. A very low temperature will cook gently but might never produce desirable browning or texture in a practical time.

180°C (about 350°F) is a moderate heat. I remember that many classic baking recipes—cakes, muffins, cookies—work well at this temperature because it allows the structure to set and the interior to cook through while the outside develops colour at about the same time. For roasting, a moderate oven gives a balance between rendering fat, browning the surface, and bringing the centre to the right doneness without excessive charring. Beyond that, there’s a practical reason: most home cooks only have one oven. If you’re cooking a meal with several components—e.g. a roast, some root vegetables, and maybe a baked pudding—180°C is a kind of “universal donor” temperature that will give acceptable results for all of them simultaneously, even if it’s not the absolute optimum for each. So it’s a convenient default that recipe writers can rely on.

Now, deep frying is a separate technique, so I need to think about why the same number shows up there. Frying oil operates by violently boiling off water at the food’s surface the moment it’s submerged. That boiling creates a film of vapour that pushes the oil away, preventing it from soaking in. That effect kicks in properly only when the oil is hot enough—around 170–180°C for most foods. If the oil is cooler, the steam isn’t generated fast enough, the food absorbs oil, and it’s greasy. But I also have to consider the upper limit: oil degrades and smokes. Many common frying fats (groundnut, canola, sunflower, even clarified butter) have smoke points not far above 190°C. So from a safety and flavour standpoint, you don’t want to go much above 180–185°C. Thus, again, 180°C is a sweet spot: hot enough for the vapour barrier, cool enough to avoid smoking and off‑tastes.

I notice the coincidence: two completely different cooking methods converge on the same figure for entirely different physical reasons. And once that coincidence becomes established, recipes and kitchen equipment reinforce it—it’s a round number people remember, thermometers are marked for it, and it’s simply “the temperature that works.”

I’ll structure my answer by first treating oven cooking (heat gradient, interior vs. exterior, versatility), then deep frying (steam bubble mechanism, smoke point), and finally point out that the initial question is really about two separate phenomena that happen to share a numerical value, with convention doing the rest.

content:
Why use yeast instead of baking powder?

Both yeast and baking powder are used to gas-fill the pastry, make it expand and thus make it soft and fluffy.

Using yeast is rather inconvenient - it can be dead already or if the yeast is submerged in too hot water it can die and also waiting for yeast to work to let it gas-fill the pastry before baking is also not that convenient. Looks like the baking powder is more convenient - it can be stored for ages, can be mixed with hot water, baking can be started immediately after mixing the pastry.

Why is yeast used then? What are those advantages of yeast tham make people use yeast and not the baking powder?

Baking powder, especially if too great a quantity is used, adds an unpleasant flavor to a baked good. Even in an appropriate quantity it can be noticeable and it certainly doesn't do anything to enhance the flavor. Many baked goods traditionally don't use a chemical leavener at all, but instead rely on technique. Creaming butter and sugar together or whipping egg whites was historically used to make cakes which rose solely based on the bubble network that was created.

Yeast, on the other hand, creates a delightful flavor that you associate with your favorite crusty loaf of bread. Yeast can be used not only in making bread but also in some excellent cakes ([St. Louis Gooey Butter Cake](http://smittenkitchen.com/2010/03/st-louis-gooey-butter-cake/), for example, although many "knock off" recipes cheat here and miss out on the true goodness). Yeast also provides a significantly different texture during the rising due to the intentional creation of a gluten network (usually something you absolutely don't want in a quick bread or quick cake) — you don't get a crumb with big, airy holes from baking powder or baking soda with an acid.

Also, in my experience baking powder lasts six months in the pantry and yeast lasts at least six months in the fridge. The shelf life is not so different.

If yeast scares you, you may want to check out some of the proponents of the [no-knead bread](http://www.nytimes.com/2006/11/08/dining/081mrex.html) technique.

For a lot more information on this subject, there is a recent publication that covers all sorts of [leavening agents](http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/1113083700).
thinking: The user is questioning the point of using yeast given its perceived inconvenience compared to baking powder. I need to answer by explaining the unique benefits yeast provides that chemical leaveners can't replicate, while also correcting some misconceptions about shelf life and difficulty. The core advantage lies in flavor and texture: yeast fermentation produces complex, desirable flavors absent in baking powder goods, and the long rise develops gluten for a chewy, holey crumb you associate with bread. Baking powder acts quickly and doesn't develop gluten, giving a tender, cake-like texture; if overused, it leaves a bitter, metallic aftertaste. I should also note that many traditional cakes rely on mechanical leavening (whipping eggs, creaming butter) instead of chemical agents, and that yeast can shine in certain cakes for its flavor. I'll address the shelf-life worry: properly stored yeast lasts months in the fridge or freezer, similar to baking powder’s relatively short active life in the pantry. To make yeast less intimidating, I can point to no-knead methods. The response should sympathize with the inconvenience, then pivot to the sensory and textural reasons yeast is irreplaceable in many baked goods, and offer practical reassurance. I’ll structure it by first stating the flavor trade-off, then explaining the texture difference due to gluten, then challenging the shelf-life assumption, and finally suggesting accessible ways to work with yeast.

content:
What does "do." mean in old recipes?

I'm reading through a book of cocktails from 1865 and I often seen the measurement for a given ingredient listed as "do.". What does this mean?

Examples:

> 40 1/2 ounces of roast and ground cocoa.  
> 6 2/3 do. ground cardamom seeds.  
> 6 2/3 do. ground Ceylon cinnamon.  
> 7 pints of alcohol, 95 per cent.  
> 20 do. water.

Or:

> 2 gallons of ground malt.  
> 6 do. water, at 142° (degrees) heat.

Or, most bafflingly:

> 1 pound = 16 ounces  
> 1/2 do. = 8 do.  
> 1/4 do. = 4 do.

I suspect it means "ditto (the above line)":
<http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ditto_mark> seems to indicate that "do." was an old way of abbreviating before the ditto mark (") became widespread.
thinking:
The user is encountering “do.” in a 19th-century cocktail recipe book and suspects it’s an old abbreviation, possibly for “ditto.” I need to confirm that by analyzing the given examples.

In the first set, the first line specifies “40 1/2 ounces,” and the following lines have quantities like “6 2/3 do.” It’s clear the missing word is “ounces” because it’s the unit just mentioned. The same pattern appears with “2 gallons” then “6 do.” where “do.” stands for “gallons.” The most telling example is the definition: “1 pound = 16 ounces / 1/2 do. = 8 do.” — here the first “do.” replaces “pound” and the second replaces “ounces,” each referring back to the respective term in the line above. So “do.” functions exactly like a ditto mark, indicating “same as the previous entry in this column.”

The term “do.” comes from the Italian “detto,” meaning “said,” and was commonly used in handwritten lists and printed books before the double quotation mark (”) became the standard ditto symbol. The user already found support in the Wikipedia article on ditto marks, which notes that “do.” was an earlier written form. I’ll structure my answer around this straightforward interpretation, illustrating it with the user’s own examples and briefly tracing its origin.

content:
Dishwasher safety - "top shelf" vs. "bottom shelf"

The instruction manual for some of my kitchen equipment says "Dishwasher safe (top shelf)".

What difference is there between what an object on the top shelf of a dishwasher experiences, and what happens to an object on the bottom shelf?

What are the risks of putting one of these items on the bottom shelf?

In most dishwashers the heating elements are on the bottom only. Lightweight plastic items might melt (soften and distort, not drip away) on the bottom, but they don't mind being in the steamy environment or being sprayed with hot detergent-laced water. They are therefore only dishwasher safe on the top shelf.

I've melted a plastic bowl or two in my time; there is a definite difference between top and bottom.
thinking:
The question asks about the practical difference between the top and bottom shelves of a dishwasher that leads to some items being labeled "top shelf only," and what risks exist if you ignore that. I need to reason from the physical design of a typical home dishwasher. Most dishwashers have an exposed heating element at the very bottom, used to heat water during the wash cycle and to dry dishes afterwards. The bottom rack sits just above this element, so items there can be exposed to intense radiant heat and possibly contact if they warp or fall. The top rack is higher up, further from the element, so it experiences a milder temperature environment—still hot and steamy, but not the direct blast of the heating element's output.

Now, why would some kitchen equipment be safe only on the top? Many items made of lightweight plastic have a relatively low softening temperature. If placed near the heating element, they can soften, warp, or distort (not necessarily melt into a puddle, but lose their shape). On the top rack, they are still exposed to hot water and detergent spray, but the air temperature is lower and there's no direct radiation, so they survive intact.

The risks of putting a "top shelf only" item on the bottom are therefore warping or melting. The item could become unusable, and if it deforms enough, it might even fall onto the heating element, potentially causing a fire hazard or damaging the dishwasher. I've experienced this myself with plastic bowls—they definitely distort when too close to the heat.

To structure the answer, I'll first explain the typical dishwasher layout (heating element on the bottom only), then describe the temperature difference between racks, then connect that to the behavior of plastics, and finally state the risk of melting/distortion. That mirrors the final answer's concise approach.

content:
Why is there cow cheese but no pig cheese?

I have always wondered what there is no cheese made from other milks other than cow, goat or sheep. Are they not suitable for humans? Do they taste bad? Is it even possible to make dairy products with them?

There are several main reasons, historically:

1. Cows, sheep and goats have udders, and can be milked by hand into a bucket. Pigs (or cats, or humans for that matter) have nipples, where you need to suck the milk out. Consider that most of the cheese in the world was invented before machinery was able to create a vacuum, this means that the only option would have been to suck milk from the pig and spit it into the bucket.
2. For making cheese, the fat/protein ratio in the milk is important. It changes, obviously, from species to species, which is why there aren't many hard yellow cheeses made of goat's milk.

Lastly, I have actually had camel's milk ice-cream, which goes to show that it's just a cultural thing mostly.
thinking:
Looking at the question, it's clear the user is puzzled by the absence of pig milk cheese, contrasting it with the common cheeses from cows, goats, and sheep, and wondering if the milk is inedible, foul-tasting, or technically impossible to turn into cheese. The natural first step is to consider the biology and historical practice of dairying. Why did my grandfather-in-law salt his beer?

My grandfather-in-law was born in England in the 1920s and fought in World War II. Somewhere along the line he acquired the habit of salting his beer before drinking it, which persisted for the rest of his life. I'm as curious about the cultural genesis of the practice as the food science of it – was there perhaps something about wartime beer that made it unpalatable without salt? I know there were other wartime food customs like [bread and scrape](http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/bread_and_scrape) so it doesn't seem implausible, but the "why" of this one isn't so obvious.

I can think of several reasons why you might salt beer:

- Salt is a natural flavor enhancer, so you'd be able to taste the hops and malt more
- Salt reduces perceived bitterness, so overly hopped beer would taste less bitter
- The salt crystals may nucleate bubble formation, giving the beer more head (briefly)

I've heard of it being done before, but never with good beer, only low quality swill. But then, since there were more quality problems with cheap brews at the time, this was probably a lot more common.
thinking:
The question asks both about the scientific and cultural reasons for salting beer, specifically within the context of an English man born in the 1920s who fought in WWII. I need to consider why someone would develop and maintain that habit. On the food science side, I recall that salt is a known flavor enhancer—it can boost the perception of malt and hop notes by suppressing bitterness and even interacting with carbonation. Salt also reduces perceived bitterness, which would make an overly hoppy or poorly balanced beer taste smoother. Another possible effect is that salt crystals act as nucleation sites, rapidly releasing dissolved CO2 and creating a thicker, longer-lasting foam head. These might all improve the drinking experience, especially if the beer itself was lacking.

Now, the historical angle: during and after the war, English beer often suffered from ingredient shortages, lower gravities, and sometimes rushed production. The resulting beer could be thin, harshly bitter, or flat. Salting would have been a practical, cheap way to compensate—masking off-flavors, adding body perception, and livening the carbonation. This trick might have been passed around among pub-goers or soldiers, and once a taste for salted beer was acquired, it could easily become a lifelong habit, even after beer quality improved. The asker’s mention of “bread and scrape” as another wartime custom supports the idea that such culinary hacks were common and persisted.

Therefore, I’ll structure the answer around listing the primary scientific reasons—flavor enhancement, bitterness reduction, and nucleation—and then contextualize it by noting that this was almost exclusively a tactic for poor-quality beer, which was widespread in that era. I’ll add a brief note that the habit would likely have stuck as a personal preference.

What should I cover bread dough with while it's rising?

If you let (bread) dough rise, the recipe always asks to cover it. Years ago, I read to cover it with a wet towel. Nowadays, I see more and more recipes that ask for plastic wrap (aka saran or cling wrap).

The towel lets air through, the wrap does not. What is the difference between the two in the end result? What is best to use and why?

I'm talking about the first as well as the second (proofing) rise. If there is a difference between the phases, please inform me.

The goal is to keep the surface of the bread from drying out.

A wet towel works fine but plastic wrap is cheaper and easier than constantly cleaning wet towels.

I have used both methods and haven't noticed a difference in the bread produced. In very dry climates, when I made bread with multiple rises I sometimes had to redampen the towel which was an added inconvenience.

Lately I have been proofing large batches of bread in a large stock pot and just use the lid of the pot as the only cover.
thinking: The question is about covering bread dough during rising, specifically comparing a damp towel to plastic wrap, and whether the first and second rises require different treatment. I need to think about why dough is covered at all: to prevent the surface from drying out and forming a skin, which would inhibit expansion and create an unpleasant texture. The covering must trap moisture close to the dough. A wet towel does this by acting as a physical barrier and providing its own moisture, but it is porous, so evaporation can still occur, especially in a dry environment. Plastic wrap is impermeable, so it seals moisture in completely. Both achieve the basic goal, but there are practical differences. When using a towel, if the rise is long or the air is very dry, the towel itself can dry out and even wick moisture away from the dough if it’s in direct contact, though a well-wrung towel placed loosely should be fine. Plastic wrap doesn’t have that issue and is disposable, but it can stick to the dough if it touches it, so some people oil the surface or leave the wrap loose. For a second proof, often the dough is shaped and exposed to more air, so covering remains important. I haven’t noticed a difference in end results between the two covers, so the choice is about convenience rather than a fundamental change in bread quality. A pot lid is another alternative that works well and is reusable. I’ll structure the response by first stating the goal, then comparing the methods on practicality and effectiveness, mentioning that both work and the main downside of a wet towel is the potential need to redampen it, then sharing my own experience with using a stock pot lid for large batches. The answer will be short and direct.The goal is to keep the dough surface from drying out and forming a skin. A damp towel can work but it’s breathable, so moisture evaporates over time, especially in dry environments or during long rises, sometimes requiring rewetting. Plastic wrap is impermeable, traps moisture reliably, and is disposable—no laundry or concerns about towel hygiene. Neither method chemically changes the dough in a way that noticeably affects the final bread, so it’s a practical choice. For convenience and consistency, many now use plastic wrap or a simple pot lid, which I’ve used with excellent results for large batches.

content:
Why are salt and pepper the "classic" dinner table seasoning?

Is there a reason we use salt and pepper on so many dishes and they can be found in any kitchen table at dinner time? Does it have to do with their flavor synergies, or were they just more available "back in the day"?

Salt is perhaps the most basic and effective flavour enhancer, and so it's fairly obvious why we have it on our dinner tables.

The popularity of pepper is down to the Romans, who were crazy about it. Thanks to the longevity of the Roman Empire, pepper was imported for hundreds of years, helping to establish it as the most popular spice, and keeping the price high.

Bill Bryson reports in *At Home* that:

> When the Goths threatened to sack Rome in 408, the Romans bought them off with three thousand pounds of pepper.
thinking:
The question is about why salt and pepper, specifically, ended up as the default table condiments in so many Western dining settings, and whether it’s about flavor chemistry or historical accident. 

Salt is straightforward: it’s a fundamental taste enhancer that suppresses bitterness and amplifies other flavors, and it has been essential for food preservation for millennia. That makes its ubiquity unsurprising—it’s not just a seasoning, it’s a biological need and a foundational culinary tool.

Pepper is more interesting. Its dominance isn’t about any unique chemical synergy with salt, but about a long historical arc of prestige and familiarity. The Roman Empire established extensive trade routes with India, and black pepper became a wildly popular luxury item among the Roman elite. They used it in both savory and sweet dishes, and its high cost meant it was a status symbol. Because the Empire lasted centuries, this demand persisted and embedded pepper deep into European culinary culture. Even after Rome fell, pepper remained an expensive, coveted spice through the medieval period, often used to display wealth at the table. Over time, as trade expanded and prices eventually fell, it had already become a deeply familiar and expected seasoning across class lines. The habit of putting a pepper mill or shaker next to the salt cellar on the table solidified, especially in French and later Anglo-American dining customs. 

The Bill Bryson anecdote about the Goths being paid off in pepper perfectly illustrates how extraordinarily valuable and desirable it was—three thousand pounds of it as a ransom underscores its status as a prized commodity like gold. So the answer boils down to: salt because it’s chemically indispensable, and pepper because the Romans made it culturally indispensable. I’ll present this by first acknowledging salt’s obvious role, then telling the pepper story with the Roman hook to make it memorable.

The solution is to thermally shield the custard using an ice-water bath: the ramekins sit in a pan of crushed ice and water, acting as a heat sink to keep the custard cool while the sugar on top melts and caramelizes under the broiler. The broiler needs to be fully preheated on high, and the rack should be on the top shelf so the sugar is close to the element. The process is fast—about 3 to 4 minutes—so constant monitoring is crucial to avoid burning. content:
Why are baking measurements such nice round numbers?

I've heard over and over that when it comes to baking, measurements cannot be ignored, and you need to be very precise. [This question](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/12875/what-does-spooned-and-leveled-mean) covers how precise a measurement of flour should be, for example. But if getting your baking just right requires being so painstaking in measuring ingredients, how is it possible that all of the amounts in recipes come out to such neat and easy numbers? I can't remember if I've ever seen a flour measurement go more specific than the nearest 1/4 cup. The smaller chemicals like baking powders are usually to the half tsp, that I've seen, but I can imagine they go down to 1/4 or 1/8. And eggs basically always come in ones, or one yolk, but there's not much you can do about that. Weight measurements are more specific of course, but have you ever seen a ratio like 4.2683 oz of flour per egg?

How accurate is this really? Does this mean if your flour measurement is off by 1/16th cup you'll be just fine? Or it just won't look the same as the one made by the person who invented the recipe? I have a hard time believing that with such complex chemistry involved, the optimal quantities are so close to large fractions of our units of measure. Is there actually a bit more fudge room with some ingredients than we're being told?

Also, if so, which ingredients are more forgiving? I'd guess that baking powders are among the least.

I've always been taught that baking is a science when it is compared to cooking. Cooking is very much 'to taste' and very individual. There are not as many things that can go wrong with a standard recipe in cooking, and you have a lot more room for creativity. You don't have to look at baking as ***that*** precise. However, unlike cooking, where you can add or subtract from a recipe with no real harm to physical structure, that does not hold in baking. For examlple, if you feel that there is too much salt in a recipe, cutting back can (and most likely will) have a cascading effect through the ingredient chain. You have to understand your ingredients and the effect they have on other ingredients. That is what makes baking a more precise science.  
And in terms of flour, it is often the most 'ranged' ingredient. Depending on flour type, miller, altitude, water temp. etc., the amount of flour in a given recipe is always a guide. Again, you have to know your ingredients. You will never see 'one and an eight cup plus 2 TBSP hard flour' in a recipe, because it is so variable for many different reasons. Flour and water are the two most flexible ingredients, and are always variable.
Hopefully this helps, I am sure someone will come along with a more scientific explanation for all different ingredients, I am just offering an experience based answer to your question.
Also, you are right, do not mess around with baking soda and powder. If you do, you are asking for trouble.
I would suppose that the rule of thumb would be that the more exacting an ingredient is (tsp, quarter tsp), you don't want to change much.
thinking:
The user is puzzled by the apparent contradiction: baking is touted as a precise science, yet recipes call for neat quantities like 1 cup, 1/4 cup, ½ teaspoon — never 1.183 cups or 4.2683 ounces. They suspect the precision advice might be overblown and want to know what leeway really exists, especially for different ingredients. I need to address this from a practical food-science and baker’s perspective, acknowledging that while some reactions are sensitive, the round numbers persist because ingredients inherently vary, and beyond a certain point, finer measurement isn’t meaningful or helpful.

I’ll recall that baking is governed by chemistry — leaveners, gluten structure, moisture balance — but also by experience. Flour, for instance, isn’t a fixed-constant material; its hydration capacity shifts with humidity, brand, and even the way it’s scooped. That’s why recipes list flour in a range-anticipating way, and bakers learn to read dough consistency rather than obsess over the last tablespoon. So a recipe’s cup-shy measurement is already a starting point, not an atomic specification. This makes seemingly coarse increments like ¼ cup perfectly functional: the real precision comes from adjusting on the fly, not from a third decimal place.

For small-quantity reactive ingredients like baking soda or powder, the teaspoon fractions are indeed as tight as they need to be. The margin for error there is narrow because even a small absolute change alters the ratio dramatically. But standard spoon measures capture that within acceptable tolerance — a ⅛ teaspoon difference matters, so you stick to the specified ½ teaspoon without doubling. There’s no need for angstrom-level precision because the chemical reactions are robust across minor weighing errors, but not robust to major misjudgments.

The user specifically asks which ingredients are more forgiving. I’ll identify flour and water as the primary cushion variables; their interaction defines dough texture, and small adjustments there are routine. Leaveners and salt are the “do not mess with” group. Eggs are pretty standardized as “one egg,” though commercial bakers sometimes do weigh them, but home recipes accept natural variation. Fat and sugar amounts have some flexibility but less than flour/water.

In structuring my answer, I’ll explain that round numbers aren’t a sign of sloppiness but a reflection of ingredient variability and practical home-baking tolerances. I’ll describe how flour is a guide, not an absolute, and why you won’t see crazy fractions. Then I’ll confirm that baking powder/soda are indeed unforgiving, and conclude with a rule of thumb: the smaller the listed measure, the less you should deviate. I’ll weave in that baking is a science in understanding ingredient roles, but an art in feel, so it’s not as rigidly precise as novices fear.

content:
What does a healthy cast iron skillet look like?

I've read plenty about how to restore and season cast iron, but I have no clue whether any of the old cast iron I've inherited could benefit from this.

Is healthy cast iron black? or should it be somewhat metallic looking (ie. a bit silvery, like steel). Does the black color come from even one seasoning process, or will it develop over time?

Is is smooth? or is it alright if there are some lumps in it's surface texture?

and finally: after seasoning, is the surface supposed to have a slight oily appearance or should it be totally dry? and will healthy cast iron leave a residue on a rag if I wipe it? Some of mine do, and I'm not sure if that is good or bad.

Ideally it should be matte to just-slightly-shiny black and very smooth. [This article](http://sherylcanter.com/wordpress/2010/01/a-science-based-technique-for-seasoning-cast-iron/) has some terrific information on the ideal oil to use (flaxseed) and method for seasoning, with actual scientific grounding.
thinking:
The user is asking for a visual and tactile description of a well-maintained cast iron skillet, including color, surface texture, and oiliness. I need to address each sub-question based on how seasoning actually works. Seasoning is a layer of polymerized oil baked onto the iron. When oil is heated past its smoke point, it undergoes polymerization, forming a hard, plastic-like coating that bonds to the metal. The color of this coating depends on thickness and the specific oil. A freshly seasoned pan often appears dark brown or bronze, not deep black. With repeated use and additional layers, it turns black. A metallic silvery-gray appearance would mean the seasoning has worn off or was never applied, exposing bare iron, which rusts. So a healthy pan should be black, ranging from matte to slightly shiny—certainly not bare metal.

Regarding smoothness, the polymerized layers need to be thin and even. If seasoning is applied too thickly, oil can pool and form sticky, lumpy spots that don't fully harden or flake off later. Old cooking residue can also become carbonized lumps. A healthy surface is very smooth to the touch, almost glassy after many cycles, because the thin layers fill in the microscopic pores of the iron. Any significant bumps or rough texture indicate a need to strip and re-season.

After proper seasoning, the surface should feel dry, not oily. If it feels greasy or leaves a residue on a rag, that means excess unpolymerized oil remains on the surface. This happens when too much oil is used during the seasoning process and not thoroughly wiped off before heating, or when the pan wasn’t heated long enough to fully polymerize the oil. A properly seasoned pan won’t leave a mark on a dry cloth; it should be hard and non-tacky. So the answer is that a healthy skillet is matte to slightly shiny black, very smooth, dry, and does not leave a residue. I’ll also point to a reliable resource—that article by Sheryl Canter on flaxseed oil seasoning—as it explains the science behind achieving that ideal surface. My response will condense these visual and textural properties into a single sentence, then offer the link for further reading.

content:
Why is it necessary to preheat an oven?

Just about every recipe advises to preheat the oven before using it. I often forget this, but luckily this doesn't seem to matter all that much. Hence my question: why would it be necessary to preheat the oven?

When you don't preheat, you cook your food at a lower temperature as your oven heats up for the first 5-15 minutes, depending on the target temperature and your oven's strength.

For forgiving foods, like a casserole, this may not affect you much - you'll just have to bake longer than the recipe says to. As long as you're careful, you'll be fine.

But if you're baking something that should be baked for a short time at a relatively high temperature, your results are going to be very different. For example, take traditional Southern biscuits: they're baked very hot for less than ten minutes. This cooks them all the way through, and browns the top and bottom. If your oven starts out cold, they're going to be done in the middle before they're brown! Beyond under-browning, you'll also run into problems like lack of rising in steam-leavened foods. Pastries, in particular, could probably be disastrous.
thinking:
The user is asking why preheating an oven is so strongly recommended when, in their experience, forgetting often doesn't ruin the dish. They’re noticing that some recipes are more forgiving than others, and they want the food-science explanation for that difference. I need to break this down from first principles.

First, consider what happens physically when you place cold food into a cold oven and then turn it on. The heating element works at full power until the air temperature reaches the set point, but that takes several minutes. During that warm-up phase, the food isn’t getting the full, steady heat the recipe was designed for. The oven’s temperature curve is a ramp, not an instant step. The less thermal mass your food has, and the more the outcome depends on a rapid initial blast of heat, the more that ramp matters.

Now, recall which cooking processes are most sensitive to temperature timing. For something like a casserole—a large, dense mass baked relatively long—the total heat energy absorbed over a longer period is what matters. If the first 10 minutes are at a lower temperature, you just compensate by baking longer, and the internal doneness still tracks because heat transfer is fairly linear. But for items that rely on rapid reactions in the first few minutes, this fails. Steam-leavened pastries (puff pastry, choux) need that immediate high heat to generate a burst of steam that pushes layers apart before the structure sets. Biscuits and scones, baked at high heat for a short time, need the outside to brown and the inside to cook simultaneously; if the heat is low initially, the interior will set and dry out before any browning occurs. Yeast-leavened items can also suffer from “oven spring” that’s stunted if the temperature climbs slowly. So the importance hinges on whether the dish depends on a kinetic race between moisture evaporation, starch gelatinization, protein coagulation, and Maillard browning that requires a specific temperature trajectory.

The user’s own experience makes sense: for forgiving dishes, preheating isn’t strictly necessary—just an aid to predictable timing. For delicate baked goods, it’s the difference between success and failure. I’ll structure the response by first explaining the oven’s heat-up delay and how it effectively lowers the cooking temperature for the first several minutes, then split the world into forgiving foods (where extended time compensates) and sensitive foods (where the dish relies on high heat from the start for rise, browning, or texture), giving the biscuit example as a clear case where the inside would overbake before the outside colors. The answer should also mention that pastries and other steam-leavened items would be particularly disastrous. The tone should match the user’s curiosity and acknowledge their observation is correct for certain foods, while explaining why preheating is non-negotiable for others.When you place food in a cold oven, the heating element runs at full power while the air gradually climbs to the set temperature. For the first 5–15 minutes, the food is effectively baking at a much lower, uncontrolled temperature. Whether that matters depends entirely on how the particular food cooks.

For a large, dense dish like a casserole or a braise, the total cooking time is long and the goal is to bring the whole mass to doneness evenly. A slow start simply means you’ll need to bake longer; as long as you monitor it, the result is much the same. The recipe’s timing becomes unreliable, but the food is forgiving.

The situation flips for any baked good that relies on a rapid, high-heat jump to create structure. Biscuits, for example, are baked hot for under ten minutes: the outside must brown and the inside must set almost simultaneously. If the oven starts cold, the inside dries and cooks through before any browning occurs. Pastries that leaven with steam (like puff pastry or choux) need a burst of heat to generate the steam that pushes layers apart; without it, they never rise properly and become dense. Even yeast-leavened breads perform an early “oven spring” that falters if the temperature rises too slowly. In these cases, not preheating doesn’t just add minutes—it produces a fundamentally failed texture and appearance.

So your observation is accurate: many casserole-type dishes survive a cold start with just a longer bake. But for high-temperature, short-bake items where the race among starch gelatinization, protein coagulation, and browning must be tightly choreographed, preheating is non-negotiable. I’ll structure my answer by first explaining the oven’s warm-up delay, then contrasting forgiving dishes with sensitive baked goods, and finally giving specific examples of what goes wrong in biscuits and pastries.

content:
Is there any truth to the idea that you shouldn't multiply seasonings when multiplying a recipe?

I often hear cooks discuss that idea that if you are multiplying, say, a recipe for 4 to be a for 32, that you shouldn't multiply some herbs, spices, or salt. I've never understood any reason why this should be true. Maybe something to do with surface area to volume ratios, or cooking times? Does anyone have a real explanation, or is this nonsense?

The notion that salt or spices *specifically* don't scale linearly sounds like nonsense to me. In any recipe involving salt and water, the salt is dissolved, so all that matters is the concentration, and that concentration is going to be the same with linear scaling.

Scaling *in general* is problematic when scaling more than 2x or 4x. When you take into account that:

- Recipes targeted at home cooks are imprecise to begin with and often use volumetric measurements that are sensitive to heat, humidity, and other environmental conditions, so the imprecision is magnified at larger scale;
- Larger portions of food may get cooked less evenly and/or at less consistent temperatures due to the volume/surface area ratio; that part is correct, but it has nothing to do with salt, it has to do with your equipment. On the stovetop, most of the heat is coming from the bottom of the pan unless you use induction, and even in an oven you've got one or two heat sources radiating heat in a specific pattern.
- Cooking *times* are also going to vary due to changes in things like rates of evaporation. The total amount of heat you're able to deliver at any given time generally does not increase as quickly as the amount of heat you *need* to deliver, so very often you need to increase cooking times.

I'm sure you probably already know all this, but the reason I'm pointing it all out is that I'm pretty sure that this odd-sounding assertion about non-linear salt/spice scaling is due to some mutation or misunderstanding of general scaling issues.

Probably, salt and spices are typically present in very small quantities in most recipes, and those quantities are already wild guesses much of the time, so the effect of compounding all this wild inaccuracy, especially with volumetric measurements, is actually pretty noticeable at large scale. Scaling sucks with these ingredients because the initial quantities and scaling method are both nonsense.

Assuming you have a precise recipe that gives *weight* measurements, and you scale by weight, then you're not going to have any problems as long as you either cook it in batches or adjust your cooking time/temp accordingly.

I suppose I could be wrong, but I spent 20 minutes digging for some evidence to contradict my claims above and came up dry; you'd think that *somebody* would have presented some evidence if the claim were true.
thinking:
The question is whether there is any scientific basis for the common advice that seasonings—salt, herbs, spices—shouldn’t be multiplied linearly when scaling a recipe from, say, 4 to 32 servings. I need to examine this from a food-science perspective.

First, I think about what salt does in a recipe. In most dishes involving liquid, salt dissolves and distributes evenly. What matters for taste is the concentration of salt in the food, typically as a percentage of the total mass. If you multiply all ingredients, including water and other liquids, by the same factor, the salt concentration stays exactly the same. So from a pure chemistry standpoint, linear scaling of salt should yield the same saltiness. There’s no surface-area-to-volume reason that would alter the dissolution or perception of salt dissolved in a liquid—once it’s in solution, it’s uniform.

For herbs and spices, the situation is about volatile oils and other flavor compounds. If you multiply the amount of seasoning in direct proportion to the total mass of the dish, the ratio of flavor molecules to food is constant. There’s no inherent mechanism by which doubling the amount of oregano in a pot of sauce, while also doubling all other ingredients, would make the flavor disproportionately strong or weak, provided the cooking process remains equivalent. Differences in extraction due to surface area or cooking time could theoretically affect how much flavor is released from whole spices or herbs, but that’s a general issue of how the food cooks at a larger scale, not a property of the seasonings themselves.

This leads me to consider why the myth persists. Scaling a recipe 8x or more creates practical problems that have nothing specifically to do with seasonings. Home recipes often use volumetric measurements—teaspoons, tablespoons—and are already imprecise. A teaspoon of a fluffy dried herb can vary wildly in mass. When you multiply an unreliable volume by 8, the error compounds. For salt, many cooks use a “pinch” or a teaspoon, but salt crystal sizes differ, so the actual mass per teaspoon is inconsistent. At small quantities, these errors might go unnoticed; scaled up, they become blatant over- or under-seasoning. The cook then blames “scaling linearly doesn’t work for seasonings,” when the real culprit is the initial measurement imprecision and the use of volume instead of weight.

Additionally, larger batches cook differently: reduced surface-area-to-volume ratio leads to slower evaporation, which can leave a dish more watery and alter how we perceive saltiness (since salt is tasted in relation to water content). Uneven heating might mean some parts of the dish are overcooked while others are undercooked, changing flavor delivery. Cooking times need to be adjusted because the heat input doesn’t scale linearly with mass. These factors affect the overall outcome, leading someone to think the seasoning ratio was off, when actually the cooking physics changed.

I realize that the claim “you shouldn’t multiply some herbs, spices, or salt” is likely a folk mutation of real scaling challenges. I recall that precise recipes using weight measurements (grams, ounces) and proper technique can be successfully scaled, provided you cook in appropriately sized batches or adjust time and temperature. There’s no evidence in food science that seasonings behave non-linearly. My search for any contrary evidence comes up empty.

Therefore, the answer I will give starts by refuting the specific claim about seasonings with the salt-concentration argument, then acknowledges the general scaling pitfalls (imprecise volumetric measures, uneven cooking, evaporation) that probably gave rise to the myth, and finally clarifies that with precise weight-based recipes and adjusted technique, scaling works fine. I’ll structure it by first stating my conclusion on the nonsense of the claim, then explaining the science for salt, followed by the real scaling issues that cause confusion, and end with the conditions under which scaling is trouble-free.

content:
transfer pizza onto stone without sticking

After I have made my pizza and put the toppings onto it, I find that I am unable to transfer the pizza on to the pizza stone in the oven.

When I try to do it the pizza goes out of shape, gets folded, the toppings get messed up and sometimes it sticks or rips. I have tried putting lots of flour under the pizza before I add the toppings but it didn't really help.

I am having to make the pizza on a metal tray and then put the tray onto the stone. Put I think that doing this prevents my pizza base from crisping properly.

What am I doing wrong? Is there some technique I should use, or am making the dough to wet, or to thin or something?

I've worked as a pizza cook, so I can give you a hard-earned answer. Cornmeal, and plenty of it. If you aren't putting cornmeal (or flour, but cornmeal works better) on the peel before you put the pizza on it, start. If you are putting it on, use more. Then put the pizza on it and give it a shake and make sure the pizza is loose before you try to shove it in the oven. If it isn't, lift up the edge that is stuck and sprinkle more cornmeal under it, then try again. The pizza should be completely free-moving on the peel before you try to transfer it to the oven.
thinking: The user can't transfer a topped pizza from their prep surface to a hot stone without it deforming or sticking, and their current workaround with a metal tray sacrifices crispness. The core issue is friction between the raw dough and the transfer surface. They tried flour, but flour can absorb moisture from the dough and become gummy, actually increasing stickiness. The key is to use a release agent that doesn't absorb moisture and creates rolling, low-friction contact points. Cornmeal is the classic choice: its coarse, gritty texture acts like tiny ball bearings, and it doesn't absorb water the way flour does, so the dough slides easily. The technique matters too: you need a generous layer on the peel, build the pizza quickly to minimize sitting time (which lets moisture seep in), and then give the peel a quick back-and-forth shake to confirm the pizza moves freely before attempting the transfer. If any part sticks, lift that edge and dust more cornmeal under it. This ensures a clean launch onto the stone, allowing direct contact for proper bottom crisping. I'll structure the answer around cornmeal as the solution, the amount needed, the shake test, and the contrast with the tray method.

Why should a stock be simmered and not boiled?

Anthony Bourdain's *Les Halles* cookbook says that a stock should NEVER be boiled, why is this? Does the higher heat extract bitterness or something else undesirable?

It seems a little strange because the bones used to make the stock were previously roasted in a hot oven.

I've only made stock once, well I guess it was a broth (see [this post](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/2960/use-any-part-of-an-animal-for-making-stock-broth/2970#2970)) but would like to improve on my technique.

Well there's a few things.

First, higher temperatures mean more volatile aroma and flavour compounds will be released, leaving a flatter-tasting stock.

Second, boiling means more motion within the liquid, which makes it harder to skim off the protein scum which forms on the surface while a stock is cooking. In addition, some of the scum will just become reincorporated into the stock via a process similar to emulsion.

Third, boiling induces faster breakdown of proteins and other particulate matter, leaving you with a cloudier end product. This is of course of very little concern for stocks which will end up incorporated into (opaque) soups or sauces.

Of the three, only the first is of any real concern to home cooks. The other two issues aren't a huge deal at the restaurant level (modulo need for clarity in consomme etc), particularly if the restaurant uses Superbags or algae filtration for clarifying stocks.
thinking:
I need to understand why simmering is preferred over boiling for stock, and specifically address the user’s hunch that higher heat extracts bitterness. I recall the basic food science: boiling is around 212°F (100°C), while simmering is in the 180–200°F range. The difference isn’t just temperature intensity but also the physical agitation of the liquid. The user notes that bones were roasted, which might seem to contradict a fear of high heat, but roasting is a dry, high-heat process that develops flavor through browning, whereas boiling is a wet extraction that can disperse impurities differently.

I think through what happens during stock-making: collagen dissolves into gelatin, flavor compounds from bones and aromatics infuse the water, and proteins coagulate as scum. At a boil, the violent bubbling drives off volatile aromatic molecules, leading to a flatter taste — that’s a straightforward chemistry point. The agitation also continuously breaks up and redisperses the protein scum and fat, making it impossible to skim off impurities and potentially creating a cloudy emulsion. The user asked about bitterness; while bitterness isn’t a primary concern, overly harsh extraction of minerals or over-cooked vegetal notes can occur, but the main clarity and flavor issues are more immediate.

I consider that the user is a home cook with one broth attempt, so I should prioritize practical science. The answer should first address flavor loss through volatility, then explain the skimming problem and cloudiness, differentiating between home and restaurant concerns. The structure will be a short list of reasons, each with a brief explanation, and I’ll clarify that the first point — loss of delicate aromatics — is the most relevant for home cooking, while cloudiness is often irrelevant unless making consommé. I’ll note that boiling doesn’t necessarily create bitterness, but can lead to a muddied, less aromatic result. The presentation will be direct and helpful for technique improvement.

content:
Is there anything I can add to homemade bread to preserve it?

I love making our own bread - we rarely buy shop bought, but it tends to go off very quickly. Part of the appeal is that it doesn't have any "junk" in it - artificial preservatives - which I'm sure contributes to the lovely flavor. Is there anything natural I can add to it to stop it going moldy so fast?

My whole wheat bread takes 4x to go off than my white bread. Even a mixture of 50% whole wheat flour will make it last longer. But that will only help if the problem is the bread getting hard too soon. That can also be prevented by keeping it in a plastic bag. You'll get the mold before the bread goes stale.

If you're keeping the bread in a plastic bag, try paper bags.

To solve the mold problem, the traditional way is to add some acidity. For example, you can add a sourdough starter. If you don't like the taste of sourdough, a poolish starter should also help. The bacteria it grows will prevent the mold growing.

I know it's not what you're asking, but freezing will also help. When you bake more bread than you eat, freeze it wrapped in a plastic bag and thaw it overnight and you will get a good, fresh bread.
thinking:
The user is asking about natural ways to preserve homemade bread, specifically to keep it from going moldy quickly, without resorting to artificial preservatives. I need to separate the problem of bread staling (getting hard) from mold growth, because the solutions differ. I recall that whole wheat flour can actually help retard staling due to its bran and germ interfering with starch retrogradation, though some might think it goes stale faster—here the note about whole wheat lasting longer suggests the user’s issue might partly be texture, not just mold. I should clarify that.

Plastic bags trap moisture and delay staling, but that moisture can foster mold. If they’re already using plastic, switching to a paper bag might allow some air exchange to reduce surface moisture and slow mold, though it will go stale faster—a trade-off. For mold, the key traditional natural preservative is acidity. Sourdough fermentation produces lactic and acetic acid, lowering pH and creating an environment hostile to mold; I remember that sourdough breads have a much longer mold-free shelf life. Even if the user isn’t a fan of strong sourdough flavor, a poolish (a wet preferment) can also develop some beneficial bacterial activity during long, cool fermentation, albeit milder, which can still inhibit mold. I’ll mention that. Then there’s freezing, which isn’t an ingredient addition but the most foolproof natural preservation method—wrap well and store in the freezer, thawing as needed. So I’ll structure my response to first diagnose whether the problem is staling or molding, then suggest whole wheat flour or bag changes for texture, move on to natural fermentation for mold inhibition, and finally offer freezing as a practical, no-additive fallback. I’ll keep the tone conversational and helpful, avoiding any judgment.

How safe is steak tartare?

How safe is steak tartare?

What can I do when preparing it make sure it is safe to eat?

Butchered meat is generally sterile except on its exterior. (That doesn't mean parasite- or botulism-free, but it's a start.)

Get the best quality you can from a source you trust. Keep it at as low a temperature as possible, and don't expose it to warm air for more than the few minutes it takes to prepare.

Cut with a clean knife on a clean surface. Put it right back into the fridge at a very low temp.

Salt and acid, if you use them in your sauce, will provide some anti-bacterial benefits, but this is not foolproof.

People all over the world eat raw meat, but it's best to start with small amounts and see how your system handles it. If you're a child/pregnant/old/sick, it's much less of a good idea.
thinking:
The user is asking two things: how safe steak tartare is in general, and what steps can be taken during preparation to ensure it's safe to eat. To answer, I need to recall the core food-safety principles around raw meat, specifically beef. Whole muscle cuts of beef are typically contaminated only on their surface from the slaughter and butchering process; the interior is essentially sterile unless the meat has been penetrated. The main risks are pathogenic bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella on the exterior, plus possible parasites like tapeworm cysts or Toxoplasma gondii in the muscle tissue. Botulism spores aren’t a practical concern for fresh, properly handled beef. So the starting point is that tartare can be relatively safe if you start with a clean, high-quality piece of whole meat and prepare the surface properly.

Now, for the preparation steps: first, sourcing is critical. A trustworthy butcher who follows strict hygiene and handling practices reduces the initial bacterial load. Keeping the meat at very low temperatures from purchase through preparation inhibits bacterial growth; raw meat should stay below 40°F (4°C) and be exposed to room temperature only for the short time needed to trim and chop. I need to emphasize that the cutting board, knife, and any grinder must be spotlessly clean to avoid cross-contamination from other foods or from the meat’s own surface after trimming. After cutting, the tartare should be returned to the refrigerator immediately until serving.

I should also address the role of ingredients like salt and acid (lemon juice, vinegar, Worcestershire sauce). They do have some antimicrobial effects—salt binds water, reducing water activity, and acid lowers pH—but their effect is limited and works best as a secondary hurdle; they cannot make heavily contaminated meat safe. Finally, I should put the risk in context: raw meat is eaten in many cuisines, but individual digestive tolerance varies, and certain populations (pregnant women, young children, the elderly, and anyone with a compromised immune system) are at higher risk of severe illness from foodborne pathogens and should avoid it entirely.

The answer will open with the sterility point, then move through sourcing, temperature control, clean equipment, ingredient hurdles, and finally the caution about vulnerable groups. I’ll present it in a straightforward, practical tone without overstating the safety or the risks.

content:
Why do tomatoes get so hot?

Ever noticed how certain foods seem to get a lot hotter than others? I almost never burn my tongue or mouth... except on tomatoes; Pizza sauce, tomatoes in panini sandwiches or spaghetti sauce.

Tomatoes always seem to get hotter and retain their heat longer than almost any other food I've encountered. And they are nearly always the culprit when I succeed in burning my mouth.

Why would that be? Is there something about their chemistry that causes them to have a higher heat capacity? Do they hold their heat longer? Or is it simply a figment of my imagination and bad luck with hot tomatoes?

Another physics digression.

All cooked food gets hot, and everything in any given dish will have the same temperature {*}. The tomatoes *don't* get hotter than the other ingredients. But they *do* have a tendency to burn more than certain other substances, so the question is "Why?".

You get burned when a portion of your flesh reaches a high enough temperature{+}. The food warms your tongue, lips, etc. by heat conduction until either you move the food or your mouth parts and the food reach the same temperature (a condition known as thermal equilibrium). What that common temperature is depends on the amount of *heat* (i.e. thermal energy) in the system. Some of the factors that come into play are:

- How much (*mass* of) food there is.
- How much (*mass* of) your mouth is involved (see below).
- The initial temperature of the food.
- The "heat capacity" of both the food and your mouth parts, which is a property of each substance that appears as a coefficient in the thermal equilibrium equation. (Don't worry, I'm not going to make you read any math.) Water has a (very!) high heat capacity, so watery foods tend to drive high final temperature and thus to burn you more easily. There is an added complication for the extra heat needed to establish a phase change (i.e. melt solids or vaporize liquids) called the heat of fusion or heat of vaporization. Again water has a high value for both of these numbers.

How fast the common temperature is reached depends on

- The area of contact between the food and the mouth.
- Another coefficient called the thermal conductivity. This one is complicated, but liquids tend to have a high thermal conductivity and solids less so. This is where soups, sauces, and melted cheese really get you. Note that your mouth parts has a pretty low thermal conductivity, so you only get to count the surface layers in finding the equilibrium temperature. Sorry.

Some consequences of all this:

- This is why you can peel the aluminum foil off of a pan that has just come out of a 400 degree (F) oven without trouble, but if you get your hand stuck in the steam plume (which is only around 212 degrees F) you get scalded: Aluminum has a low heat capacity, and steam has a (very, very!) high one.
- Small bites help in two ways: less total heat means a lower common temperature, and may allow you to move the food around in your mouth, reducing the temperature of any one part.
- Some foods are just dangerous this way. You know what they are from experience: steam, hot soups and sauces, melted cheese, etc.

{*} Well, sort of. But take that as true for any particular region of any particular dish.  
{+} What temperature is that? Good question. Maybe there is a medical professional around, 'cause I don't know. I'd guess around 140--150 degrees F (call it 60--65 degrees C), but don't quote me.
thinking:
The user is asking why tomatoes—especially in the form of pizza sauce, panini fillings, or spaghetti sauce—seem to burn the mouth more frequently than other foods, despite all parts of a dish being at the same temperature. This is a common experiential puzzle that can be explained with basic food-science physics. I need to untangle the misconception that tomatoes “get hotter” and instead focus on why they transfer heat so effectively to the mouth, causing burns. 

First, the core misunderstanding is about temperature versus heat content. In a mixed dish, all components reach roughly the same temperature during cooking, so the sauce or tomato slice isn’t actually hotter than the pasta or bread. The difference lies in how much thermal energy they carry per gram and how quickly they release that energy into the tongue. I’ll recall key thermal properties: water has a very high specific heat capacity (about 4.18 J/g°C), meaning watery foods—like tomatoes, which are >90% water—store more heat energy at a given temperature than less moist ingredients. That stored heat then has to be dumped into the mouth tissues when contact occurs, potentially raising the tissue temperature to a damaging level despite the food not being hotter initially.

Next, thermal conductivity matters. Liquids and semi-solids (sauce, melted cheese, tomato pieces in sauce) have higher thermal conductivity than solid, drier foods like bread crust or meat chunks. So the heat rushes into the mouth’s surface layers faster, reaching a tissue-damaging temperature before you can react. The high water content also means the food can maintain a higher final equilibrium temperature with the mouth because the tissue (which has its own heat capacity) can’t absorb all that energy quickly enough without itself heating up. Moreover, sauces cling to the palate or tongue, increasing contact time and area, which amplifies the burn. This is analogous to why steam (also water) scalds worse than dry hot air at the same temperature.

I also need to acknowledge the user’s observation about “retaining heat longer.” That’s partly a result of the higher heat capacity—more energy needs to dissipate for the food to cool down—and partly a perceptual effect: because the burn already happened, any lingering warmth feels hazardous. So, it’s not a figment of the imagination; tomatoes in saucy forms really do pose a higher burn risk. The response should correct the misconception, then break down the physics in an accessible way, tying back to everyday examples like foil vs. steam. The structure will start with a clear thesis that temperature isn’t the issue, then list the contributing factors (heat capacity, conductivity, adhesion), and finally give practical takeaways and safety notes. The tone will be conversational but informed, just as in the provided final answer.

content:
How to succeed with making omelette

Sounds simple but I seem to fail every time, that is it turns into scrambled eggs instead. How do you make it so that you can flip it over both without it breaking and before it burns?

This depends on which type of omelet you want to make, I'll run through the three types I know how to make.

The thick Waffle House style omelet (it's the kind that poofs up and is about an inch thick all the way around, IHOP also serves this omelet) is achieved by beating the eggs and incorporating a LOT of air in to the mixture. Restaurants do this by using a milkshake machine to whip the eggs. This type of omelet is easy to flip and cook, you just put enough butter to coat the pan, pour off any excess and then pour your egg mixture in to the pan (you are going to have to use an omelet pan for this). Let the omelet cook while occasionally swirling the pan in a circular motion. When the omelet has cooked most of the way through flip by either the toss in the air and catch in the pan method (not for beginners!) or the fork and spatula method (place spatula underneath and hold omelet onto the spatula with a fork on one corner). This will yield a thick fluffy omelet but it can be hard to work enough air into the eggs at home.

The second type is the French omelet and it doesn't require flipping at all. The french omelet is what you see in fine dining brunches if you see it at all in the U.S. This omelette is made by mixing your eggs and pouring the mixture into a medium low heat pan. As it cooks you take a fork and pull the cooked egg off the bottom and into the center of the omelet. [Here is a video that goes more in depth](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VxSQBaknmqo&feature=related).

The third type is what I call the grandma omelet. It's made in a frying pan instead of an omelet pan and features a fairly flat egg wrapped around some cheese and other toppings. For this omelet you need medium heat. You should coat the pan with butter and pour in the egg mixture to a heated pan. Let cook for a minute or two, then swirl the uncooked egg to the outside of the pan use a fork to lift the very edge to allow the uncooked egg to take the place of the cooked next to the pan. Let the egg cook till desired doneness (side note: your omelet should and will have a small amount of uncooked but heated egg, it should be not runny, but still not be entirely set) and add toppings and fold over. Then serve.

To address your scrambled egg problem, you need to let the egg set more before attempting the flip and lowering the heat on your pan will take care of the burning. Just remember that eggs are extremely delicate and respond better to lower heat and close attention.

Also the names are just the ones I use in my head, if somebody knows the correct terminology, let me know and I'll update to reflect it.
thinking:
The user is describing a common frustration: eggs intended to be an omelette end up as scrambled eggs, and they specifically want to know how to flip without breaking or burning. I need to diagnose why that happens. The scrambling likely comes from moving the eggs too much or too early — before a solid enough skin of cooked egg forms on the bottom to hold the mass together. Burning while waiting for it to set points to heat that’s too high. So the first instinct is to say: let the egg set more, and lower the heat. But the answer can be more helpful if I recognize that “how to flip” depends entirely on the style of omelette they’re attempting. I recall there are several major omelette techniques, and some don’t even require a flip at all, which sidesteps the problem.

I’ll structure the advice by describing three distinct styles I know from my own cooking experience. For a thick, fluffy American diner-style omelette (what I informally call the Waffle House style), aeration is key — beating a lot of air in gives it structure, making it easier to handle. The flip still requires confidence or tools, but the airy mixture is more forgiving if the heat is moderate and you wait until it’s mostly cooked through. For a French omelette, there is no dangerous flip: you use low heat and continuously push cooked curds to the center, eventually rolling it out of the pan. This completely avoids the flipping issue. For a simple flat “grandma” style (basically a country omelette cooked in a frying pan), you lift the edges to let raw egg flow underneath, then fold it over without any aerial flip. Each of these addresses the breaking problem in its own way.
