White pepper vs. black pepper

Other than color, what is the difference between white pepper and black pepper? I thought it was purely a color thing so that black pepper wouldn't ruin the color of, say, a white sauce. We tried white pepper in a few dishes and in all cases, they were wretched. (FWIW: one recipe was Alfredo sauce.) The only things I can come up with are:

- There is a substantial difference between the 2 and we apparently do not like white pepper
- There is not a substantial difference but we got a bad batch of white pepper
- There may or may not be a difference, but the recipes we tried should not have included this spice

Which is correct?

They don't taste identical at all, and even more important, they don't smell the same. White pepper has a distinct "barnyard" odor. People do indeed use them when black flecks might be unpleasant, but in most cases I'd rather go pepperless or just live with the color.
thinking:
The user is asking specifically about the flavor difference between white and black pepper, not just color. They had a bad experience using white pepper and suspect either a fundamental taste difference, a bad batch, or that the recipe shouldn't have included it. They want to know which is correct.

I recall that black and white peppercorns come from the same plant, Piper nigrum. The difference lies in processing. Black pepper is made from unripe green drupes that are cooked briefly and dried with the skin on, which develops its pungency and a complex, sharp, slightly floral aroma.

White pepper comes from fully ripe berries that are soaked (retted) in water to remove the outer pericarp, then the inner seed is dried. This fermentation step produces a very different flavor profile—earthy, musty, with a distinct "barnyard" or even cheesy note, due to compounds like skatole and other fermentation byproducts. So there is a substantial chemical difference in aroma and taste, not just color.

Given that, the user's bad experience is likely because they were expecting a neutral pepper flavor just without black flecks, and instead got hit with that barnyard note. A delicate cream-based Alfredo sauce would amplify that musty flavor, making it seem "wretched." It's not a bad batch necessarily (though low-quality white pepper can be even more funky), it's that white pepper genuinely tastes different, and the recipes may have called for it for color reasons without the cook realizing how much it would alter the flavor. The third option—that recipes should not have included it—is a matter of taste, but the fundamental error was treating them as interchangeable.

I can structure the answer by first clarifying that they are not simply color variants, then explaining the processing difference and the resulting "barnyard" aroma, and finally noting that while it is used to avoid black specks, the flavor is so distinct that many would prefer to omit it. I'll avoid repeating the exact phrasing of the final answer but will build toward that same conclusion.The core of the question is why white pepper made dishes “wretched” when the cook assumed it differed only in color. To reason forward, I need to establish that the processing of white versus black pepper creates genuinely distinct flavor profiles, not merely visual differences.

Black pepper is produced from unripe green peppercorns that are briefly cooked and dried with their dark outer skin intact, which preserves sharp, pungent, and mildly floral volatile compounds. White pepper starts from fully ripe berries, which are soaked for days to ferment away the outer husk, leaving the pale inner seed. That fermentation step introduces new aromatic molecules—most notably skatole and related compounds—that give white pepper a characteristic musty, earthy, “barnyard” smell completely absent from black pepper. The difference is chemical, not cosmetic.

The user’s experience with Alfredo sauce makes sense: a delicate cream-based sauce would amplify that funky note, making it taste foul to someone expecting a clean, neutral pepper heat. It’s unlikely to be just a bad batch, because the off-putting quality they describe aligns perfectly with white pepper’s inherent flavor. The idea that the recipes shouldn’t have included it touches on the real issue: many cooks reach for white pepper only to avoid black flecks, without considering how much it changes the dish’s flavor. Ultimately, the surprising taste is the primary explanation.

I plan to structure the response by immediately stating they taste totally different, then explaining the processing and the resulting “barnyard” odor, and finally noting the common visual-only justification while sharing a personal preference to avoid that flavor.

content:
Is it safe to eat a cooked steak that (briefly) touched the plate that was holding the raw meat?

So I just finished preparing a perfect-looking steak, and as per usual, my apartment's hypersensitive smoke detector decided to go off. Not wanting to put the steak back into the pan, in one brilliant flash of boneheadedness, while I was scrambling for a rag to start whipping away the smoke, I dropped the steak in the only other vessel that was on the countertop - the same plate that was holding the meat before I cooked it.

I figured that since the *inside* has already been cooked, I could probably just sear the outside again on high heat for about 30 seconds to kill any surface bacteria that it might have picked up. Which I did. Doesn't really look any the worse for wear, but I haven't totally convinced myself that this is safe.

Anyone run into this scenario before and survived it? Is there anything else I can do to guarantee safety without totally ruining the steak?

If you're at all like me, you are reassured by hard numbers and measurables. This should help.

In this situation one of the likely pathogens would be one of the *Salmonella* species. *Salmonella* is killed by temperatures in excess of 130 F (55 C). However, it's not an *instant* death. The time to kill *Salmonella* decreases exponentially as the temperature increases.

The following table represents all the temperature and duration to kill 99.9999% of the most heat-resistant strain *Salmonella senftenberg*. This species is as much as 30x more heat resistant than a "normal" *S. typhimurium*.

```
   Temperature | Time
---------------|------
 140 F (60 C)  | 60m
 150 F (65 C)  | 10m
 160 F (70 C)  | <2m
```

For any given temperature the proportion of bacteria killed is constant. 1/6th the time kills 90%, 1/3rd kills 99%, 1/2 kills 99.9% etc.

USDA guidelines to kill *Salmonella* and *E. Coli* are as follows:

```
   Temperature | Time
---------------|------
 135 F (57 C)  | 86.4m
 140 F (60 C)  | 8.6m
 145 F (63 C)  | 2.7m
 150 F (65 C)  | 51.9s
 160 F (70 C)  | < 6s
 165 F (74 C)  | < 2s
```

So, needless to say, re-searing your steak at a typically high stove top temperature (at least 300 F [149 C]) for even a fraction of a second will result in utter devastation to whatever beastie population you may have picked up in recontaminating your meat. Chances are, if the steak came *hot* out of the pan, and you removed it from the plate quickly, the residual heat alone would be enough to kill it. The re-sear certainly doesn't hurt though.

A good rule of thumb is to wash plates as you go. If this is not possible or convenient you should minimally *remove* the plate from your vicinity by putting it in the sink or dishwasher as soon as you have taken the food off of it.
thinking:
The question describes a common kitchen mishap: a cooked steak briefly touched a plate that held raw meat, then was quickly re-seared. The core concern is whether the re-sear is sufficient to eliminate any pathogens that may have transferred from the raw meat juices. To address this, I need to recall the relevant food-safety microbiology and heat-transfer principles.

First, raw meat surfaces often carry bacteria like *Salmonella* and *E. coli*. These are killed by heat, but the kill rate depends on temperature and time—not an instantaneous process, but exponentially faster at higher temperatures. The steak’s interior was already cooked, so the only potential recontamination is on the surface.

Second, I recall that typical pan-searing temperatures are far above 300°F (150°C), well into the range where pathogen-kill times are measured in seconds or fractions of a second. Even a brief 30-second sear will rapidly bring the surface temperature above 165°F (74°C), where USDA guidelines indicate *Salmonella* and *E. coli* are killed in under two seconds. The residual heat from the just-cooked steak may have already begun that process before the pan was even applied, but the re-sear guarantees it.

Third, I should consider whether the steak’s surface could have dried or formed a slight crust from the initial cook, reducing how much liquid it could pick up from the plate, but even if wet, the subsequent heat treatment is decisive. The practical advice about washing or removing the raw-meat plate is a helpful safety habit that addresses the root cause.

With that science in mind, I plan to structure the answer by presenting the time-temperature kill data in a clear table, then logically applying it to the described scenario—showing that the re-sear far exceeds the lethal conditions for any transferred bacteria. I’ll close with the reassurance that this is safe and a simple rule to avoid the situation.

Pasta: is simmering equivalent to roiling boil?

I recently got into a surprisingly heated argument with a friend about what level of boil you should cook your pasta at. He (an engineer) argued that the heat transfer would remain the same regardless of the level of the boil and that anything above a simmer would be a waste of energy. I looked at it less from a heat transfer point of view and argued that a higher boil would increase agitation and cause the noodles to stick less to each other.

So what is it? Is a higher boil actually a waste of (a minuscule amount of) energy?

You should boil noodles. Simmering is *not* the same as boiling. Boiling water is 212 ℉ (100 ℃). Simmering water is in the range of 185 ℉ to 200 ℉ (85 ℃ to 93 ℃).

Your engineer friend is under the mistaken assumption that simmering is somehow a weaker boil than a rolling boil, but still 212 ℉. It's not.

You are correct in your assumption that the more vigorous rolling boil will agitate pasta and help prevent sticking.
thinking:
The question hinges on a common misconception about what "simmering" means. Many people, including the engineer friend, assume simmering is just a less vigorous version of a boil, with the water still at 212 ℉ (100 ℃). But in cooking terminology, simmering is a distinct temperature range—typically 185 ℉ to 200 ℉ (85 ℃ to 93 ℃)—well below the boiling point. So the first thing to correct is that simmering water is not 212 ℉ with fewer bubbles; it’s literally cooler water. That alone means the heat transfer to the pasta will be slower, and cooking time will be longer. The engineer’s argument that heat transfer remains the same regardless of boil level only holds if the water temperature is the same, which it isn’t.

Then there’s the agitation factor. In a rolling boil, the violent bubbling creates constant movement that physically separates pasta strands or pieces, reducing the chance they stick together. Simmering, with its much gentler movement, won’t provide that same mechanical anti-stick action. So the questioner’s intuition about sticking is spot-on—it’s not just about heat transfer but about the physical dynamics of the water.

The energy waste argument also falls apart under scrutiny. Even if a rolling boil uses a little more energy to maintain the higher temperature, the faster cooking might offset that because the pot is on the heat for less time. But the deeper flaw is the misunderstanding of simmering’s temperature, so the whole premise is shaky.

I’ll structure the response by first clearly defining the temperature difference, then explaining why that matters for cooking speed and sticking, and finally acknowledging that the questioner’s agitation point is correct while the engineer’s energy claim is based on a false assumption.

As per the question - how to I test that a knife is sharp enough?  
And/or, how do you know when a knife needs sharpening?

---

### Edit:

Yesterday I attempted (I feel quite successfully) to hone my knives for the first time ever (requiring me to purchase a honing steel), which immediately made a rather noticable difference (I shall be honing them regularly from now on).

Not sure whether additionally sharpening them as well would be a good idea?

The suggested tomato and paper tests make sense, and I shall try them in the near future and see..

I usually notice when cutting onions and tomatoes. With a very sharp knife cutting an onion doesn't cause much tears at all. What is the purpose of creaming butter with sugar in cookie recipes?

I got distracted while assembling the dry ingredients for a cookie recipe and added the sugars, which were supposed to be creamed with the butter first. Fortunately, the sugar was added last and I was able to salvage enough to cream it.

What does creaming the butter and sugar actually do? Had it been on the bottom of the bowl under the flour etc, could I have just beat everything together?

The recipe is simple and just calls for creaming and then adding egg, and after that, dry ingredients. It's nothing fancy.

Creaming puts the air bubbles into the mixture. The baking powder only helps enlarge the bubbles, not make them. In cookies the creaming plays another essential role, which is to help dissolve the sugar. To [cream the butter keep it cool and do it for a few minutes](http://www.nytimes.com/2008/12/17/dining/17bake.html) (at 65°F, harder in the summer).

It has [recently been discovered](http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/jf990435+) that cookie dough is different from cake batters. Sugar is part of the structure of the cookie and not just a sweetener, tenderizer, and browning agent. It forms the base upon which the fats and the starch granules of the flour are embedded. The sugar needs to dissolve for the matrix to form.

If you beat the whole thing, it will be harder to get bubbles in and you may end up overworking the dough. The cookies will end up flat and tough.
thinking:
The question is about the fundamental purpose of creaming butter and sugar in cookie recipes, sparked by a real-world mixing mishap. I need to unpack the food science behind this technique, particularly for cookies, where it plays a more complex role than simply mixing ingredients. First, I recall that creaming is not just about combining; it’s a mechanical process that incorporates air. When solid butter and crystalline sugar are beaten together, the sharp sugar edges cut into the fat, creating countless tiny air pockets. These bubbles act as nuclei for any chemical leavening (baking powder/soda) to enlarge during baking, giving lift and a tender crumb. Without this initial aeration, the final texture would be dense.

However, the asker’s cookie recipe is “nothing fancy,” and cookies behave differently from cakes. I remember a key piece of food science: sugar in cookies isn’t just a sweetener or tenderizer; it forms part of the physical structure. There’s that 1999 study revealing that sugar must dissolve and later set into a glassy matrix that holds the fat and starch granules together. Creaming begins that dissolution by working the sugar into the butter’s small water content and fat phase, starting the formation of that structural syrup. If the sugar isn’t properly dissolved via creaming, the crystals remain large and don’t melt uniformly during baking, weakening the cookie’s internal scaffold and causing excessive spread and a tough, gritty texture.

Now, to the direct question: had the sugar been at the bottom of the bowl mixed with flour, could they just beat everything together? That would bypass the creaming step entirely. If you start by beating butter into a flour-sugar mixture, the flour coats the fat immediately, inhibiting air incorporation because the butter particles are separated by dry ingredients and can’t trap air as effectively. The sugar crystals are also coated, slowing dissolution. Plus, overbeating to compensate would develop gluten from the flour, making the dough tough. So the cookies would likely spread flat and turn out hard and chewy in the wrong way. The answer should first clarify the dual purpose (aeration and sugar dissolution), then highlight the cookie-specific structural role of sugar, and finally explain why mixing everything at once would fail, tying it back to the user’s scenario. I’ll structure the response by starting with the air-bubble explanation, moving to the sugar-structure insight, and concluding with why the all-in-one beating would yield poor results, referencing the necessity of deliberate creaming.The purpose of creaming butter and sugar in cookie recipes is twofold: it aerates the dough and helps dissolve the sugar. When you beat butter and crystalline sugar together, the sharp sugar creates tiny air pockets in the fat. These air bubbles act as nucleation sites for any baking powder or soda, allowing the cookies to rise and develop a tender crumb. Without this aeration, the final texture would be dense and flat.

In cookies specifically, sugar plays a structural role beyond just sweetness or browning. Research shows that sugar must partially dissolve to form a syrup-like matrix that holds the fat and starch granules together. Creaming initiates this dissolution by working the sugar into the butter’s moisture and fat, ensuring the sugar melts uniformly during baking and sets into a glassy framework. If this step is skipped, the sugar crystals remain too large, leading to excessive spread, poor structure, and a tough, gritty texture.

Had you beaten everything together—flour, sugar, butter—you would have gotten poor results. The flour would coat the butter immediately, blocking its ability to trap air, and the sugar would stay coated and undissolved. Beating longer to compensate would overwork the gluten, making the cookies tough and flat. For a proper cookie structure, the creaming step is essential.

How to rest meat but not let it get too cold?

Having read [this question](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/623/why-should-i-rest-meat-after-cooking) I am persuaded that resting meat is good for its flavour. But if the meat has a good temperature straight after it's been cooked, it seems as though it will be too cold after resting it for a few minutes.

How do you rest meat in such a way that it is not too cold for eating?

Straight after it comes out of the pan it will usually be too hot to eat. Regardless of resting or not, you can't fully taste things which are too hot, they need to come down to a comfortable temperature before you eat them.

Some things you can do to stop the meat being too cold when you serve it:

- You can rest the meat wrapped in foil, this will stop it from getting too cool too quickly if you are not ready to serve once its had the time to rest.
- you can rest it and then warm it again before you eat it, either under a hot grill for a little, or in an oven.
- serve it with a hot sauce which will warm the meat
- serve it on a warmed plate which will stop it cooling more too quickly on the table

Although I think you are worrying too much about nothing IMHO. Even once rested the meat will still be at a good temperature, especially as you have not cut it yet and most of the heat will be retained in the middle of the meat.
thinking:
The user’s concern is that rested meat will be cold. My first thought is that they might be overlooking how hot the meat actually is when it first finishes cooking. Straight from the pan or oven, the surface can be dangerously hot, and the internal temperature is often above the ideal eating range. Scientifically, our ability to taste flavors is blunted at very high temperatures, so food needs to cool somewhat to be enjoyable. Resting inherently brings it to a more comfortable temperature.

But the question is how to actively prevent it from becoming unpleasantly cold during that rest. I recall that in kitchens, meat is often tented loosely with foil—it traps some heat but still allows steam to escape, so the surface doesn’t get soggy. That slows down the cooling rate significantly. Another approach is to rest it uncovered and then briefly reheat it before serving: a minute under a hot broiler or in an oven brings the exterior back up without overcooking the center. Warm sauces can also contribute thermal energy to the plate. Finally, a warmed plate is a classic restaurant technique to prevent the food from losing heat the moment it’s served.

Beyond those tricks, the meat’s thermal mass works in our favor. As long as it remains whole, the center retains a great deal of heat, and conduction continues to warm the outer layers even during resting. So in practice, after a typical rest of 5–10 minutes, the meat is still comfortably warm. I’ll structure the answer to first correct the starting-temperature assumption, then offer those practical measures, and end with a reassurance that it usually isn’t a problem.

content:
Does it matter what kind of sugar is used in baking?

The baking recipes I use specify many kinds of sugar e.g. caster, raw, white, soft etc.

Generally, I always just use raw sugar, mainly for convenience.

Does it really make a difference?

Yes!

Sugar is often used as a "wet" ingredient in baking. That means it needs to be dissolved in the water in order to prevent too much gluten from being produced (making the result fluffy/flaky, and not chewy). Different sugars hold different amounts of moisture (for example, brown sugar holds more than white) and using sugar with crystals that are too large (or too small) will make the texture come out completely wrong. Too small and your cake will be rubber; too large and your biscuit will fall apart.

Also, if you're using the sugar for creaming (with fat), you generally need to use a coarser sugar. Superfine sugar will dissolve too quickly and won't allow enough air to be incorporated. Confectioner's sugar is good for creaming but has completely different properties from crystal sugar - it's been "processed" and has cornstarch added, so you can't just substitute in equal quantities.

Of course, it goes without saying that the taste is different as well. But even more important than the taste are the solubility characteristics which, as explained above, will have noticeable effects on other parts of the recipe.

It does depend what you're baking; if the sugar is being used purely for flavouring, then you can use whatever sugar you like. Much of the time in baking though, sugar is used for more than just sweetening, and it's important to be aware of that. If the sugar is being creamed or dissolved, don't substitute unless you're sure you know what you're doing.
thinking: I need to consider what the user is really asking: they default to raw sugar as a one-size-fits-all substitution, so they want to know if that’s undermining their baking. At first glance, I might think it’s just about sweetness level or minor color differences, but then I remember sugar plays several functional roles in baked goods beyond taste—solubility, moisture retention, gluten interference, and creaming aeration. Raw sugar has large, coarse crystals and a bit of molasses; caster sugar is finely ground to dissolve fast; brown sugar has high moisture from molasses; confectioner’s sugar often contains cornstarch. If the recipe uses sugar dissolved in liquid, undissolved coarse crystals could leave a gritty texture and fail to limit gluten development, making cakes tough or rubbery. Conversely, using too fine a sugar where aeration is needed (creaming) could make the mixture collapse because it dissolves before trapping air. The “wet” ingredient concept—where dissolved sugar acts like a liquid to inhibit gluten—makes crystal size crucial: too small and too much dissolves too quickly, promoting gluten over-tenderizing; too large and not enough dissolves, leading to chewiness. For creaming, coarser sugar’s sharp edges cut pockets in the fat; superfine won’t do that. So I’ll structure the response to first confirm yes, it matters, then explain the moisture/solubility angle with crystal size effects, then address creaming and confectioner’s sugar differences, note taste is secondary, and finally add the caveat that it depends on the sugar’s role in the recipe—if it’s just flavoring, substitution might be fine, but when sugar is structural, know what you’re doing.

content:
Why not put knives in the dishwasher?

What is it about the dishwasher that harms knives?

The only reasons I've found are:

- You could get cut... I personally have a greater change of getting cut by trying to wash them by hand.
- The blades can damage the plastic-coated metal shelves... so I put them in the silverware-holder instead of on the rack (it's 100% plastic, no metal).
- The blade could get nicked by being knocked into other silverware... so put the blade by itself in a section of the silverware-holder in the DW.

Expensive knives can survive a trip through the dishwasher, but like others have mentioned, they can bump into things, end up with coatings of detergents and such, suffer damage to wood, etc. Why would you do that to an investment?

Cheaper knives will just straight out rust/corrode, even if you remove them and dry them right after the cycle. Yeah, you can scrub it off, but you're also losing metal from the blade, possibly starting rust in areas you can't dry, and generally degrading the knives.
thinking:
The user is asking why dishwashers harm knives, having already considered and dismissed some commonly cited reasons—personal injury from sharp blades, damage to dishwasher racks, and nicking from other utensils. They've proposed workarounds like placing knives in the plastic silverware basket, alone. So they're really asking: beyond those physical collision risks, what is it about the dishwasher *environment* itself that causes damage? I need to explain the chemical and thermal processes that degrade knife materials, even when the knife is safely isolated from impacts.

First, I recall the key factors: dishwasher detergents are highly alkaline (high pH) and often contain abrasive particles, bleach, and rinse aids. The combination of high heat, prolonged moisture, and these chemicals attacks metals and handle materials. For knife blades, even those labeled stainless, the high pH can strip away the passive chromium oxide layer that prevents rust, leaving the metal vulnerable. The intense heat and moisture also cause thermal expansion and contraction, which can loosen handles, especially wood, and get water into tiny crevices between blade and handle, initiating corrosion you can't wipe away. Cheap knives often use lower-grade stainless steel with less chromium and more carbon, or even non-stainless steels, which rust easily in such conditions. Even if you pull them out immediately after the cycle, microscopic rust can start in areas where water has wicked in.

Expensive knives may be made of higher-quality stainless (like VG-10, X50CrMoV15) that resists corrosion better, but the harsh detergent can still cause pitting, clouding, or dulling of the edge over time. Wooden handles soak up water and swell, eventually cracking or loosening rivets. The drying cycle's intense heat exacerbates all of this. So the answer is that physical damage from bumping is real, but the core issue is the chemical and thermal assault that degrades the blade and handle, making the knife lose its edge, rust, or fall apart prematurely.

I'll structure the response by first acknowledging the user's points, then explaining the hidden mechanisms: detergent chemistry, heat and moisture, effects on cheap vs. expensive knives, and why even careful dishwasher placement can't avoid these problems. I'll conclude by framing it as a risk to an investment, as the final answer does.To answer this, I need to get past the obvious collision risks and focus on what the dishwasher environment itself does to knife materials. The user has already dismissed cut hazards and physical nicks by suggesting safe placement, so the real question is about chemical and thermal damage.

I recall that dishwasher detergents are highly alkaline, often with a pH of 11 or 12, and contain aggressive agents like sodium hydroxide and bleach. Combined with the heat (typically 130–170°F) and prolonged moisture, this environment attacks even stainless steel. The high pH can strip away the chromium oxide layer that makes steel "stainless," exposing the iron to water and oxygen and causing rust or pitting. The heat also accelerates chemical reactions and thermal expansion, which can break down adhesives in handles, swell and crack wood, and allow water to wick into microscopic gaps between the blade and handle—places no towel can reach after the cycle.

Cheap knives usually use lower-grade steel (like 420 stainless or even carbon steel) with less chromium or more impurities; they rust quickly even after a single cycle, and the rust can start in crevices where it's impossible to dry. Expensive knives made from higher-chromium alloys are more resistant, but repeated exposure to harsh detergents can still cause edge dulling from micro-pitting, water spots that require abrasive polishing, and cumulative damage to handle materials. The physical bumping the user is avoiding is secondary to all of this.

I'll structure the response by first acknowledging the user's specific points, then explaining the dishwasher's chemical and thermal attacks, the difference between knife qualities, and why even careful placement can't protect against corrosion and handle degradation. That leads logically to the final answer's framing: it's a needless risk to an investment, especially for cheap blades that outright rust.The user has already considered and dismissed the risk of cuts, rack damage, and blade-to-blade nicking by proposing to isolate the knife in a plastic basket. Therefore, the core of the question is: what else in the dishwasher environment causes harm, even without physical collisions? I need to think about the chemical and thermal processes that affect knife materials.

Dishwasher detergents are strongly alkaline (pH around 11–12), often containing bleach, caustics, and abrasives. This chemical bath, combined with the sustained high heat of the wash and dry cycles (typically 130–170°F), corrodes and degrades metals and handles. Even stainless steel relies on a thin, passive chromium oxide layer to resist rust; the harsh alkaline and oxidative environment can strip that layer, opening the door to pitting, rust spots, and dulling of the cutting edge. Wooden handles swell from water absorption, then shrink and crack from the drying heat, loosening rivets or causing the handle to separate from the tang. Water also wicks into the microscopic gap where the blade meets the handle, initiating rust you can never wipe dry.

Cheap knives are typically made from lower-grade stainless with less chromium or even high-carbon steels that are not truly stainless; they rust rapidly, sometimes after a single cycle, and the rust can develop in crevices where it's impossible to remove without grinding away metal. Expensive knives use more corrosion-resistant alloys, but even they can suffer from micro-pitting that degrades the edge and water spots that require abrasive cleaning, slowly thinning the blade. The physical isolation from other utensils doesn't protect against this chemical and thermal assault, which is the real reason the dishwasher harms knives. I'll structure the response by acknowledging the user's specific points, then explaining the dishwasher's chemical and thermal damage mechanisms, and finally distinguishing the effects on cheap versus expensive knives to justify the final answer's conclusion about protecting an investment.

Nonstick cookware or not?

I am looking to replace my >10 year old Calphalon nonstick cookware. I can see the nonstick surface coming off the pans, and am starting to worry about how much of that is getting into our food.

I love the ease of cleaning nonstick cookware, but am wary of buying it again. Should I opt for nonstick or not?

I'm with @Ward -- I like being able to scour my pans for those times when even [deglazing](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/261/how-do-you-clean-a-cast-iron-skillet/509#509) doesn't work. I'd say to look at replacing your set bit by bit -- which items do you cook that really need non-stick, and what pan do you cook it in? Maybe replace your more beat-up items with something not non-stick, try cooking with it, and see how well you like cooking with them -- it's possible that you won't like it, and it'd be better to be out the cost of only a piece or two than a whole set. You could even try out a few different materials -- cast iron, stainless, anodized aluminum, etc.

It also might take a little time to get used to cooking with out the non-stick. One mistake I've seen people make is not giving their pans enough time to pre-heat. (I think it was the Frugal Gourmet who'd say "Hot pan, cold food, food won't stick" ... which isn't entirely true, but you'll have much less problems with a hot pan).

content:
When is a cooking oil not appropriate to substitute for another?

Frequently recipes call for a particular kind of oil for making use of certain characteristics (taste, heat tolerance, health, etc.). It's well known you can substitute cooking oils in most cases (vegetable oil for canola oil).

Are there circumstances in which it is *not* appropriate to substitute cooking oils?

Actually, there are really only a few oils you *can* substitute for each other, at least without any significant side effects.

The oils which generally *are* used interchangeably are peanut oil, canola/rapeseed oil, and sunflower oil. These oils have similar smoke points, don't impart any really noticeable flavour, and tend to be used primarily for high-heat cooking (pan-frying, deep-frying), so if you're paranoid about saturated fat for instance, you can substitute sunflower oil for peanut oil. Corn oil is in the same group, but I rarely see that used anymore. You can also use the "light" olive oil, but that *will* change the flavour of the dish. I *believe* walnut oil has similar properties, but it's considerably harder to find.

But keep in mind that oils are used for far more than frying. Many have highly-specialized uses:

- Extra virgin olive oil is most commonly used in sauces and salad dressings ("oil and vinegar" almost always means olive oil, there really is no substitute);
- Chili oil is really more of a condiment than a cooking oil. Even if you could cook with it, the result would be inedible due to the heat.
- Toasted sesame oil is used as a flavourings in Asian dishes. It's useless as a cooking oil (and cooking with it would be a terrible waste). *Regular* sesame oil, on the other hand, is often bought in a refined form and **is** generally used as a cooking oil.
- There are a lot of other more esoteric types of oil such as palm oil and coconut oil, which you really don't want to use unless you know what you're doing (you can ruin the flavour).

I could go on, but for now I'll refer you to the [Types of oils and their characteristics](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooking_oil#Types_of_oils_and_their_characteristics) as a starting point. Cooking oils really **aren't** freely interchangeable in all situations; even if you've accounted for smoke point and flavour, sometimes a significantly different fat content (i.e. grapeseed oil which is mostly polyunsaturated vs. canola oil which is mostly monounsaturated) can seriously mess up a delicate recipe.

It's better to be asking which oils you **can** substitute in a specific situation than to assume everything goes and list the "exceptional" circumstances.
thinking:
I need to think about what the question is really asking: it assumes that cooking oils are generally interchangeable, and wants to know the exceptions. But my knowledge of cooking says that’s backwards—most oils have distinct roles, and only a handful are truly neutral enough to substitute for one another without affecting the dish. First, I recall the key properties that determine whether an oil can substitute: smoke point (for high-heat cooking), flavor profile (neutral vs. pronounced), and fat composition (which affects texture and health claims). I think of the common oils used for frying: peanut, canola, sunflower, and sometimes corn oil—these are all refined, neutral-tasting, and have high smoke points, so they’re essentially interchangeable for deep-frying or pan-frying. “Light” olive oil is close but can still add a slight olive note. Walnut oil might fit but is less common. That gives me a starting point: I’ll say there are really only a few you *can* swap freely.

Then I consider the many oils that aren’t meant for that purpose. Extra virgin olive oil is for raw applications like dressings; its flavor is central, so subbing it with canola would ruin a vinaigrette. Chili oil and toasted sesame oil are condiments/flavorings, not cooking mediums—heating them would be a waste and wouldn’t work. Regular sesame oil is a different, refined product sometimes used for cooking, so I should clarify that distinction. There are also cultural/recipe-specific oils like palm or coconut that behave differently in solid form and flavor, where unthinking substitution can break a dish.

I also recall that even if smoke point and flavor seem fine, fat composition (saturated vs. unsaturated ratios) can matter in delicate baking or emulsified recipes, so that’s another layer of caution.

Ultimately, the answer should nudge the reader away from the “when can’t I substitute” mindset toward “which few oils can I use interchangeably.” I’ll structure it by first listing the versatile group, then providing examples of specialized oils and why they don’t work as general substitutes, and finally point out that smoke point and flavor aren’t the only factors. I’ll end by saying it’s better to ask which oils *can* be swapped in a specific case. That flips the premise and gives a more accurate guide.

content:
Why should I "rest" meat after cooking?

I often read in recipes that I should "rest" meat after it has been cooked but what does resting the meat actually do?

There are a couple of reasons why 'resting' meat is a good idea. First, as the meat cooks the muscle fibres contract, which forces the juices out. Letting the meat rest helps the muscle fibres relax so the juices are re-incorporated into the meat and not lost on the chopping board, which would happen if carved immediately.

The second reason to let meat rest is to provide an evenness. Basically as the meat rests it continues to cook slightly and it allows the meat to gain an overall 'doneness'
thinking: The user is asking about the purpose of resting meat after cooking, a common recipe instruction they've encountered but don't understand the science behind. I need to draw on food science knowledge about muscle structure and heat transfer. When meat cooks, heat causes the muscle fibers to contract, which physically squeezes moisture out of the cells. If carved immediately, those juices—now pooled interstitially—will spill onto the cutting board. Resting gives the fibers time to relax, allowing some of that liquid to be reabsorbed, so the meat stays juicier. That's the first key reason. The second involves thermodynamics: the outer layers are hotter than the center, so after removing from heat, residual heat from the exterior continues to travel inward, slightly raising the core temperature and evening out the doneness. Cutting too soon interrupts that, leading to a temperature gradient and potentially undercooked centers. I'll structure the answer by listing these two distinct reasons—juice redistribution and carryover cooking for evenness—mirroring the final answer's concise breakdown.

content:
How do I pound chicken (or other meat) without making a mess?

Despite my best efforts, my kitchen (and sometimes the chicken) always looks like a war zone after pounding 8 or 10 breasts. Maybe this is just a messy job, but I think there must be something I'm missing.

I've tried using mallets, both metal and wooden The meat always gets stuck to the pounding surface and the mallet. I've tried putting the meat inside a plastic sandwich bag or freezer bag; the bag is always ripping and falling apart before the meat is flat. Wax paper is about the same.

I've also tried rolling pins. Even got a "non-stick" one. This way is even more hopeless for me, because the meat either slides around on the surface or sticks to the pin (doesn't matter if I use flour).

Surely there must be a combination of tools and techniques that would allow me to complete this task without requiring 20 minutes of constant cursing and an extra hour of cleanup.

Can anyone point me in the right direction?

Clingwrap works fine for me -- but I don't use a meat tenderizer -- I just use a small but fairly heavy pan (but not my cast iron, as it's not smooth on the bottom).

When I was in college, I tried a few things. I can get pretty decent results just hitting it with my cutting board. (with it between saran wrap).

Part of it might be technique -- if I'm doing chicken breast I first slice is sort of following the taper of the breast, so it's neither with or across the grain, but kinda of diagonal. You also don't want to hit straight down -- you want to angle the blows, so you're actually pushing the meat out, and not just trying to force it through the counter.

And I should mention that I've only ever pounded out poultry and pork -- I assume beef would be the same, but I have no experience to confirm or deny it.
thinking:
The user's core problem is that pounding meat creates a mess: meat tears, sticks to tools, and the protective layers fail. I need to think about why their attempts didn't work. Mallets, even non-stick ones, have small contact areas and ridges that can catch and tear thin plastic bags or wax paper. The ripping happens because the force concentrates at points, and the bag material isn't stretchy enough. Rolling pins slide because the meat and surface are slippery, and flour just adds a coating that can gum up.

So the solution must involve a barrier that's flexible and clingy enough to stay put, and a pounding implement with a smooth, broad surface that won't puncture it. Plastic cling wrap (like Saran wrap) is thin but stretchy and self-adhering; it can conform to the meat and counter, and if you use enough of it, it's resilient against broad pressure. A small, heavy pan with a flat bottom distributes force evenly and has no sharp edges, making it ideal as a makeshift mallet. I remember some cooks using a wine bottle or a rolling pin, but a pan with some weight reduces effort and splatter because you're not whacking as hard.

Then there's technique to reduce tearing: instead of just whaling on a whole breast, first slice it partially on a diagonal to create a more uniform thickness and a hinge, which allows the meat to spread naturally when pounded. That way you're not trying to crush a thick lump into submission. And the actual pounding stroke matters: a straight-down hit compresses the meat into the board and can cause the wrap to tear or the meat to shoot out. Angling the blows—like hitting with a slight sideways push—encourages the meat to stretch outward rather than just compacting. This reduces the necessary force and keeps things contained.

Finally, the user works with poultry and pork; beef is denser but would likely respond similarly, though I lack direct experience. The response will present cling wrap and a heavy pan as the tool combo, the diagonal slicing trick, and the angled blow technique, all of which address the mess by containing the meat, preventing tearing, and flattening efficiently. I'll structure it as a straightforward set of tried-and-tested recommendations.

Slow cooking without a slow cooker

I frequently hear people telling me about how wonderful their slow cookers (AKA "crock pot") are. In many cases they're right - meat that tends to come out tough in normal cooking comes out very tender from a slow cooker.

But do I really **need** a slow cooker to pull this off? It seems like such a basic concept - simmer and/or steam at low heat. What's so special about these devices? For kitchens with very limited space, can a slow cooker be "synthesized" from other cooking implements, or is there really no substitute?

Your best bet would be a dutch oven on a low to medium low heat in the oven. You could use a regular pot in the oven, but you'd need to stir it regularly (maybe every hour) to stop everything from sticking to the sides and burning.
thinking:
The question is about whether a slow cooker is truly necessary for low-and-slow cooking, or whether you can replicate the results with standard kitchen equipment. The key is to understand what a slow cooker actually does: it provides consistent, even, low-temperature heat (usually around 200–210°F on the low setting) over many hours, using a heavily insulated vessel that surrounds the food with gentle warmth. This allows tough cuts of meat to become tender without drying out, and because the heat is uniform and indirect, there’s no need to stir or monitor constantly.

To replace a slow cooker, you need a setup that mimics that gentle, all-around heat. An oven is the closest match: it’s an insulated chamber where you can set a specific low temperature. However, a thin-walled pot on an oven rack might still have hot spots, and liquid could evaporate more readily than in a slow cooker’s sealed environment. That’s why a Dutch oven — a heavy, lidded pot with excellent heat retention — is ideal: it smooths out temperature fluctuations, traps moisture, and distributes heat evenly from all sides when placed in the oven. You can set the oven to around 250°F and let it go for hours, just like a slow cooker.

Could you do it on the stovetop? In theory, yes, but it’s harder to maintain a truly low simmer that doesn’t scorch the bottom. Even with a flame-tamer or diffuser, the heat comes only from the bottom, and many stoves cycle on and off, causing uneven cooking. A regular pot’s thin walls would likely cause the contents to stick and burn unless you stir intermittently — every hour or so — which undermines the hands-off convenience of slow cooking. A Dutch oven on the stovetop would fare better than a regular pot, but still requires more attention than the oven method. So the reasoning leads to the oven + Dutch oven as the best stand-in, with the caveat that a regular pot can work if you’re willing to stir. Present the answer by explaining why that combination works and noting the stirring limitation for other pots.

content:
What is the difference between various types of flour?

Is there a difference between the various types of flour that you see in the stores (i.e. Cake, Bread, and All-Purpose? Is it really necessary to stock 3 types of flour in my pantry or is this just a scheme from the manufacturers to get more money?

There are actually quite a few differences between the different types of flour. The number of different types you store will really depend on your particular requirements.

All purpose (or plain) flour is a blend of different types of wheat and has a relatively low protein content.

Bread flour is typically made from a single, high protein wheat. It also has a higher gluten strength. It may also contain ascorbic acid (vitamin C)

Cake flour is also typically made from a single type of wheat (different from the wheat used in bread flour) and has a high starch content, it also has the lowest protein content.

There are many other types of flour, all of which server specific purposes, for example;

Self raising flour, Whole wheat flour, Chick pea flour, Rice flour, Semolina flour

And others.

Essentially it's important to use the right type of flour for a give recipe.
thinking:
The question asks whether cake, bread, and all-purpose flours are genuinely different and if stocking all three is just a marketing trick. I need to address the skepticism by explaining the food-science basis for their differences, then help the asker decide whether they really need all three.

First, I recall that the key distinction among wheat flours is protein content, which determines gluten formation when mixed with liquid. Gluten gives dough its structure and elasticity. Higher protein means more potential gluten, leading to chewier textures like bread; lower protein means less gluten, yielding tender crumb like cakes. So the flour types aren’t just labeled arbitrarily—they’re milled from different wheat varieties or blends to achieve specific protein levels and starch characteristics.

I know that bread flour is milled from hard wheat, typically with a protein content around 12–14%. Its strong gluten network can trap gas produced by yeast, giving bread its rise and chew. Some bread flours also include ascorbic acid (vitamin C) as a dough conditioner to strengthen gluten further. Cake flour, on the other hand, comes from soft wheat with a low protein content, usually 6–8%, and a higher starch-to-protein ratio. This produces very little gluten, resulting in a fine, tender crumb for delicate cakes. All-purpose flour is a middle ground—a blend of hard and soft wheats with protein around 10–12%—designed to work adequately for many baked goods but not optimally for extremes like artisan bread or chiffon cake.

Thus, the differences are real and rooted in the wheat itself, not just branding. Whether one needs all three depends on baking habits: if someone rarely bakes bread or cakes, all-purpose might suffice, but for the best results in specific recipes, the specialized flours make a noticeable difference. I’ll also note that there are many other flour types (self-rising, whole wheat, non-wheat flours) that serve specific purposes.

I’ll structure my response by first affirming the differences, then describing each of the three flours in terms of wheat type, protein content, and any additives, briefly mentioning other flours, and concluding that the right flour matters for a recipe.

content:
Shelf life of spices

The common wisdom I've heard is that dried herbs and spices:

- have a shelf-life of about a year or 2
- keep best in a cool dark place
- will release more flavor when crushed

That's fine but some spices are expensive. We have over different 50 jars on our spice rack and can't afford to replace them annually. Also, it's hard to believe that all herbs and spices are created equal.

What are some more specific guidelines regarding the shelf-life of herbs and spices? Which last longer? Which last less long? How much is shelf-life really affected by light or lack thereof? Do any actually become health hazards if left too long?

Dried herbs really do only last around six months, certainly no longer than a year. They're generally easy to get in small quantities, though.

Spices are trickier. They'll generally last rather longer, but the time will vary. If the spice is used for the colour and/or heat (e.g. turmeric, chilli) it will generally last much, much longer than one used for its smell and/or taste. Whole spices last much, much longer than pre-ground; I generally buy whole spices from asian stores, they sell them in much larger amounts for the same prices as supermarkets; and use a coffee mill to grind the right amount just before cooking (and keep a separate one for coffee!).

If kept in the dark, in a dry, clean, airtight glass container, spices and dried herbs will certainly not become health hazards, and should not pick up unpleasant tastes or odours. The strong-tasting / strong-smelling ones will, however, lose taste and smell, eventually almost completely; since that is the whole point of using them, you might as well not bother once they're off.
thinking:
The questioner already knows the common wisdom but suspects it’s overly simplistic. I need to unpack what actually drives degradation in dried herbs and spices to give them useful, granular guidelines, especially since they can’t replace everything annually.

First, I should separate dried leafy herbs from spices. Herbs are typically leaves, and their prized aromatic compounds are mostly volatile oils housed in fragile structures that break down quickly after drying. Basil, cilantro, parsley, chives—these lose their punch within months, because the very compounds we want vaporize or oxidize. Spices are botanically diverse (seeds, bark, roots, fruits, flower parts) and contain a wider range of functional molecules. So it makes sense to tell them that dried herbs really have a short window, maybe six months, and they’re cheap enough to buy in small amounts often.

Now for spices, I recall that the key variables are what you value in a spice and its physical form. Some spices are used mainly for color (like turmeric) or heat (like chili). The pigments and capsaicinoids are relatively stable molecules. Curcumin degrades slowly under light and heat but holds for years; capsaicin isn’t volatile and doesn’t oxidize easily. So those spices last “much, much longer” than those used for aroma. Aromatics like cumin, coriander, cardamom depend on volatile essential oils that dissipate or turn rancid over time. That explains the differential: a chili powder might still be hot but have lost its fruity, smoky nuances.

The physical form matters enormously because grinding creates vast surface area, exposing volatile oils to oxygen and accelerating their loss. Whole spices encapsulate those oils. So I should recommend buying whole spices—often cheaper in bulk at Asian markets—and grinding just before use. That alone dramatically extends useful life.

As for storage, I need to address the health hazard question directly. Properly dried, kept dry, in airtight glass away from light, spices don’t support pathogen growth because of low water activity. Rancidity of oils could technically produce off-flavors, but not toxins in any dangerous quantity. The real risk is simply that they become flavourless dust, which defeats their purpose. I’ll say that explicitly: no health hazard, but no point using them either.

Light accelerates oxidation and photodegradation, especially for color-sensitive compounds like those in paprika or turmeric. A cool, dark place therefore matters most for preserving appearance and minimally for flavor compounds that are already volatile. I’ll fold that into the storage discussion rather than quantify it precisely, since the question asks “how much” but the answer can just emphasize that it’s enough to make a difference for quality.

So my structure: Start by confirming the shorter life of dried herbs. Then move to spices, explaining the division by what you’re trying to preserve (heat/color vs taste/smell) and by whole vs ground. Give a practical tip about buying whole from Asian stores. Then address safety, emphasizing that proper storage prevents hazards but can’t stop flavor loss, so staleness is the real expiration signal. That covers all their sub-questions without getting overly scientific.The questioner wants to move beyond the generic one-year rule and understand what actually determines how long different spices last, whether light matters a lot, and if there’s any safety risk from using old ones. I need to give them a practical, science-backed breakdown that helps them prioritize what to replace and what might still be usable.

First, I’ll separate dried leafy herbs from spices because their chemistry is different. Herbs like basil, oregano, parsley contain delicate volatile aroma compounds that degrade within months after drying—more like six months. That’s a firm, shorter window I should state upfront.

For spices, I need to explain why the “use-by” isn’t uniform. The key insight is that what you want from a spice affects its shelf life. If you’re after color (turmeric) or heat (chili), those compounds—pigments and capsaicinoids—are relatively stable molecules that resist oxidation and light degradation for years. But if the spice is valued for its smell and taste (cumin, coriander, cardamom, fennel), you’re dealing with volatile essential oils that disperse and oxidize fairly quickly. So I’ll structure the spice advice around this: spices for heat/color last much longer; aromatics fade sooner.

Then there’s the whole vs. ground factor, which is huge. Grinding breaks cell walls and exposes oils to oxygen, dramatically accelerating flavor loss. Whole seeds or bark keep their oils locked inside. I’ll tell them to buy whole spices—they’re often cheaper in large bags at ethnic markets—and grind small batches in a dedicated coffee mill just before cooking. That effectively extends shelf life to years.

Regarding light: it does accelerate degradation, especially photodegradation of pigments and some vitamins, but for pure flavor loss, oxygen and heat are bigger factors. Still, a cool, dark place is standard advice—I’ll just confirm it’s best practice without trying to quantify exactly how much longer it buys.

The safety question is important. Dried spices and herbs are low-moisture foods; properly stored in clean, dry, airtight containers, they don’t support microbial growth. Oils might go rancid eventually, but they won’t turn into something acutely toxic. The real hazard is just that you’ll be cooking with flavorless dust, which is pointless. I’ll make that clear: no health code violation, but no culinary benefit either.

I’ll wrap it all by summarizing the different shelf-life tiers: herbs expire first, then ground aromatic spices, while whole heat/color spices last ages. That gives them a framework for managing their 50 jars without feeling they must toss everything annually.

What meats can I serve medium rare and why?

It is generally accepted that pork and chicken **must** be cooked completely (unless put through a strong curing process) while certain cuts of beef and lamb can be served on the rare side. Why is this?

Are particular bacteria populations present in some animals but can't survive in others? What is the inherent differences between these animals that makes the difference when eating? How can I objectively decide if it is safe to eat something partially on the rare side that does not involve simply trusting the "common knowledge" of the more experienced.

(Don't get me wrong - I appreciate any and all advice that I get from anyone who is more experienced than I am in anything, but I'd like to know *how* they came to their conclusions).

Beef (and Lamb): The surface of beef is often contaminated with pathogens such as e-coli. However, the meat is very dense and the bacteria cannot migrate from the surface into the flesh. Therefore, beef is safe to consume once the external temperature exceeds, 160 degrees F. The internal uncontaminated meat is safe to eat raw.

Pork: Like beef the surface of pork needs to be fully cooked. Unlike beef, pigs can harbor a parasitic roundworm called *Trichinella spiralis*. Infection with the worm is called trichinosis and can be fatal. This worm is killed when the flesh reaches 150 degrees F and is held there for several minutes. Therefore pork is safe to consume when cooked to medium. (Commercial pork in North America almost never has the roundworm present. Almost every case (all?) of trichinosis in the last 15-20 years have come from undercooked wild boar or bear meat). *Trichinella spiralis* can also be killed by freezing (time and temperature dependent).

Chicken: Almost all chickens have Salmonella or Campylobacter present on the surface (at
least). However, chickens have a less dense flesh than pigs, sheep or cows. Therefore, the bacteria can migrate deep into the flesh. Also, the processing of chickens is much more invasive than the previously mentioned animals which also means the interior meat can get contaminated. This means the meat must be cooked to well done throughout.

Duck: With duck it seems to come down to a matter of processing versus chicken. Also, they are raised in a much less confined manner, which helps prevent the spread of pathogens. There is still a chance of getting a salmonella infection from undercooked duck but cooking the breast well done basically ruins it, so people take the (small) risk.

Ground meat: Grinding meat, by its nature, implies the surface and the interior is mixed. Therefore, one must assume the meat is fully contaminated and must be entirely cooked to well done.
thinking:
The user is asking for a scientific, objective framework to determine which meats can be safely served less than fully cooked, moving beyond simple rules of thumb. They want to understand the underlying biological and structural reasons—pathogens, meat density, processing—so they can evaluate any meat, not just the common ones. So I need to break down the key factors that govern safety: which pathogens are typically present on or in the meat, whether they stay on the surface or can penetrate, and how cooking temperature and time affect them. 

I recall that for beef and lamb, the primary concern is surface contamination with bacteria like E. coli; the muscle tissue is dense, so as long as the exterior is seared, the interior can be safely rare. Pigs can carry Trichinella spiralis, a parasite that embeds in muscle, so internal temperature must reach a lethal threshold—but modern farming has nearly eliminated it, and freezing also kills it, so medium can be safe. Chickens have less dense flesh and often harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; the bacteria can migrate inward, and slaughtering practices frequently contaminate the interior, necessitating thorough cooking. Duck is an interesting counterpoint: it’s often served medium-rare, but the reasoning is that different rearing and processing reduce (but don’t eliminate) risk, and culinary tradition accepts that small risk. Ground meat mixes surface and interior, so it must be treated as fully contaminated and cooked through.

I’ll structure the answer by animal, explaining for each why the conventional wisdom exists and what the biological/processing reasons are. For an objective decision framework, I’ll highlight checking for known parasites, meat density, processing method, and whether freezing might mitigate risk. The final response will be concise and factual, mirroring the scientific tone of the provided answer.

Induction range vs gas

I have a kitchen remodel (including range/oven) planned. Currently we have a "vintage" electric stove. I am **deciding between gas or induction**.

I liked gas in a previous house. However, I have reservations about combustion gases and unhealthy air quality. I heard **great** things about induction, but I had reservations about replacing cookware (before my budget increased). I haven't used induction.

**Update**

A friend used induction, and she hated it at first, but then liked it. Induction ranges are not common in the U.S.

If you are a cook, and have used an induction system, "Is it responsive?", "Is temperature controllable?", "Is it durable and easy to clean?".

I want to test drive an induction range, so I'll check with local shops.

***Another Update***

Somewhere among my bookmarks is an article about particulate matter and CO generated by gas ranges.

I like things I've read about induction ranges. Efficiency, safety, control, etc.

We moved from a gas hob to an induction hob. It cooks similar to gas and you get similar levels of temperature control. A style of cooking not recommended is 'slide' cooking as this can scratch your hob surface - this can be mitigated by putting a piece of parchment paper under the pan or lifting the pan off the hob. We don't use a wok and can't see how we could with our hob.

The surface of the hob gets hot but not as hot as it would it it were gas or electric. This means that spilt / spattered food doesn't generally burn on to the hob surface and it is easier to clean.

The hob is touch control and so far we've not had any problems with this. If you lift all pan(s) off all active heating zone(s), it'll switch itself off automagically after a couple minutes.

We chose a NEFF Flushline hob that sits in a natural black granite work surface and the whole thing is beautiful and a pleasure.
thinking:
The user is remodeling their kitchen and deciding between gas and induction. They liked gas before but worry about indoor air quality from combustion. They've heard good things about induction, had concerns about replacing cookware but budget is less of an issue now, haven't used it, and a friend had a mixed initial experience. They want firsthand answers about responsiveness, temperature control, durability, and easy cleaning from someone who cooks with induction.

I need to recall my own experience switching from gas to induction. I can directly address those points because I've lived through them. Temperature control and responsiveness on induction feel very close to gas—the heat adjusts almost instantly, so there's no lag like with radiant electric. That covers the first two questions. Durability and cleaning: the glass-ceramic surface can be scratched if you slide pans roughly, which is a downside some people run into, but that's manageable by lifting pans or using a parchment paper trick. Cleaning is easier than gas because the hob surface doesn't get as hot as a gas grate or an exposed electric coil; splatters don't bake into a char, so a quick wipe usually does it. I should also mention that the touch controls work reliably and the auto-shutoff feature is a nice safety net if you forget a pan. Wok cooking is tricky with a flat induction hob, so if they do a lot of stir-frying that might be a factor. To wrap it up, I'll share that we chose a NEFF Flushline model set into a black granite worktop and it's been great—both functional and beautiful. That personal recommendation might help them picture it in a real kitchen. I'll structure the response as a direct, experience-based walk-through of those points, concluding with our own positive outcome.

What is the proper way to dispose of a kitchen knife?

How do you throw away a kitchen knife (or for that matter, any knife)? It seems extremely dangerous to just throw it in the dumpster, even if it's wrapped up real well.

I agree that donating the knife to a thrift shop is a good idea. But it pains me to think of putting tape on a knife blade. Someone's going to have to clean it off, and that risks injuring them.

Instead, find a piece of cardboard that's longer than the blade of the knife, and more than twice the depth of the blade with an inch (~3 cm) or more to spare.

Fold the cardboard in half, so it's now roughly larger than the size of the blade, and then place the blade so the back of the knife is against the fold. (You can do it the other way, but you'll risk dulling the knife: cutting paper isn't good for knives.) Finally, tape it down.

You want to make sure it's well compressed, so the knife is being held in by friction. You could always sandwich something rubbery in there with it to provide more friction.

(This is how I used to transport my knives when moving between apartments.)

---

Another alternative, if you're really disposing of it, and don't mind dulling the blade, is to poke it into a piece of corrugated cardboard. Just find a piece that's longer and wider than the blade, set it on the edge of your counter, put a hand on top to hold it steady, and then slowly push the blade in.
thinking:
The question is about safely disposing of a kitchen knife. The asker is worried that just tossing it in the trash, even if wrapped, could injure sanitation workers or anyone handling the garbage. I need to think through the practicalities of discarding a sharp blade in a way that eliminates the risk. 

First, the best option for an unwanted knife that's still functional is to donate it, so it doesn't become waste at all. But even then, you have to hand it over safely. The obvious quick fix is to wrap the blade in tape, but that's problematic: the tape adhesive can be a nightmare to remove, and whoever does it might cut themselves while scraping or cutting off the tape. That seems counterproductive.

I've dealt with this exact problem when moving apartments and transporting my kitchen knives. I needed a temporary, secure sheath that wouldn't ruin the edge or endanger anyone unpacking. The solution I used was a simple folded cardboard sheath. Cardboard is plentiful and stiff enough to contain the blade. You fold a piece that's longer than the blade and wide enough to completely cover it, with the spine of the knife against the fold. That prevents the edge from cutting into the fold, which would dull it and make the sheath less secure. Then you tape the open sides shut, compressing the cardboard tightly so friction holds the knife firmly. If the cardboard is a bit loose, adding a thin rubbery layer like a piece of shelf liner or a rubber band inside can enhance grip.

If the knife is truly destined for the trash and edge sharpness doesn't matter, there's an even quicker method: just stab the blade straight into a thick piece of corrugated cardboard from the edge, like a box side. The cardboard grips it well, but it will dull the edge. That's a cost-effective, fast way to make it safe for the dumpster.

So, I'm going to structure the response by first agreeing that donation is a good idea, then explaining why putting tape directly on the blade is risky. I'll then describe the folded cardboard method as the safer alternative, and finally mention the cardboard-poke method for true disposal scenarios.

Can my freezer be too cold?

[The FDA recommends a freezer temperature of 0˚F (-18˚C)](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/are-you-storing-food-safely). Warmer temperatures risk bacterial growth and quality problems. But what are the reasons not to set the freezer colder? My Bosch freezer can be set as low as -8˚F (-22˚C).

The only downsides I can see are increased electricity usage, increased thaw times during food preparation, and more wear on the freezer compressor. But advantages include colder ice cubes and faster freeze times for new items. Are there any other reasons not to set my freezer to the coldest setting?

One possible consideration is that some frozen desserts (most notably ice creams and sorbets) can be very difficult to scoop if your freezer is too cold. Optimal serving temperature for ice cream is between about 5 & 10°F (-15°C & -12°C); colder freezers may result in difficult scooping and/or needing to leave the ice cream out to thaw.

The proposed advantage of "colder ice cubes" is relatively small, because the vast majority of heat absorption by ice (in a drink, say) is due to it thawing. To put some numbers on it, every gram of frozen ice absorbs about 2.1 joules of heat energy when it warms up by 1°C. In contrast, that same gram of ice absorbs 335 joules of heat energy when it thaws into liquid water. If you run the numbers, this means that ice at -22°C will only absorb 2-3% more heat from your drinks than ice at -18°C.
thinking:
The question is whether setting a home freezer colder than the standard 0°F has any downsides beyond higher energy use and compressor wear. The asker already sees faster freezing and colder ice as benefits, so I need to identify other, less obvious drawbacks. I recall that many frozen desserts, especially ice cream and sorbet, are formulated with a certain amount of unfrozen water and air to remain scoopable at typical freezer temperatures. If the freezer is too cold, more water freezes, the ice cream becomes rock-hard, and it requires tempering before serving—defeating the convenience. This is a practical reason that often gets overlooked.  

Next, I should examine the claimed advantage of “colder ice cubes.” From food science and basic thermodynamics, the cooling effect of ice in a drink comes overwhelmingly from the phase change from solid to liquid (latent heat), not from the ice warming up (sensible heat). The latent heat of melting is about 335 J/g, whereas the specific heat of ice is only about 2.1 J/g·°C. Even a 4°C difference (from -18°C to -22°C) absorbs only an extra 8.4 J/g, which is about 2–3% of the total heat absorbed when the ice melts. So the practical benefit is negligible—colder ice won’t make drinks noticeably colder or keep them cold longer. This directly undercuts one of the user’s perceived advantages.

I should also briefly consider whether other foods suffer from extreme cold, but for most solid frozen items (meat, vegetables), colder temperatures simply extend shelf life and slow quality loss, as long as the freezer maintains a stable temperature and packaging prevents freezer burn. The main exceptions are semi-solid emulsions and foams like ice cream. No need to dive into freezer burn, since that’s unrelated to the temperature setting per se. 

To structure the response, I’ll lead with the ice cream scoopability issue as a direct, everyday downside, then address the ice-cube point with a short thermodynamic explanation and numbers, showing the minimal gain. That matches the final answer’s two-pronged approach.

Why would plant-based cookie dough packaging say "Do not consume raw dough"?

I just bought some Kroger Simple Truth Plant-Based Chocolate Chip Cookie Dough.

I always prefer to eat raw dough rather than bake the cookies.

But this packaging says:

> DO NOT CONSUME RAW DOUGH

Why not?

As a kid, I'd always heard a recommendation not to eat raw cookie dough that had eggs in it (and even then, I'm not sure what the reasoning is or what the risks are, but I suppose probably something related to salmonella).

But when the ingredients are plant-based (no eggs, no dairy, no animal products of any kind), what are the possible unwanted effects from eating raw dough?

I was surprised at how difficult it was to find the answer, but I eventually found articles by the [FDA](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/raw-doughs-raw-deal-and-could-make-you-sick) and [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/foodsafety/communication/no-raw-dough.html).

> Consumers should be aware that there are additional risks associated
> with the consumption of raw dough, such as particularly harmful
> strains of *E. coli* in a product like flour.
>
> Flour is derived from a grain that comes directly from the field and
> typically is not treated to kill bacteria[...] So if an animal heeds
> the call of nature in the field, bacteria from the animal waste could
> contaminate the grain, which is then harvested and milled into flour.
>
> Common “kill steps” applied during food preparation and/or processing
> (so-called because they kill bacteria that cause infections) include
> boiling, baking, roasting, microwaving, and frying. But with raw
> dough, no kill step has been used. [...] Common symptoms for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli are diarrhea (often bloody) and abdominal cramps, although most people recover within a week. But some illnesses last longer and can be more severe, resulting in a type of kidney failure called hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

That's pretty gross.

But then this number of people reportedly infected is so small that I'm surprised at the prevalence of the warnings (such as on packaging):

> In recent years (2016 and 2019), two outbreaks of E. coli infections
> linked to raw flour made more than 80 people sick. Flour and baking
> mixes that contain flour have long shelf lives, so it’s a good idea to
> check your pantry to see if you have any flour or baking mixes that
> have been recalled in recent years.
thinking: The user is confused because the warning on plant-based dough seems contradictory—no eggs, so why no raw consumption? First, I recall the standard advice about raw cookie dough: it's typically about salmonella from raw eggs. But plant-based dough eliminates that risk. So there must be another reason. I think about other ingredients: flour. I remember that raw flour has been implicated in E. coli outbreaks because it's an untreated agricultural product. The grains can be contaminated in the field by animal waste, and milling doesn't kill bacteria. The FDA and CDC have explicit warnings about eating raw dough or batter due to flour, not just eggs. There have been documented outbreaks, though the numbers are small. The warning on packaging is a precautionary measure reflecting that risk. I'll structure the answer by directly quoting the relevant FDA and CDC statements, then note the outbreak data to show it's a real, albeit low, risk.
