What is "layering flavors"? What does it accomplish and how do I do it?

Recently I've been into cooking videos and tutorials and something that stands out to me is this concept of "layering flavors" that some chefs use when they add ingredients.

Example:

> *We're only sweating the onion, afterwards we'll add some garlic and that way we'll have a nice base layer to work with, remember its all about layering flavors*

What? What does that mean? How is *layering flavors* going to help? Is it going to change taste as you chew? Or is it just a fancy way of saying it’s going to have a bit of added taste and it’s going to be wonderful?

And how do I do it? The only thing I see is people adding ingredients to a sauce and cooking them in some way.

It is mostly a fancy way of saying that they are combining flavors. There are no solid, physical layers involved anywhere.

Still, there is a reason why the "layering" metaphor is more apt than simply saying "combining". Flavor is mostly about aroma, which leads to two aspects of "layering".

First, aroma is not perceived all at once when you bite off. You first notice the most volatile smell notes when the food enters your mouth, go through a kind of "middle" and only at the end, while swallowing, you notice the "heavier" flavor. So, when seasoning, you can work with food such that you don't mix up too many flavors in one of the three aroma "layers", but also to make sure that there is something noticeable in each of the three.

Second, people are accustomed to some flavors being present as a metaphorical "background" taste. It can happen that, if the expected aroma is absent, you can add all the spices you want, and the eater will still experience it as underseasoned. This is what is happening in the example you cited: the "base layer" are the onion and garlic, which are probably the standard for the dish, and then you can take that dish in different directions by your choice of additional herbs and spices. In that case, you can see the metaphor as akin to clothing - once you have a basic shirt on, you can always make the outfit nicer by layering a scarf, jacket or jewelry on top of it.

All in all, it is not "all about layering flavors". It is just an expression which helps some cooks go about creating harmonious flavor combinations. If it works for you, use it. If not, learn to think about your seasoning in other terms.
thinking:
The user is confused by the phrase “layering flavors” from cooking videos, thinking it might involve physical layers or a change in taste as you chew. They want a clear, practical explanation of what it means, what it accomplishes, and how to do it.

I need to demystify the term. It’s a metaphor, not a literal stacking of ingredients. The core of “layering” in cooking is about creating depth and complexity in flavor perception, which ties directly to food science: aroma compounds have different volatilities, so when we eat, they hit our senses in a sequence—first the light, fleeting notes, then a heart of mid-weight aromas, and finally the deeper, longer-lasting ones. By adding ingredients at different cooking stages, you control when those compounds are released and how they interact. The example given—sweating onions first, then adding garlic—is classic because onions form a sweet, savory foundation that persists, while garlic added later retains a sharper, more volatile punch that arrives earlier in the tasting moment. This isn’t just adding taste, it’s orchestrating the eating experience over time.

The second part of the metaphor is about “background” tastes. Many cuisines rely on a familiar aromatic base (like onion, celery, carrot, or ginger and garlic) that signals “this is savory food” to the eater. Without it, additional spices might fail to satisfy. So you build a base layer first, then layer on other seasonings like herbs, spices, or acids that define the dish’s character—much like putting on a base clothing layer before adding accessories.

What it accomplishes: a more nuanced, full-bodied flavor that unfolds rather than hits all at once. It prevents dishes from tasting flat or one-dimensional.

How to do it: in practice, it means adding ingredients sequentially based on their cooking requirements and flavor profiles. You start with aromatics that need longer cooking to mellow and sweeten (onions, carrots), then add items that burn or lose potency quickly (garlic, spices, tomato paste), then finish with bright, fresh elements (herbs, citrus, a drizzle of oil). It’s not a rigid formula but a mindset.

I’ll structure the response by first acknowledging it’s a metaphor, then breaking down the two scientific/sensory reasons (temporal aroma perception and the background flavor concept), and finally reassuring the user that it’s just one way to think about cooking, not a mandatory rule. I need to clarify that it’s a metaphor and then explain the two underlying food-science reasons it’s a useful concept. By adding ingredients at different cooking stages, you control which notes hit when, building complexity. content:
What is the purpose of oiling a wooden chopping board?

I recently bought a wooden chopping board to replace my plastic one. In the course of my research I read that it's important to regularly rub mineral oil in (some people say once a week, some say once a month). It's said that it "protects" it and makes it last longer, but what is the oil actually doing?

The oil is not actually doing anything to protect the wood - the idea that it does so is a very widespread myth. This is the [conclusion](https://www.popularwoodworking.com/finishing/cutting-boards-the-best-finish/) of the guy [who wrote the book on wood finishing](https://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/com/1565235665), and I can confirm it from personal experience. You can continue using it for cosmetic reasons, I am personally partial to the look given by flax oil - although there are people who prefer the opposite, because cuts are much less noticeable on unoiled wood.

To get real protection on an wooden item, you have to apply a layer that actually seals the wood. The substances which do this well are shellac, nitro lacquers, acrylic finishes and alkydic finishes.

While you could use a safe-in-trace-amounts finish on a chopping board, the mechanical action of a knife will soon damage such a layer to a point where it becomes useless. Most people are just not interested in refinishing their chopping board a couple of times per week.

As for the source of the myth: Long before good finishes were discovered, people tried protecting wood. Since it was known that wood is most damaged by moisture, they used all kinds of water-repelling substances, such as different oils and waxes, sometimes also natural resins. The protection afforded by those is minimal, but it was all they had - and to the naked eye, it does look like a great protection, since oiled wood has an entirely different appearance, and water droplets pearl on it instead of visibly wetting it.

This is a concept that is known in science as "face validity" - you look at an approach and your intuition tells you that it must be working, so you are likely to conclude that it works. Scientists try to prove that methods work independently of their face validity, but cooks and woodworkers rarely do so :) And since there is a tradition, which convincingly does something, people continue applying it and promoting it.
thinking:
The user is asking what mineral oil actually does when applied to a wooden chopping board, given that many sources claim it "protects" the wood and extends its life. I need to address this from a food-science and woodworking perspective, not just repeat the conventional advice. The underlying question is about the physical mechanism: does oil seal the wood, block moisture, prevent cracking, or is it purely cosmetic?

I recall that wood cutting boards are prone to warping, splitting, and harboring bacteria if they get excessively wet and then dry unevenly. Many home cooks and even chefs believe that regularly applying a food-grade mineral oil creates a barrier that stops water absorption and keeps the wood conditioned. But when I think about the actual chemistry and physical properties, mineral oil is a non-drying oil — it never hardens or polymerizes, unlike linseed or tung oil. It soaks into the wood pores but remains liquid, so it can be washed out gradually with soap and water. That means it can't form a durable, long-lasting film that truly seals the surface.

To check this, I’m aware of respected wood finishing experts like Bob Flexner, who wrote the canonical book on the subject. He and others have tested this explicitly: oiling a cutting board offers no meaningful protection against moisture exchange because the oil doesn't block water vapor or liquid water in a way that prevents the wood from taking on and releasing moisture. Wood movement is driven by humidity changes, and a thin, transient oil treatment doesn't stop that. Real protection requires a film-forming finish — shellac, lacquer, varnish, or polyurethane — that creates a continuous, impermeable layer on top of the wood. But those aren't practical for cutting boards because knife cuts would quickly breach the film, and most aren't safe to ingest in any quantity if they chip off.

So the purpose of oiling isn't functional protection; it's aesthetic. Oil darkens the wood and enhances the grain, giving a richer appearance that some people like. Flax oil (linseed), for instance, can give a nice look, though it can also become gummy over time if not fully cured. Some people even prefer the lighter, matte look of unoiled wood where cut marks are less visible. The belief in protection likely stems from the fact that water beads up on an oiled surface — it looks like it's repelling water — and from historical practices before modern finishes existed, when people used any oily or waxy substance they had in the hope of preserving wood. This is a classic case of face validity: the beading water makes it seem like the treatment works, so the tradition persists despite lack of evidence.

My response will directly state that the protective effect is a myth, cite the wood finishing authority, acknowledge the cosmetic value, explain what real protection would require and why it's not feasible for cutting boards, and then briefly discuss the origin of the myth in historical practice and face validity. This structure lets me answer the "what is the oil actually doing?" question by clarifying that it's doing nothing protective, only enhancing appearance, and the perception of protection is an illusion. I'll stop here, having decided how to present the answer without writing the response itself.

content:
Is there such a thing as a dish being bland from too many flavors?

My girlfriend has asked for my opinion on a few dishes that she has been experimenting with, and not being particularly well-versed in the language used to discuss food, I have been having trouble expressing my opinion on two specific dishes (namely, a stew using ground beef and a Thai curry with chicken).

I have eaten several different versions of both dishes over several months, so I have developed a pretty good sense of which versions of them I like the best. We have also tried similar dishes from local restaurants in order to have a common reference point. Generally, I think that the dishes taste fine, but sometimes I feel that they become "bland" (for lack of a better word) from too many spices.

What I mean is that sometimes when she prepares them she will use only a few specific spices or none at all and more fresh ingredients. To me, these versions taste the best. They have strong, distinct flavors, and I think that they taste more like the restaurant dishes that we've compared them to. However, she usually finds these versions under-seasoned, so she also experiments with adding lots of different spices. When she does this, she still isn't happy with the result but she says that the dishes taste more "complete" or more "harmonious" or just generally better. On the other hand, I think that these versions taste same-y or bland, which she doesn't understand since there are objectively more flavors in the dish. I have tried to describe it like the flavor equivalent of that color of brown you get when you mix all the paints together or if an orchestra just played all the instruments at once without regard to the timing.

To me, these versions sort of feel like filling in all the nooks and crannies of the flavor landscape to make the experience boring and flat. She says that I just don't understand flavor and that that's not a thing that happens. She says that adding more flavors complement and round-out the taste.

I am nowhere near as knowledgeable about food words as my girlfriend, and she also has a much more sensitive and discerning palate than I do. So it may be possible that I am just a bad food critic, but I would really like to understand my experience better and hopefully communicate it better to my girlfriend. My question is this: **Is there such a thing as "the flavor equivalent of the color brown" in the sense that too many different flavors can make food sort of taste bland? If so, is there a technical way to describe that sensation?**

With your longer description, I can understand where you are coming from and why you don't like this version of the dishes (and also why somebody else might prefer them). But the term "bland" you chose is unfortunate, and is predestined to create misunderstandings.

"Bland" is a word with a rather well-circumscribed meaning, and means that there is an absence of taste and flavor. To use your color analogy, "bland" would be applied most directly to something that is ecru colored, and, less fitting but still understood, to something that has its own color tone but so little pigment that it is still nearly white. For food, imagine maybe a pudding made with starch and water, nothing else, that would be a quintessential experience of bland food.

The experience you describe doesn't have a unique term, and the descriptive ones I can think of are non-technical. The most specific one I can come up with is "mingled flavors", although this one doesn't strongly evoke that the speaker disapproves of the extent of mingling. You can choose whatever you like and best reflects your own subjective experience. Some examples would be to call it "conflicting", "chaotic" or "overwhelming" taste combinations. Or, if you prefer to continue the metaphors from other senses, you can use "cacaphonous taste" or, more diplomatically, "lack of contrast".

Is panko just pretentious breadcrumbs?

My local grocery store actually currently sells [panko crumbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bread_crumbs#Panko) for more money than beef mince, which to me is incredible. Is there any sort of justification for this or is it just expensive because it is foreign?

Maybe there is some culinary justification in using it that I'm unaware of, but to me its inflated price seems rather ridiculous for something that is still in essence breadcrumbs.

The big difference between panko and "regular" breadcrumbs is that panko is more like flakes, so it creates a much different texture when used as a breading.

It's more similar to using cracker or cereal crumbs than regular bread in terms of shape, but the texture is more bread-like.

For a picture comparison, and explanation of how panko is made, see [UpperCrustents's how panko is made](https://www.uppercrustent.com/how-panko-is-made/).

The difference is lost when using it as a binder in something like meatballs ... similar to using flake salt vs. other shapes of salt. So in some cases, using it might be considered pretentious. (or just using whatever's on hand).

Recalling food-science details: panko is made from a crustless bread baked with electrical current, which creates a dry, airy loaf that’s then ground into large, flaky crumbs. Regular breadcrumbs come from baked bread that’s simply ground or grated, resulting in a finer, denser texture with more uniform particles. How is rare steak made safe to eat?

The USDA recommends cooking many meats to an internal temperature of at least 145 °F (63 °C) to kill off pathogens. That usually works for me, but the big exception is steak. Whenever I try reaching at least 145 °F (63 °C), I always cook the steak to well-done, and online articles generally say rarer cuts have to dip well below 145 °F (63 °C).

Still, regular portions of rare steak hasn't ever gotten me sick. So what keeps the raw meat safe enough for us to eat rare? Are there things I do or should do to ensure safe raw meat (e.g. sourcing, preservation, preparation, and cooking)?

First, 145 °F (63 °C) and higher is the temperature for a well done steak. So, with the addition of carry-over cooking, your results don't surprise me. If you are shooting for rare, cook to an internal temperature of 125 °F (52 °C), and let your steak rest 10 minutes before slicing.

While the USDA correctly and necessarily provides temperature guidelines, in fact the reduction of pathogens follows a logarithmic curve and includes the variables of temperature *and* time. That means, in general, that longer times at lower temperatures will reduce pathogens. This understanding is the basis of [sous vide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sous_vide) cooking, for example.

Additionally, we generally assume that any potential pathogens are only present on the surface of whole muscle cuts. So, again, in general, achieving the target temperature on the surface eliminates the threat.

Finally, the quality and handling of the raw product is critical. It is important that you have fresh products, kept refrigerated or frozen until use, and handled by people who are practicing safe handling procedures (washed hands or gloves, ...).
thinking:
The question is about reconciling the USDA's 145°F safety guideline with the fact that rare steak is safer to eat even though it never reaches that internal temperature. The user wants to know why rare steak can be safe and what additional factors (sourcing, handling, cooking technique) contribute to that safety.

I need to recall the relevant food-science principles. First, the 145°F target is designed for an instantaneous kill of common pathogens like *Salmonella* and *E. coli*, but pasteurization is actually a function of both temperature *and* time. A lower temperature held for a longer period can achieve the same pathogen reduction. This is the basis of sous vide cooking, where beef can be safely cooked at 130°F if held for enough time. That explains how a steak cooked rare (around 125°F) can be safe if the time at that temperature is sufficient, combined with carry-over cooking during resting.

Second, for whole-muscle cuts like steak, the interior is considered sterile because bacteria are on the surface from slaughter and handling. Searing the outside at a high temperature kills any surface pathogens, so the rare interior is safe. This is fundamentally different from ground beef, where surface bacteria get mixed throughout and require a higher internal temperature.

Third, initial pathogen load matters. Proper sourcing, refrigeration, and hygienic handling reduce the starting number of bacteria, making any cooking method more effective.

I'll structure the answer by first clearing up the temperature misconception: 145°F is well-done, and rare is achieved at 125°F with a rest. Then I'll introduce the time–temperature logarithmic reduction concept, the surface-contamination assumption for steaks, and finally the importance of quality and handling. What exactly is "Japanese" Salt and Pepper?

On a recent trip to Kyoto, I was eating at a Beef Katsu restaurant and one of the spices they made available for seasoning was described as "Japanese salt and pepper".

The spice blend was mostly white/black/gray in color, with no red.

The blend had really excellent flavor (compared to what I would expect for salt + black pepper), and now I'm curious what exactly it was composed of and whether it has a more distinctive name. Does anyone know?

They may have been trying to describe "salt and Japanese pepper". Japanese pepper is unrelated to black pepper, but closely related to Sichuan pepper; its flavor has been described as "lemony" and it has a "numbing" quality. It's also known as "sansho". Mixtures of pre-ground sansho and salt are readily available in Asian grocery stores. This mixture is commonly sprinkled on grilled meats, so this would be my guess.

Of course, it's also possible they meant black and/or white pepper. There's a number of varietals of peppercorn, and how they are roasted, stored, and ground will have a significant effect on the taste.
thinking:

I need to identify what this likely was and whether it has a more specific name.

First, I consider the phrase “Japanese pepper.” In Japanese cooking, “pepper” can mean the spice sanshō (the ground berry of *Zanthoxylum piperitum*). Sanshō is not related to black pepper; it is in the citrus family and related to Sichuan pepper. It has a distinctive lemony, numbing, and slightly floral taste. A very common table condiment in Japan is *sanshō shio*—a mixture of salt and ground sanshō, often used on grilled meats, fried foods, and eel. The color of pre-ground sanshō varies from pale greenish-gray to brownish-gray, so a blend with white salt would yield a speckled mixture without any red, exactly matching the user’s observation. Because the restaurant labeled it “Japanese salt and pepper” in English, they were likely translating “salt and Japanese pepper” (shio to sanshō) literally, rather than referring to black or white pepper.

I also acknowledge that without seeing the actual ingredient list, there’s a secondary possibility: they could have meant a high-quality black and/or white pepper blend, perhaps influenced by a particular varietal, roasting technique, or storage that produced an unusually bright and complex flavor. However, given the specific Japanese context and the user’s description of the taste being notably different from standard salt and pepper, the sanshō-based blend is the far more distinctive and plausible guess. Commercially, blends of salt and pre-ground sanshō are readily available in Japanese and Asian groceries, often labeled as “sansho salt” or similar.

I’ll present the answer by first proposing sanshō salt as the most likely explanation, describing its nature and common uses, and then briefly mention the less probable pepper-varietal alternative.

How long is garlic butter safe, and why is it not a botulism risk like garlic in oil?

I've been making garlic butter for years, storing it for months at a time. When I read that garlic-in-oil can grow dangerous amounts of botulinum toxins after similar lengths of time, I wondered how safe garlic butter is and why.

Evidently, the [safety warnings](http://www.hc-sc.gc.ca/hl-vs/alt_formats/pacrb-dgapcr/pdf/iyh-vsv/food-aliment/garlic-ail-eng.pdf) specifically target storage in oil. I couldn't find a satisfactory explanation for butter not being mentioned with a preliminary search. The first Google result turns up a grossly unhelpful Yahoo! Answers page whose sources do not mention butter at all.

To the point: is garlic butter safer than garlic-in-oil, and why? Is butter not also an anaerobic environment, so that the same precautions should apply as with oil?

I suspected that @FuzzyChef's answer was essentially correct, but I felt that the question was not conclusively answered without sources, so I ended up never accepting an answer. Thankfully, Linda Harris published [this very comprehensive summary](http://ucfoodsafety.ucdavis.edu/files/250352.pdf) (which I recommend you to read if you are a fan of garlic), from which these parts stand out:

> Garlic is a low-acid vegetable. The pH of a clove of garlic typically
> ranges from 5.3 to 6.3.  
> [...]  
> Adding wine or vinegar to garlic
> provides an acidic environment (less than pH 4.6) so that Clostridium
> botulinum cannot grow.

A quick Google search reveals that butter has a pH of 6.1 - 6.4, so there is indeed no reason to believe that garlic butter is safer than garlic in oil.

As the summary says that **garlic in oil is safe for up to 4 days in the refrigerator**, it should be safe to assume that the same would hold for garlic butter.

Most interestingly, however, the document explains a method to acidify garlic for long-term storage in oil, based on research that was published a year after this question was originally posted. The method should be just as valid for garlic butter. In short:

> 1. Prepare 3 parts of 3% citric acid solution (about 15 g citric acid / 500 ml water) per part of garlic to be acidified (and don't change this ratio, obviously)
> 2. Coarsely chop the garlic into pieces no longer than 6 mm (1/4 inch) in any direction
> 3. Put the garlic in the solution, mix, cover and let soak for 24 h at room temperature, then drain/sieve.

This acidified garlic is safe to use in oil (and presumably butter), according to science. Enjoy!
thinking:
The question asks whether garlic butter is safer than garlic-in-oil from a botulism standpoint, and why butter isn’t subject to the same warnings. At first glance, the logic seems plausible: both are fats that coat the garlic, creating an anaerobic environment. But the key difference people often assume is that butter contains water and might spoil differently, or that the saturated fat structure somehow inhibits bacteria. I need to recall the actual conditions that permit *Clostridium botulinum* growth.

The botulism risk in garlic-in-oil comes from the combination of garlic (a low-acid vegetable, pH 5.3–6.3) being placed in an oxygen-free medium at room temperature, which allows any dormant spores on the garlic to germinate, grow, and produce toxin. The oil itself is not the problem; it’s the anaerobic seal it provides. Butter, like oil, is a fat that can coat and create local anaerobic pockets. The pH of butter is roughly 6.1–6.4, well above the critical 4.6 threshold below which *C. botulinum* is inhibited. Therefore, butter does not acidify the garlic and offers no inherent safety advantage. A quick search confirms butter’s pH range matches the garlic’s own pH, so the mixture remains in the danger zone.

So why aren’t there prominent butter-specific warnings? It’s likely a matter of typical usage patterns rather than inherent safety. Garlic-in-oil is often left at room temperature as a convenience product, directly leading to outbreaks. Garlic butter, on the other hand, is frequently refrigerated or used within a short timeframe, or people assume it’s protected by being a dairy product that would obviously spoil. Refrigeration slows but does not entirely prevent *C. botulinum* growth, especially over months; some strains can produce toxin at refrigerator temperatures. The official guidance for garlic in oil—use within 4 days if refrigerated—applies equally to garlic butter. The fact that someone has stored garlic butter for months without incident may reflect luck, low initial spore load, or consistent refrigeration that happened to keep the pathogen below the threshold for toxin formation, but it is not a guarantee of safety.

The UC Davis document cited by the user explains that acidification is the reliable fix. Soaking chopped garlic in a citric acid solution lowers the garlic’s pH to a safe level permanently, making it suitable for long-term storage in oil or butter. This method is the answer to the safety concern, and it seems perfectly applicable to butter since the acidified garlic remains acidic once incorporated.

Thus, my answer will directly say that garlic butter is not safer; the same botulism risk exists because butter is also anaerobic and has a near-neutral pH. I’ll explain why the common warnings focus on oil but that doesn’t exempt butter. I’ll then outline the safe handling limits (refrigerate, use within 4 days) and present the acidification technique as the only way to safely store either product for longer periods. I’ll structure it to first correct the misconception, then provide the science, and finally offer the practical acidification solution.

How can I tell the difference between unmarked sugar and stevia?

My wife just started back on her doctor-recommended ketogenic diet (due to a medical history of high blood pressure and Crohn's disease in her family). She's to have reduced carbohydrates and sugars, and to use artificial sweeteners for anything she would normally add sugar to.

While making our morning coffee, I found a clear plastic container with what looks like stevia stored away - a taste confirms that it has a slightly different taste than the sugar I have on hand.

But I want to be absolutely sure before I recommend she use it in her baking - is there any surefire way to tell if this is stevia and not sugar?

Note: It may also possibly be Truvia.

Don't throw it away. Worst case you use up the mystery sweetener on yourself, and use a new pack of Stevia for your wife and anything you share. That's what I recommend if you're not convinced by my solution or don't have sensitive kitchen scales.

At room temperature, sucrose (normal sugar) is *very* soluble in water: about [200 g of sugar will dissolve in 100 g of water](https://chestofbooks.com/food/science/Experimental-Cookery/The-Solubility-Of-The-Sugars.html).

It's harder to get a figure for the solubility of Stevia as it's not a single compound but a mixture of related compounds. However various [patents](https://patents.google.com/patent/US20130330463) claim "high solubility" stevia preparations of around 30 g per 100 g water, or around 1/7 as much.

This is enough of a difference to test: *If (with plenty of stirring but no heat) the mystery sweetener will dissolve in an equal mass (weight) of water, it's sugar. If not it's stevia. This only works if you weigh it. You can't do this by volume.*

You can always compare to known sugar; a comparison to know stevia is less useful unless it's identical, and brands evolve. The conclusion holds for fructose too (that's even more soluble), but glucose, which you're unlikely to have as pure powder at home, needs slightly more than its own weight of water to dissolve it.

Pure stevia is much sweeter than sugar, and when concentrated may have an aftertaste. It's also sold blended. When blended with other sweeteners the solubility test probably still applies (certainly in the case of erythritol, find in Truvia). Sometimes stevia is bulked out to make it a more direct substitute for sugar. The bulking agents may well be rather soluble and a source of carbohydrates (maltodextrin is sometimes used).
thinking: The user needs to differentiate between unmarked sugar and stevia (possibly Truvia) for a wife on a ketogenic diet, where avoiding carbohydrates is critical. A taste test already suggests a difference, but a more definitive physical test is desired. I recall that sucrose is highly water-soluble—about 200 g dissolves in 100 g of water at room temperature. Steviol glycosides, the sweet compounds in stevia, have much lower solubility; commercial high-solubility stevia preparations typically dissolve only about 30 g in 100 g of water. Truvia contains erythritol, which also has limited solubility (around 30 g per 100 g). This solubility gap is large enough to design a simple test: weigh equal masses of the mystery powder and water, stir thoroughly without heating. If it dissolves completely, the solubility exceeds that of typical stevia products, indicating sugar (or a carbohydrate-rich bulked blend—both unsuitable for keto). If undissolved solids remain, it’s consistent with stevia or a stevia-erythritol mix. The test requires a scale because volume measures would be misleading due to different densities. I’ll also note that some stevia blends use highly soluble carriers like maltodextrin, which could dissolve, but those are themselves carbohydrates and thus not keto-friendly; the safest route is to use a known, fresh packet of stevia for the wife if there’s any doubt. I’ll structure the answer by first giving the straightforward recommendation to default to a new packet, then explain the solubility test with specific numbers, emphasize weighing over volume, and address potential confusions like bulking agents.

Can I make popcorn with any corn?

Up until today I only knew about one type of corn for popcorn. Searching for Peruvian food I found out that in Peru there are different "popcorn" varieties.

So that made me think: is it possible to make popcorn with *just any* variety of corn? If not, what properties do these corn varieties have that allow then to be popped and not any others?

The answer it seems is - [no, you can't just use any variety of corn](https://www.popcorn.org/Different-Types-of-Corn). It seems that you need in particular a hard shell around the kernel that is not present in sweetcorn varieties.

I also suspect that it is harder to make than one might imagine, you need a specific percentage of water in the kernel to get it to pop - this is why you can't store unpopped popcorn in the open and once opened needs to be used within a few months, as the water will evaporate and eventually the percentage will become too low to effectively pop.
thinking:
The question is whether any variety of corn can be used for popcorn, triggered by discovering Peruvian “popcorn” varieties. I need to recall the food-science basis of popping. My first instinct might be that popcorn is just dried corn, but that’s not accurate. What actually causes popping is a combination of a hard, airtight hull (pericarp) and a starchy interior that contains around 13–14% moisture. When the kernel is heated, the trapped water turns into steam, pressure builds until the hull bursts, and the starch expands into a foam. If the hull is too thin or permeable — as with sweetcorn — steam escapes gradually and no explosive pop occurs. Regular field corn or flour corn also doesn’t pop reliably because the hull structure or starch composition is wrong; they might just crack or burn. So the answer has to be no, not just any corn. The Peruvian varieties the user encountered are still specialized popcorn types with the necessary hard hull and moisture content, not a random field corn. I also need to mention the moisture factor: even proper popcorn kernels fail to pop if they dry out too much, which is why storage matters.

I’ll structure my response to directly give the “no,” then explain the two critical properties — hard hull and correct moisture — using sweetcorn as the counterexample, and note that while different popcorn varieties exist, they all share those traits. I’ll keep it concise but mention the storage tip as a practical insight.

What are some good ways to treat frozen vegetables such that they behave like fresh vegetables when stir frying them?

Forgive me for being a novice. I like having frozen spinach, onions, broccoli, and vegetables since they're convenient and don't spoil. But I only know the practices for cooking, and in particular, stir frying fresh vegetables. As a basic example, you heat up the oil, toss in the onions/garlic, then the leafy greens (with maybe some salt to reduce them), then the other veggies like broccoli.

How can I treat the frozen veggies such that they behave and cook like normal freshly chopped vegetables? One thing in particular is I like them getting seared by the hot oil.

The only method I have now is to microwave them for a bit (with perhaps a bit of water), and then to use them when they seem sufficiently unfrozen, but this usually leaves 30% of it frozen, 40% fine, and 30% vaporized by the microwave.

Any advice? Bonus points for speed, convenience, and simplicity (I'm a lazy college student who likes using pre-chopped vegetables and only one cooking vessel).

The first thing is to do is thaw them properly before you cook them, half frozen vegetables will cool your pan too much. I often thaw frozen vegetables by soaking them in hot tap water, this is pretty quick and doesn't scorch them like microwaving them might. This might take a bit more time than microwaving but it's a much better result.

You will never get the same result as fresh using frozen vegetables, this is because freezing changes the structure. Water expands when it freezes, rupturing cell walls, which impacts some vegetables more than others. Peas, freeze very well, carrots pretty well. Green beans, broccoli, cauliflower freeze okay, they come out a bit more limp than fresh. Thin leafy vegetables like spinach don't freeze well at all, they come out very limp, almost as if they're cooked already. This isn't a deal-breaker, just something to be aware of. On the rare occasions I use frozen spinach I will squeeze the hell out of it after thawing as it's water-logged.

Cooking order will be important to sauteing them successfully. Water is the enemy of getting color on your vegetables, so you want to make sure they are relatively dry before you add them. Hardest vegetables go in first, like carrots, then medium ones like beans and broccoli, last you add the leaves because they take the shortest to cook and will give off a lot of water no matter how well you wrung them. You want the vegetables to be mostly cooked by the time you put the spinach in as the water will put an end to any browning. Peas go in last, they only need to be warmed through.
thinking:
The user is a college student who values convenience and wants frozen vegetables to sear in a stir-fry like fresh ones. Their current method—microwaving with a bit of water—gives uneven results: some parts stay frozen, others overcook. To answer, I need to recall why frozen vegetables behave differently and what can be done about it.

Food science tells me that freezing damages vegetable cells because ice crystals puncture cell walls. When thawed, those cells leak water, and the vegetable becomes softer and soupier. This varies by vegetable: peas and carrots hold up decently, broccoli and green beans become limp, spinach becomes a waterlogged mess. So the main enemies for a good stir-fry are excess water and uneven thawing. Water prevents browning and creates steam rather than searing. Uneven thawing leaves frozen chunks that cool the pan.

If they want a sear, the first priority is to thaw vegetables completely and evenly. The user’s microwave method partially cooks them and leaves dry spots. A better method is to soak them in hot tap water, which thaws quickly without the harsh, uneven heating of a microwave. After thawing, draining and drying are critical—excess surface water must be blotted off. For spinach, squeezing out water after thawing is necessary because it releases so much liquid.

Cooking order matters greatly. Since water from leafy greens will kill any browning, hardest, driest vegetables (like carrots) should hit the hot oil first. Then medium-textured ones like broccoli or green beans go in. The limp, waterlogged spinach (thoroughly wrung out) goes in last, after the others are mostly cooked, just to wilt and warm. Peas only need a quick finish. This sequences the release of water to minimize steaming.

I should also manage expectations: frozen vegetables will never be exactly like fresh because of the structural damage, but the right technique can still yield a satisfying stir-fry. The answer will walk through a clear, lazy-friendly method: hot water thaw, dry, then cook in order of hardness and water content.

Why is putting hot milk in a thermos not recommended?

A colleague of mine just got a new thermos (inox), [this model](https://thumbs.dreamstime.com/z/aluminum-thermos-open-cup-17409838.jpg), and actually read all instruction, and we were surprised to read that it is not recommended to pour hot milk in the thermos.

My opinion was that:

1. Unlike tea of coffee, a lot of [micro-organisms](https://www.uoguelph.ca/foodscience/book-page/types-microorganisms-and-their-activity-milk) live in milk, will end up being a favorable place for those micro-organisms to generate a culture (which will be more and more difficult to get rid off, and will contaminate any other fluid poured in the thermos)
2. If you don't wash it straight away, it will really stink.
3. The milk being full of water-insoluble proteins/fat, it will "coat" the internal thermos walls (gross!) - I've already seeing that "coat" forming in plastic containers, and I guess it won't be any different in inox containers.

I've actually not found an answer online, so I thought that here I could find some experts. I realize this could be a cross-question for [Biology SE](https://biology.stackexchange.com/), but I felt it more food-related.

It depends on the design. Some can't be washed properly, and milky liquids are much harder to clean off by rinsing than water or most water-based drinks

My genuine Thermos brand flask wouldn't be a problem because all the surfaces that come into contact with the food are accessible.

My previous small cheap flask had a pouring system in the lid that meant the contents passed through a non-washable chamber (clipped together in a way that wasn't designed to be opened). My flask is mainly used for kayaking, it has to be made up beforehand as fiddling about with powders when on a riverbank in the pouring rain doesn't tend to get you a hot drink when you need it. At that point it would have gone in the bin even if I hadn't just broken it.

A point mentioned in the comments is that the instructions for [one particular Thermos](https://www.thermos.co.uk/UK_careuse_stainless_steel_vacuum_flask.aspx) say *This product must NOT be used for keeping milk products or baby food warm or cool, to avoid the possibility of bacterial growth.* This is the only reference to *warm* contents in these instructions; the word used elsewhere is *hot* (excluding washing-up instructions). *Warm* implies attempting to maintain temperatures in the danger zone. Why do shrimp / lobster / crab turn pink or red when cooking?

Cooking is a form of chemistry - so there must be a *scientific* reason behind this.

*Why do all crustaceans turn pink or red when cooked?*

Crustaceans like shrimp, lobsters, crabs and crayfish have a pigment called [astaxanthin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astaxanthin) in their shells.

Astaxanthin belongs to the terpines class of chemicals of which the carotenoid **¹** class is a subdivision and, in a marine environment, gets produced by [an algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haematococcus_pluvialis) that is subsequently consumed by crustaceans (and other animals like salmon, red trout, red sea bream *and flamingos* **²** )

As Astaxanthin absorbs blue light, it will appear as its [opposing additive colour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_color): a deep red. The more this deep red is diluted, it will subsequently become red, orange or yellow in colour.

> While the crustaceans are alive, astaxanthin lies wrapped in the tight embrace of a protein called crustacyanin. The protein holds the pigment so tight, in fact, that it’s flattened and its light-absorption properties are changed. The astaxanthin-crustacyanin complex then winds up giving off a blue-green color. ³

This can be observed if you have aggressive live lobsters you want to cook: just put them in the sink full of water with a glass of white wine added for a few minutes and they will ~~get drunk instantly as they've never had alcohol in their lives~~ *relax* and the blue colouring can then be clearly seen at the fronds of their [carapace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carapace).

The astaxanthin-crustacyanin complex gets:

> separated when a crab or lobster is cooked. Crustacyanin is not heat-stable, so introducing it to a boiling pot of water or a grill causes it to relax its bonds with astaxanthin, unravel and let the pigment’s true bold red color shine through. ³

**Note ¹:** Carrots have given carotenoid its name  
**Note ²:** Eating minuscule shrimp containing this carotenoid is what turns flamingos pink: pink flamingos will be more well-fed than pale flamingos...  
**Note ³:** [Sourced here](https://mentalfloss.com/article/31483/why-do-crabs-and-lobsters-turn-red-when-you-cook-them)
thinking: I need to explain the color change in cooked crustaceans. The question explicitly asks for the scientific reason, so I'll recall the relevant food chemistry. I know that many red, orange, and pink colors in seafood come from carotenoid pigments, specifically astaxanthin. This is the same pigment that makes salmon and flamingos pink; crustaceans get it from eating algae that produce it. But live lobsters and shrimp often appear bluish, greenish, or brown, not red. So the red must be masked somehow. I remember that astaxanthin is bound to a protein called crustacyanin in the shell. The protein interaction changes the pigment's arrangement or conjugation, altering its light absorption so it reflects blue-green light instead of red. That's why a live lobster can look dark blue-green. When you cook it, the heat denatures the crustacyanin protein, causing it to unwind and release the astaxanthin. Freed, the pigment reverts to its natural state, absorbing blue light and reflecting red/orange wavelengths. That's the core mechanism. I can also mention the "drunk lobster" trick to reveal the blue color before cooking, as a practical demonstration of the protein-pigment complex. To structure the answer, I'll first introduce astaxanthin and its source, then explain the crustacyanin masking, the heat-induced release, and maybe briefly note the broader occurrence of this phenomenon in other animals. That covers the science clearly.

Does meat need to be washed before preparation?

I don't even remember where I have learned that, but I've always thought it common knowledge: Before a piece of meat gets seasoned, or malleted for tenderizing (sorry, don't know the English word for that), or marinated, or thrown into the pan, or ground, it should be first washed under the faucet, and then patted dry. When I think of it, it also makes sense to me, because the bacteria are always on the meat surface, never inside. So I don't think it is a vestige of the time one got bloodied cuts from the village butcher, but that it applies to the modern meat pieces sold on absorbent pads too.

And then I read [this question](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/14556/do-you-use-paper-or-cloth-towel-for-patting-a-meat-dry-before-frying), which presumes patting (but doesn't mention washing). Most of the answers and comments seem to indicate that patting isn't always considered necessary, and there is no mention of washing the meat or of the dripping water from the washing. In fact, the answers and comments wouldn't make much sense if one assumes that the meat has been just washed.

So is washing compulsory, is it optional but a good idea, is it plain useless, or does it even have disadvantages for the meat?

It's neither necessary nor a particularly good idea; it does little to remove bacteria from the surface of the meat (which you're about to cook, remember) and runs the risk of spraying/dripping bacteria all over the kitchen.

The FSIS has an article on it [here](https://www.fsis.usda.gov/wps/portal/fsis/topics/food-safety-education/get-answers/food-safety-fact-sheets/safe-food-handling/washing-food-does-it-promote-food-safety/washing-food):

> Washing raw poultry, beef, pork, lamb, or veal before cooking it is not recommended. Bacteria in raw meat and poultry juices can be spread to other foods, utensils, and surfaces.

The only exception would be something like vac-packed, wet-aged meat where you need to remove the salt, but that's a matter of preference.

I have never washed a piece of meat in my life and I'm still here!
thinking:
The user has a deeply ingrained habit of washing meat before preparation, thinking it removes surface bacteria and is common knowledge. They’re now questioning that practice after reading a discussion that presumes meat is patted dry but never mentions washing. The core of the confusion is whether the washing step is still necessary, beneficial, or perhaps even counterproductive. They want a clear verdict: compulsory, optional, useless, or harmful.

I need to recall the relevant food-science and food-safety principles. The bacteria of concern on raw meat (like Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli) are predominantly on the surface, not inside whole cuts. The user's instinct that surface washing might remove them seems logical, but the key misconception is about sanitation. Washing under running water doesn't reliably remove pathogenic bacteria from the meat surface—it mostly just wets it. More critically, the splashing action of water hitting the meat and bouncing into the sink area can aerosolize bacteria-laden juices, spreading microscopic droplets onto countertops, clothes, and other foods. That's a well-documented cross-contamination risk.

The kill step for surface pathogens is cooking to a safe internal temperature. Since meat is going to be cooked, any surface bacteria will be destroyed by the heat. So the washing step provides no meaningful safety benefit and introduces a real hazard. This is the consensus of food safety authorities like the USDA's FSIS, which explicitly says not to wash raw meat or poultry. The answer should cite that guidance.

I also need to consider whether there are any valid exceptions. The user might have encountered processes like rinsing a brined turkey or washing salt off vac-packed wet-aged beef. That's not a safety step—it's a flavor or texture preference to remove excess salt or purge. The answer can mention that as a niche scenario where rinsing and patting dry is done for culinary reasons, not hygiene.

So the structure of the response will be: directly refute the necessity and wisdom of washing, explain the dual reasons (lack of efficacy and cross-contamination risk), cite the official FSIS stance, briefly note the non-safety exception for salt removal, and close with a light personal anecdote that underscores how unnecessary the practice actually is. That covers all parts of the question without overcomplicating it.

Why does diluted half & half not make a substitute for whole milk?

I noticed that cutting half & half with water does not make it taste like whole milk. What is the reason for this?

I'm trying to apply some systems thinking to my understanding of ingredients.

The difference between whole milk (or any milk, really) and half-and-half is one of fat content, not overall concentration. Half-and-half gets its name from being a 50/50 blend of milk and cream, which normally separate because the less dense fats concentrated in cream float naturally to the top of the mostly-water milk. However, milk also contains a number of other proteins, sugars, etc. that give it flavor. When you dilute half-and-half with plain water, you're diluting the fat content (potentially down to a similar range as contained in whole milk) but you're *also* diluting all those other flavorful components. You wind up with something that has the right fat level but not enough of anything else, and which tastes somewhat flat and flabby by comparison with proper milk.
thinking: I need to understand why diluting half & half with water doesn’t yield a whole-milk-like flavor. Half & half is a blend of equal parts milk and cream. Whole milk has roughly 3.25% milkfat by weight, while half & half has around 10–18%. If I add water to half & half to cut its fat percentage down to that of whole milk, I’m simply reducing the concentration of everything in the half & half—not only fat, but also milk proteins (casein and whey), lactose, and minerals. Whole milk, however, has a full complement of these non-fat milk solids at a typical level of about 8.5%. Diluting half & half with water lowers the fat to the target range, but it also drives the protein and sugar content well below what whole milk provides. The flavor and mouthfeel of milk depend on both the fat and the non-fat components; proteins contribute body and a subtle savory note, while lactose adds sweetness. Without enough of those, the mixture tastes watery, flat, and lacking the characteristic richness of whole milk. So the simple fat-correction overlooks the fact that half & half starts with a much lower ratio of non-fat solids to fat, and watering it down only makes that imbalance worse. I’ll structure the explanation around the distinction between fat content and total milk solids, emphasizing that milk’s flavor comes from more than just fat.

Why use a kettle to heat water?

Whenever I need to heat up water for a French press or hot chocolate, I do it in the microwave. Is there a good reason to use a kettle instead of the microwave to heat water?

Bear in mind that I'm using an electric kettle, rather than a stove-top one.

First, the advantage of a kettle is that it is quite efficient, and turns itself off once the water is boiling.
This as opposed to the microwave, which only stops after a set time, rather than relying on the condition of the water.

Second, a microwave can cause water to superheat, particularly in a ceramic or glass container. This means that there is a certain risk that the water will "jump out" at you once you add something to it or put a spoon in.

Additionally, most kettles have more power than the average microwave, so the kettle is probably faster to boil water.
thinking:
The user asks why someone would use a kettle instead of a microwave for heating water for a French press or hot chocolate. The underlying assumption is that the microwave seems convenient, so we need to identify the practical advantages of the kettle. I'll focus on electric kettles since they are common and have features directly relevant to the comparison.

First, consider efficiency and control. An electric kettle is purpose-built for boiling water: a heating element is immersed in the water, so nearly all the electrical energy is transferred to the water as heat. Once the water reaches boiling point, a thermostat or bimetallic strip triggers an automatic shutoff. This means you don’t have to guess a time and the kettle won’t continue heating dry, which is both convenient and safe. A microwave, by contrast, requires the user to estimate the time needed, which can vary with water volume and container, leading to under- or over-heating.

Next, safety regarding superheating. Microwaves can heat water without inducing the normal convection currents you’d see with a bottom-heated container. If the container is very smooth (like ceramic or glass), the water can exceed its boiling point yet remain still, without forming bubbles. When the user adds a spoon, sugar, or coffee grounds, this disrupts the superheated state and causes a sudden, violent boil-over, posing a scald risk. A kettle, with its heating element at the bottom and often a roughened surface, promotes nucleation and boiling at the expected temperature, eliminating that hazard.

Finally, speed. Most electric kettles draw 1500‒3000 watts, while a typical microwave might be 700‒1200 watts. Even accounting for efficiency differences, the higher wattage means the kettle can bring the same amount of water to a boil faster.

These points collectively make a strong case for using an electric kettle. I’ll structure the answer by first noting that I’m referring to an electric kettle, then presenting these three reasons in a clear, concise list.

Can one bake a cake with a cooked egg instead of a raw one?

[This recent question](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/75148/is-there-any-way-to-bring-an-egg-to-its-natural-state-not-boiled-after-you-coo) about a person who wanted to bake a cake but only had a cooked egg left suggested me an even stupider one: **is it possible to bake a cake with a cooked egg instead of a raw one?** After all, the egg is going to end up cooked inside the cake anyway.

I imagine that it's going to be tricky to mix it with the dough, but with a hand mixer and a sufficient amount of violence everything is possible.

Or are the chemical processes of boiling an egg and cooking it inside the dough fundamentally different?

I would say no. The function of the egg in the cake is to go in raw, mix with the other stuff, and once the raw egg has penetrated and coated the other ingredients thoroughly, bind it all together with that bouncy, sticky solidified eggy property which comes into existence as the egg cooks.

Cooking the egg first all by itself, then adding to a cake would be like drying some crazy glue, then grinding up that hardened crust and putting the resulting powder between two things you want to stick together. The gluing action is all over when the glue has dried.
thinking:
The question asks whether a cake can be made using an already cooked egg (like hard-boiled) instead of a raw one. The underlying intuition is that since the egg will be cooked inside the cake anyway, maybe the pre-cooking doesn't matter. I need to consider what eggs do in a cake batter and whether those functions can survive being cooked separately first.

In baking, raw egg serves several roles: it provides moisture, but more importantly, the proteins in the raw egg unfold and coagulate during baking, binding the flour, fat, and sugar into a cohesive structure. Raw egg also helps emulsify fats and liquids, trap air for leavening, and then sets into a network that gives the cake its crumb. If you hard-cook an egg first, the proteins have already denatured and coagulated into a solid mass. They can't dissolve into the batter, coat starch granules, or form a new continuous network upon baking. The cooked egg would just be small rubbery bits suspended in the batter, unable to glue the ingredients together. No amount of mixing or violence will revert those proteins to their raw state — protein coagulation is irreversible in this context. The result would be a crumbly or dense mess, not a proper cake.

I might initially think that because the egg ends up cooked, it's the same, but that's a misunderstanding: the critical step is that raw egg undergoes coagulation *in situ* alongside the rest of the batter. Pre-coagulating the egg is like trying to stick two pieces of paper together with powdered, already-dried glue. The binding power is gone. So the answer is firmly no. I'll structure the response by explaining the egg's function, why pre-cooking prevents that, and including an analogy to dried glue to make it vivid, just as the provided final answer does.

Why did James Bond heat up the knife for his foie gras?

I was reading Fleming's *Casino Royale* and ran into the following curious detail, when describing James Bond's meal:

> Later, as Bond was finishing his first straight whisky ‘on the rocks’ and was contemplating the paté de foie gras and cold langouste which the waiter had just laid out for him, the telephone rang.  
> ...  
> Bond shook himself, then he picked up his knife and selected the thickest of the pieces of hot toast.  
> **He dipped the knife into the glass of very hot water** which stood beside the pot of Strasbourg porcelain and reminded himself to tip the waiter doubly for this particular meal.

Now, from the text, it seems he's about to put foie gras on a toast. As far as I'm aware it's quite soft and not hard to cut with the knife and spread.

**What exactly is the point of dipping the knife into hot water then?**

From this [link](http://www.seriouseats.com/2012/12/food-lab-pan-seared-foie-gras-how-to.html)

> The key to slicing and portioning foie is to treat it like a rich
> mousse-cake: Make sure to heat up your knife under running water in
> between every slice. A cold knife will catch and stick in the foie,
> causing it to tear or crumble. A hot knife will melt the fat as it
> goes through, leaving you with clean, smooth surfaces to sear.
thinking: The question asks why James Bond dipped his knife in hot water before using it on foie gras. Foie gras is a fatty liver preparation, rich in rendered fat at room temperature. To understand the technique, I recall that cold or room-temperature fat can be firm and waxy, while gentle heat liquefies it. A cold metal knife would drag against the semi-solid fat, causing the delicate liver to tear or crumble under pressure. By warming the blade, the knife melts a microscopic layer of fat on contact, acting as a lubricant. This allows the blade to glide through cleanly, producing smooth, intact slices and making it easier to spread on toast. The hot water bath is a simple way to reheat the knife between strokes, maintaining the effect. I’ll structure the response by explaining this principle: the hot knife melts fat to prevent sticking and tearing, drawing a parallel to slicing other soft, fatty foods like a mousse-cake.

What's the difference between hollandaise, mayonnaise, and aïoli?

I was following a [recipe by Gordon Ramsay](https://youtu.be/WkrMRk2qdqo?t=4m25s), that included a hollandaise.
However while making it I couldn't help but think I was making a warm mayonnaise.

This brings me to my question: What's the difference between mayonnaise, hollandaise, and aïoli?

(Gordon Ramsay did say he was making a "modern version" of hollandaise using olive oil instead of butter, so I expect what he did isn't a hollandaise in the usual sense?)

[Mayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayonnaise), at its most basic, is egg yolk and oil, with a little vinegar, whipped into an emulsion.

[Aioli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aioli) starts with oil and garlic, and sometimes vinegar or lemon. Some versions (French-Provençal, apparently) add egg yolk for an end result close to mayonnaise, but the yolk is not required.

[Hollandaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollandaise_sauce) is a cooked sauce made from egg yolk and butter, sometimes flavored with lemon and pepper. I think it must have a much larger ratio of egg yolk to other ingredients in it, since it remains brightly yellow and thick.

[Bearnaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9arnaise_sauce) is a variation of hollandaise, which uses white wine vinegar to emulsify the egg yolks and butter, and flavors the resulting sauce with shallot, chervil, and tarragon. Like an aioli, it is not defined by the emulsion but by the flavoring agents. Adding terragon and capers, or tarragon and shallots, to a hollandaise (or other egg-yolk emulsion sauce) will produce a 'faux-bearnaise'.

The garlic defines the aioli, which is also the only one that can be made without egg yolk. The choice of butter rather than oil makes a hollandaise, and it is cooked as a sauce to set the yolks (which neither of the others require). The yolk and oil combination itself is the central concept of mayonnaise, while it can be flavored, it doesn't have to be.

The sauces are quite similar, though, and an emulsion of egg yolk with seasonings might be called by any name. The difference between a garlic mayo and a french-style aioli are likely to be pretty subtle. Likewise, a mayo flavored with lemon and pepper will be hard to distinguish from a hollandaise which uses oil - although hollandaise is usually cooked to set it, so the texture may be different. And a aioli with butter will be very similar to a hollandaise with garlic. Adding tarragon and shallot to any of them is likely to produce a bearnaise type sauce.

All three recipes are very loose and broadly defined, since they can be tweaked a lot depending on preferences - so it makes it hard to pin down other factors like ingredient ratios that might distinguish the recipes. The sauces that add flavorings or substitute ingredients will tend to be named one or the other based more on recipe origin, familiarity, and marketing rather than any clearly defined difference.
thinking:
I need to break down what defines each sauce at its core, because the user's experience—making something called hollandaise that felt like warm mayonnaise—points straight to the common confusion around emulsified egg-yolk sauces. They already suspect Ramsay’s olive-oil version isn’t standard, so my answer needs to clarify the canonical differences first, then address why the lines get blurry.

I recall that mayonnaise is fundamentally a cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, usually with an acid. Hollandaise is a warm emulsion, cooked gently, and the fat source is butter, not oil. That cooking step sets the yolk proteins and gives a different texture. Aïoli is classically a garlic and oil emulsion, made without any egg, though many modern recipes add yolk and turn it into garlic mayonnaise. So the key differentiators are the fat (butter vs. oil), the presence of garlic, and whether heat is applied to thicken the yolks.

Checking my initial instinct: calling hollandaise a “warm mayonnaise” is tempting but inaccurate, because mayonnaise isn’t cooked and uses oil. Aïoli with egg is very close to garlic mayo, but the traditional Provençal version is eggless, so “garlic” is the defining feature, not the egg. Béarnaise is a related derivative that uses a flavor base of tarragon, shallots, and sometimes wine vinegar, but the question is mainly about the first three.

Is butter ever the same after having been melted?

I was recently doing some experiments with butter which involved melting it gently in the microwave and pouring it into dishes. It seemed to me that after the butter had cooled and re-solidified, it wasn't really the same. The color was yellower, and the texture somewhat grainy.

Obviously if I microwave the butter a lot, the water will boil off. But I microwaved on low power, stirring frequently, hoping to minimize water loss.

Is there some change that happens to butter when it's melted and then cooled? Or am I imagining things?

Butter may look totally amorphous, but there's actually a fair amount of structure in the fat, in particular fat crystals that make it firmer. Melting it disrupts all that structure, and it can't regain it just by resolidifying, so the structure of previously melted butter really is different.

You might notice that this is similar to chocolate: if you take smooth, snappy tempered chocolate, melt it, and let it resolidify, the texture will often be grainy, soft, or even crumbly. That's also thanks to fat crystals, in that case in the cocoa butter.

To back up a bit, let's look at how butter is made. Churning is the most well-known step, but there's more:

- **Aging (heating, cooling, and storing the cream).** The cream is heated and cooled, with resting periods at various temperatures, which encourages formation of certain kinds of fat crystals. (The details of this process vary; for example [different temperatures can be used depending on the hardness of the milkfat](http://www.webexhibits.org/butter/aging.html).)
- **Churning.** This damages the fat globules, causing them to release fat, which forms much of the mass of the butter and lets it collect into grains.
- **Working/kneading.** After draining off the buttermilk, the grains are kneaded together. This evens out small amounts of buttermilk trapped in the grains, and fat crystals can also come together into larger networks.

So the final butter actually has three forms of fat in it: fat crystals, free fat, and fat globules. The fat crystals make it firmer, and the free fat and globules make it softer. This also explains why butter isn't all the same texture. For example, from On Food and Cooking:

> Feeds rich in polyunsaturated fats, especially fresh pasturage, produce softer butters; hay and grain harder ones. The butter maker also influences consistency by the rate and degree of cooling to which he subjects the cream during the aging period, and by how extensively he works the new butter. These conditions control the relative proportions of firming crystalline fat and softening globular and free fat.

So when you melt and resolidify butter, it's not just a simple solid to liquid to solid thing. You're disrupting the crystals, and potentially even rupturing a few more fat globules. That means a couple things:

- There's likely more free fat and less crystals, which explains why previously melted butter can be much softer than the original butter.
- The crystals that do remain or reform won't have the same structure as the original ones, since you didn't follow the same heating/cooling/storing regimen. That explains the graininess you noticed. It's possible that working/kneading the butter might even that back out to some extent.

The exact texture of your previously melted butter will probably vary, depending on how hot you melted it and how fast you cooled it afterwards.
thinking:
I need to figure out what’s happening to the butter on a physical level beyond simple phase changes. The user mentions minimal water loss, yet the butter feels grainier and looks yellower after resolidifying. That suggests the fat itself is reorganizing differently.

Butter isn't just a homogeneous blob of fat; it's a complex microstructure. I recall from food science that milk fat contains a mix of triglycerides with different melting points, and during butter manufacture (aging the cream, churning, working) specific fat crystal networks are intentionally formed. Those crystals give butter its characteristic firmness and smooth mouthfeel. When heated past a certain point, all crystals melt completely, erasing that carefully built structure. On cooling, the fat recrystallizes, but not in the same organized way—the uncontrolled cooling produces larger, uneven crystal aggregates, which explains the grainy texture. The color change might be due to how light scatters differently off this new crystal arrangement or minor redistribution of carotenoids, but the texture shift is the more robust signal.

This is essentially the same principle as chocolate tempering, where cocoa butter must crystallize into a specific polymorph to be glossy and snappy; untempered chocolate is soft and grainy. So the answer should first acknowledge that the structure is destroyed, then compare to chocolate, then break down how butter gets its original structure through aging, churning, and working, and finally explain that without that controlled process, recrystallization yields a different product. This covers the user’s observation directly. I’ll structure it by leading with the crystal disruption idea, then the chocolate analogy, then the butter-making details, and finally tie it back to the changes the user noticed.

How should I keep the vegetables from flying off the board when I cut them?

Whenever I chop veggies like onions or carrots they sometimes just fly off the chopping board into the open space of the kitchen. Carrots do that especially often – I cannot chop them (dicing is also problematic) without the occasional pieces flying off the board.

What am I missing here? I try to imitate Jamie Oliver and Gordon Ramsay chopping videos bit by bit.

Use a sharp knife, dull knives don't slice, they split the same way an axe splits logs and that will generate that sideways force that throws carrot bits.

Also learn to practice your slicing and chopping technique. You shouldn't be dropping the blade straight down like a axe or guillotine. You should be moving the blade in a orbital movement, so that you are slicing in a forward direction while the blade is on its way down to and through the carrot. By slicing properly much less of your veg will have that energy buildup because they won't "snap" apart but will be sliced apart neatly.

Search YouTube for Basic Knife Skills and watch several videos, then practice, and start slowly. You will get faster with time and time only, don't rush it or you'll get sloppy and may hurt yourself.
thinking:
The problem of vegetable pieces flying off the board usually comes down to two things: knife sharpness and cutting technique. When a knife is dull, it doesn't sever the fibers cleanly. Instead, it acts like a wedge, building up pressure until the vegetable suddenly splits apart. That sudden release of energy can send pieces flying, especially with dense, brittle vegetables like carrots. The same thing happens if you bring the blade straight down in a guillotine-like chop—the entire force is directed vertically, compressing the vegetable until it fractures laterally.

Imitating chefs like Jamie Oliver or Gordon Ramsay requires more than just speed. They use a sharp knife and a slicing motion: the blade moves forward as it descends, following a slight elliptical or orbital path. This shears through the vegetable gradually rather than splitting it all at once, so there’s no sudden snap to launch pieces. The forward component also stabilizes the cut, keeping the vegetable in place.

Beyond that, a sharp knife is non-negotiable—it glides through fibers with minimal resistance, so you don’t need to force it. The answer should emphasize these two points clearly, then recommend the asker find basic knife skills videos, start slow, and build speed without rushing, because control comes first. I’ll structure it as: (1) sharp knife to prevent splitting, (2) proper orbital slicing technique to avoid the snap, and (3) practice with patience.

How can 100% peanut butter have more protein than 100% peanuts

I am looking at:

- 100% peanut butter (no added salt, sugar, oils or anything else)
- 100% roasted peanuts (no added salt, sugar, oils or anything else)

When looking thought different sources, I can always notice the following:

- Peanut butter has more protein (as % of calories) than peanuts

example sources (I've looked through a dozen more, but please check others, maybe mine are not representative?):

<http://www.waitrose.com/shop/ProductView-10317-10001-5588-Waitrose+LOVE+life+roasted+peanuts>

<http://shop.wholeearthfoods.com/collections/award-winning-peanut-butter/products/whole-earth-100-nuts-crunchy-peanut-butte-227-g>

Why is this? If no ingredients are added, how is it possible for the macronutrients to change (as % of the calories). Different levels of roasting cannot be the reason because they should not change macronutrients disproportionally.

The only explanation I can think of is if in the process of making peanut butter, some part of the peanut is removed and that part contains a low protein amount. Some sources say that when peanut butter is made, the 'bitter heart of the peanut' is removed. Could that explain it?

If anyone has some insight I would be very interested to learn.

There's definitely some rounding going on because the peanut butter has 100.1g of nutrients per 100g of product. This isn't enough to explain the discrepancy. Adding up the nutrients on the roasted peanuts gives 95.4g. I think we can assume the other 4.6% is water. So perhaps more water has been driven off the peanut butter.

What I think is more likely (though could be additional) is that there's *significantly* less fat in the peanut butter (48.1% vs 51.7%). While this could be down to different varieties of peanut, I suspect some fat is removed in the processing, perhaps to avoid an oil slick on the surface.

Most likely of all is just different source data. Different peanuts may have been used in the calculations -- whether that is consistent with the actual ingredients used is another matter. In fact if you look at nutrition information for raw peanuts online, you'll get a range of values. There's nothing special about peanuts, the same is true for bananas. I'm sure if you look at the scientific literature on any foodstuff, you'll find a range of values published, reflecting natural variation as well as measurement variabilility -- this will then propagate to the values published to the consumer.
thinking:
I need to make sense of a puzzling nutritional comparison: two products that are both 100% peanuts, yet the peanut butter shows a higher protein share of total calories than the whole roasted peanuts. The user has provided specific links, so I'll mentally pull up typical label data for such products. Whole Earth crunchy peanut butter (just peanuts) often lists around 48g fat, 27g protein, and 12g carbs per 100g, with a total that may slightly exceed 100g due to rounding. Roasted peanuts from Waitrose might show around 52g fat, 26g protein, and 13g carbs, summing to about 95g – the remainder being mostly water. Right away I notice the peanut butter has less fat and more protein proportionally. The question is how that shift happens when no other ingredients are added.

I consider physical changes during processing. Roasting drives off moisture, but both products are roasted, so water content shouldn't differ massively unless the peanut butter is ground while hot and loses more steam, or is roasted longer. A small water loss would concentrate all macros, but it wouldn't change the protein-to-fat ratio. The fact that the peanut butter is lower in fat suggests some fat may be physically removed. In natural peanut butter production, the grinding releases oil; if the paste is allowed to settle, some surface oil might be poured off before jarring to reduce separation, which would lower the overall fat percentage and thus boost the relative contribution of protein and carbs to the energy. That's a plausible manufacturing step even in a "100% nuts" product, as no non-peanut ingredients are added.

But I also know that different peanut varieties and growing conditions lead to substantial differences in oil and protein content. The nutrition figures on a label are averages from a database or batch testing, not necessarily a direct analysis of the exact nuts in that jar. The Waitrose peanuts and the Whole Earth peanut butter likely source peanuts from different farms or regions; the labeled fat content for the roasted peanuts is around 52g, while the peanut butter is around 48g, which falls within the known natural range for peanut composition. The slight rounding error (100.1g total) just adds a small distortion.

So the core reasons are likely a combination of minor water loss, possible fat skimming, and – most importantly – the use of different peanut stocks for the nutritional calculations. I'll structure my answer by first noting the rounding oddity, then discussing how processing might remove water or fat, and then emphasize that natural variation and separate source data are the most probable causes, with the caveat that labels often aren't a direct chemical analysis of that exact batch.
