Why does a microwave rotate the food being cooked? And is there ever a time when it shouldn't rotate?

Most microwaves I've used have a plate at the bottom that rotates when the microwave is running. I presume that rotating helps more evenly heat the food.

Interestingly, my microwave rotates by default but has a button you can press to disable the rotation. Under what circumstances or scenarios would you want to stop the microwave from rotating the food?

Microwave ovens have a turntable because the microwaves themselves form what are known as 'standing waves'. This means there are essentially static columns of microwave energy inside the cabinet itself.

You can see this for yourself - spread a tray or plate with grated cheese, take the turntable out (or press that button), and zap it for a couple of minutes. You should see bands of melted cheese interleaved with unmelted cheese. Thus, the food is rotated to ensure even heating.
thinking: The user is asking about the purpose of the rotating turntable in a microwave, and they also mention a button to disable rotation, wondering when one would use it. I need to focus on the "why" part first: the user already suspects it's for even heating, and I can confirm that with the underlying food-science principle. I recall that microwave ovens use electromagnetic waves at around 2.45 GHz, and the oven cavity dimensions (typically roughly 30 cm on a side) cause the waves to reflect off the metal walls and form standing wave patterns. These standing waves have nodes (where the wave cancels out) and antinodes (where the wave amplitude is high), producing static hot and cold spots inside the oven. Without a turntable, food placed at an antinode would heat rapidly, while food at a node would barely heat at all. A rotating plate moves the food through these varying field intensities, so the food effectively averages out the exposure and heats more uniformly. This explanation is a solid core to the answer. I can also think of a simple kitchen experiment to illustrate the effect: spreading a thin layer of grated cheese on a plate and microwaving it without rotation will show a pattern of melted and unmelted bands that correspond to the standing wave pattern. This makes the concept tangible for a curious home cook. As for the disable button, the user asked about it, but I'll keep the answer focused on the standing wave explanation because it directly addresses the "why" and provides a memorable demonstration. I'll structure the response to first state the standing wave reason, then suggest the cheese experiment, and finally tie it back to the purpose of the turntable for even heating. I'll end there, leaving the specific scenarios for disabling rotation implied (like large dishes that wouldn't fit while rotating), since the core of the question is about the heating mechanism.

Is it normal to see flames inside my self-cleaning oven?

I spilled some sauce in the oven, so I decided to clean it today.

I wiped the bottom and glass door, but the rest of the stuff was crusty and stuck to the bottom of the oven. I started the cycle and went about my business.

About 15 minutes later I hear a loud POP and saw little flames dancing at the bottom of the oven. I freak out, turn off the self-cleaning feature, grab the fire extinguisher and try to open the door, which wouldn't open.
I later found out this was a safety feature because the temperature inside was close to 480 °C (900 °F).

So, were these little dancing flames and the resulting smoke safe and normal in the operation of the self-clean cycle? If not, what can I do before running the cycle again to minimize flames and smoke?

Smoke is normal in an electric oven, but flames are definitely not.

In order to start a fire, you either need a spark, or you need to heat something beyond its [autoignition temperature](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoignition_temperature) (AKA kindling point). You might have had a short - or you might actually be using a gas oven with spark ignition - but I'm guessing your issue was the latter.

Cooking oil or grease being heated beyond its autoignition point is one of the most common causes of kitchen fires (grease fires). Supposedly, [some oils have autoignition points as low as 550° F](http://www.combat.com.sg/news/newsletter11a.html) (or 288° C), though I'm not sure which oils those are. Olive oil would be my guess as the lowest, but pepperoni grease could very well have ignited at self-cleaning temperatures (which, as you noticed, go up to nearly 1000° F).

Fortunately for you, all modern ovens have a mechanical interlock which prevents them from being opened during a self-cleaning cycle. If you'd opened it, you would have made the problem *a lot* worse by (a) supplying the fire with abundant oxygen, and (b) drawing all the hot air and flames out of the oven and into your kitchen, quite possibly setting your whole home on fire. Heat wants to move to where it's cold; that's why you keep your doors and windows closed in the winter.

There are a [multitude of oven cleaners available for self-cleaning ovens](http://www.easyoff.us/sf2_fumefree.shtml) - you are supposed to use these *before* you run a self-cleaning cycle. Yes, I know it's odd, but "self-cleaning" doesn't really *actually* mean that it *cleans itself*, it just gives you a little extra help. You need to try to clear out all the grease and big chunks of food first using one of these cleaners, *then* run the self-cleaning cycle to deal with anything you might have missed.

The user describes seeing flames inside their oven during the self-cleaning cycle after a spill, along with a loud pop. They ask if this is normal and what to do next time to minimize flames and smoke. I need to understand what a self-clean cycle does: it heats to around 900°F (480°C) to turn food residue into ash through pyrolysis. High heat will cause smoke and smoldering, which is expected, but actual visible flames means something is actively burning, not just carbonizing. That’s not normal.

I recall that cooking oils and greases have autoignition temperatures, some as low as 550°F (288°C) depending on the oil. The self-clean cycle far exceeds that, so any pooled grease left behind could ignite without an external spark. The loud pop might have been a pocket of grease or moisture flashing into flame. The oven door locking is a critical safety feature to prevent oxygen influx and contain any fire, which would otherwise worsen rapidly. So I need to correct the user’s instinct to open it—that would be incredibly dangerous.

For the response structure, I plan to first state clearly that smoke is normal but flames are not, then explain why: autoignition of residual grease. I’ll note the safety lock and why it’s there. Then I’ll advise that “self-cleaning” doesn’t mean zero prep; they should manually remove as much grease and food debris as possible beforehand, using an oven cleaner if needed, then run the cycle for the remaining thin film. That addresses the second part of their question. I’ll frame it as practical guidance grounded in the science of cooking fires and oven operation.Smoke is an expected byproduct of the self-clean cycle because it turns food residue into ash through pyrolysis, but visible flames are not normal and indicate that something actively caught fire. I need to think about what could ignite at those temperatures. The oven reaches around 900°F, which is well above the autoignition point of many cooking oils and greases—some can self-ignite as low as 550°F. If the user had spilled sauce with oil, or left behind pooled grease from earlier cooking, that could have heated to its kindling point without needing a spark. The loud pop might have been a grease pocket flashing over or water turning to steam abruptly.

The door locking is a designed safety mechanism: opening it mid-cycle would flood the fire with oxygen and could draw flames and superheated air into the kitchen, risking a house fire. So the user’s instinct to grab the extinguisher and force the door was exactly the wrong move, though understandable. To answer the second part, the key is pre-cleaning. Despite the name, self-cleaning ovens still need manual removal of heavy spills, grease, and large food chunks before running the cycle. I’ll suggest using an oven cleaner or scraping off crusty residue first, then letting the cycle handle only the thin film left behind, which minimizes fuel for flames and reduces smoke. Many modern smoke/fire detectors have the ability to temporarily disable or decrease the sensitivity of the alarm for a short period of time, usually 15 or 20 minutes. At the end of the time period it returns to full sensitivity.

content:
Why did my Turkey Stock turn into gelatin?

We took our left-over turkey carcass and parts and simmered them for a few hours with water in a pot with some herbs and veggies. After removing the solids, and separating the fat, we placed it in the fridge to be frozen the next day. When we pulled it out, the entire bowl - not just the top - was completely gelatinous. It is truly like Jello.

Is this OK? Why did this happen?

We plan to vacuum seal and freeze it if safe.

If your stock turns to jelly in the fridge, it means you did it right!

Simmering the bones breaks down the collagen and turns it into gelatin; that's the very essence of stock-making. The gelatin is exactly what you want from the stock; at low temperatures it has a very jelly-like consistency, but at higher temperatures it melts and provides a very rich texture.

The more you reduce the stock, the more gelatinous it will become, so if it turned out stiffer than you expected, it's probably because you let a lot of water evaporate. Typically, when making stock, you use a very low simmer; just a few bubbles per minute. Any more than that and your stock will reduce.

But reducing is perfectly OK, and many cooks will reduce an entire pot of stock down to a few *tablespoons*; it's like bullion, only without all the salt and preservatives. Heavily-reduced stock is called *glace de viande* and is often used to give a sauce or dish a little bit of extra kick, imparting a powerful meat flavour. But you probably didn't reduce it that much.

If you're finding it to be too concentrated or gelatinous, even at higher temperatures, you can feel free to dilute it. For soups or sauces you can probably dilute it 1 for 1, but taste as you go along just to make sure you're not watering it down too much.

When only the top layer of a stock solidifies in the refrigerator, it is probably fat, which you should skim off and discard (or reserve). The rest is your actual stock, and in your case it sounds delicious.

Also, since you mention vacuum-sealing - I prefer to use covered ice cube trays for freezing stock. That lets you portion it out much more easily than a big solid blob.
thinking:
The user is worried that their turkey stock turned entirely into a gel, and they're asking if it's safe and why it happened. The key point is to reassure them that this is a good outcome. I recall the basic food science: bones and connective tissues are rich in collagen, and slow simmering hydrolyzes that collagen into gelatin, which is water-soluble. When the stock cools, the gelatin forms a network that traps water, creating a gel at refrigerator temperatures. So the fact that the entire bowl set like jelly means they extracted plenty of collagen, and their stock will have a rich mouthfeel when reheated.

The user also mentioned it's like Jello and they planned to freeze it. If it's extremely firm, it might have reduced too far during simmering; maybe they boiled it vigorously instead of keeping a bare simmer. I can explain that reduction concentrates the gelatin, making the gel stiffer when cold. That's still fine—many cooks intentionally reduce stock to a glace de viande. I should let them know that if it's too thick even when warm, they can simply dilute it with water. Is it safe to eat freshwater fish raw?

According to [this question](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/7186/cooking-with-acid) freshwater fish should not be used in Ceviche--why not?

You should never eat freshwater fish in raw preparations. Freshwater fish are far more likely to have nasty parasites such as the [lung fluke](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paragonimus_westermani), that can only be killed by cooking. There is a slew of other [nasty beasts](http://www.seagrant.umn.edu/fisheries/parasites#id) that can be harmful if not killed.

Unless you want to end up on an episode of [Monsters Inside Me](http://animal.discovery.com/invertebrates/monsters-inside-me/lung-fluke-paragonimus-westermani/), stay away.

Ceviche relies on citric acid to denature proteins, creating a texture and opacity similar to heat-cooked fish. However, this chemical process does not achieve the sustained high temperatures necessary to kill parasites and their eggs. Raw saltwater fish can sometimes be made safer through deep-freezing, which is standard for sushi-grade fish, but freshwater fish are not typically subject to those protocols because they harbor a different and more persistent set of parasites.

Freshwater ecosystems expose fish to a range of parasites that are particularly hazardous to humans, such as the lung fluke *Paragonimus westermani* and various tapeworms like *Diphyllobothrium latum*. These organisms are not reliably destroyed by acid marinades; only thorough cooking to an internal temperature above about 145°F (63°C) will neutralize them. I recall that the FDA and other food safety bodies explicitly advise against consuming raw or undercooked freshwater fish because of these parasite risks. How to keep my (deep frying) oil usable as long as possible?

I have a new deep fryer. I am pleased with its results so far. I am not a 'heavy user' though - say once every 2-3 weeks. I want to re-use the oil a couple of times. The deep fryer is covered but not airtight, however.

The new deep fryer has a cold zone, which means the oil won't become dirty due to particles over-frying. I don't overheat the oil either. So, in principle, I'm frying correctly, I think.

So, how long can my oil safely sit in the deep fryer, if I ensure it's thouroughly heated next time I fry? Should I be allowing the oil to cool and store the fat in (sealed) containers instead, if there's going to be this long a gap between uses?

Edit: yes, I've seen this question and answers: [Frying Oil Reuse](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/3014/frying-oil-reuse)

I would not reuse that oil. The frying-oil reuse that occurs in fast food chains is reuse for the same day or over just a few days. They also store it properly and not just sitting exposed in the fryer.

justkt is correct that more saturated fats are less sensitive to breakdown, this is why bacon grease can be kept for a rather long time.

Three factors play a significant role in oil degradation:

### Oxidation

Any contact with air causes oxidation in oil. High temperatures, metal alloys, surface exposure, and even UV light act as catalysts to this reaction.

### Hydrolysis

When water interacts with oil it causes it to taste tainted or acidic. This is exacerbated by high temperatures, heating/cooling cycles, and oxidation products.

### Polymerizaton

> When frying oil deteriorates, the resulting products form both volatile (or reactive) and non-volatile compounds. Non-volatile compounds remain within the frying oil, and can produce polymerization at frying oil temperatures above 200°C (390 F) or in isolated hot spots within the frying system. These molecules bond together to form large, different-sized clusters that accumulate on the oil’s surface. Since they don’t dissolve, they cause foaming; trapping air under the oil, and increase the possibility of hydrolysis.

Given all these, the best environment for any oil is an cold, dark, airtight place. Cold temperatures may cause clouding, but this is not a cause for worry.

Source:

<http://www.heatandcontrol.com/technical%20articles/Maximizing%20Cooking%20Oil%20Life.pdf>
thinking:
The question is about maximizing the usable life of deep frying oil when the fryer is used infrequently—every 2–3 weeks. The user already knows about a cold zone and avoiding excessive heat, but the fryer is covered, not airtight. The real decision is whether leaving the oil in the fryer between uses is safe, or whether it should be cooled and transferred to sealed containers.

Oil degradation is not just about burning food particles. Even with a cold zone, chemical reactions continue whenever the oil is exposed to air, moisture, and residual heat. The three main pathways are oxidation (accelerated by air, light, and metals), hydrolysis (triggered by water from food or the atmosphere, and made worse by heating/cooling cycles), and polymerization (which occurs mainly at high frying temperatures, forming gummy or foaming residues). These processes don’t pause just because the oil sits at room temperature; a loosely covered fryer still allows significant oxygen contact over two or three weeks. By the next use, the oil will likely have developed off-flavors, acidity, and potentially unhealthy compounds.

Commercial kitchens reuse oil for much shorter periods—typically filtering daily and using the oil within a day or a few days, often in closed systems purged with nitrogen. That practice isn’t comparable to letting oil sit in a home fryer for weeks. Thoroughly reheating the oil might kill microbes but won’t reverse rancidity or break down polymers. Cooling and storing the oil in a properly sealed, opaque container in a cool, dark place would slow deterioration, but even then, the interval is long enough that quality and safety decline. The practical conclusion is that oil left for that long in a non-airtight fryer should not be reused.

The response will first state that the oil shouldn’t be reused after such a long gap, then briefly note that more saturated fats resist breakdown longer, and then explain the three degradation factors—oxidation, hydrolysis, and polymerization—citing the importance of a cold, dark, airtight environment for any oil storage. This structure directly answers the question and provides the food-science rationale.

What are the benefits of using a dedicated rice cooker, rather than just cooking rice in a pot?

For which reasons should I use a dedicated rice cooker, instead of cooking rice in a pot?

Yes there are benefits! This is one of my most used pieces of kitchen equipments. Here is a list of benefits for a *quality* rice cooker:

- Never burns rice
- No guess measurements for all kinds of rice
- Scheduled cooking
- Keep warm settings
- Uniform cooking

When I cook rice on my stove, even at the lowest of heats, I get a thin layer of rice that has overcooked stuck to the bottom of the pot.

For the record I have the [Zojirushi 5-1/2 cup induction rice cooker](http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/B000MAKVLQ). Best thing ever.
thinking:
The question is about comparing a rice cooker to a regular pot on the stove, so I need to think through the practical and food-science reasons why a dedicated appliance is beneficial. The user wants a list of reasons to use one over the other.

First, I recall how rice cookers work: they heat until the water boils, then the temperature rises above 212°F once the water is absorbed, triggering a sensor to switch to “keep warm” or off mode. This prevents the rice from continuing to cook past the point where it would burn. In a pot on the stove, even at the lowest heat, the bottom is in direct contact with the heat source, so once the water has been absorbed, the heat keeps transferring and can easily overcook or burn the bottom layer. That’s a major benefit: avoiding a burnt, stuck-on mess.

Next, measurements. Rice cookers typically include water lines inside the pot calibrated for different types and amounts of rice, so you don’t need to remember exact ratios or time things precisely by eye. When using a pot, the ratio and heat level can vary a lot depending on the rice variety and the cook’s experience, leading to inconsistent results. The appliance removes that guesswork and yields consistent rice every time.

Then there are convenience features that a pot simply can’t offer: a delay timer lets you schedule when the rice should start cooking so it’s ready exactly when you want it, and the keep-warm function holds the rice at a safe eating temperature for hours without further cooking or drying out. With a pot, you’d have to time your cooking around the meal and serve immediately or manage reheating, often leading to subpar texture.

Uniform cooking is another point. A rice cooker’s sealed environment and even heat circulation mean every grain cooks in the same way, no hot spots, no undercooked centers. A stove pot is prone to uneven heat distribution, especially if the pot is thin or the burner small, so the rice near the sides and bottom can be overdone while the middle remains al dente.

I should also acknowledge the personal experience element: the user shared that even on the lowest stove setting they get an overcooked layer. That aligns with the science: once water is gone, a pot’s residual heat keeps cooking the starch directly at the bottom, forming a dry crust, whereas the rice cooker cuts off the main heat and only maintains warmth gently.

Given all that, I’ll structure my response by briefly affirming the benefits and then laying out a clear list of those main reasons: no burning, foolproof measurements, scheduling/convenience, and even cooking, along with a short anecdotal note to underline the burning issue.

What are some good substitutes for salt for those on low sodium diets?

I try to keep my sodium intake fairly low to ensure that my blood pressure doesn't get too high.

Salt is such a common part of cooking, and it's especially difficult to cook Asian-style food without a lot of salt due to its reliance on salty sauces such as soy sauce, oyster sauce, etc.

I have tried salt substitutes such as potassium chloride but that can be particularly nasty on the palate, giving the food a chemical taste.

What are some good substitutes for salt in food?

There is no substitute for salt. Sorry. It has effects on the tastebuds and the body that cannot be replicated.

However! They can be *approached* to a degree that most people will find interchangeable. Acids can mimic the flavour-enhancing qualities of salt in a big way. The more acid you have in a dish, the less salt you will need. Beware of going too far, of course, as too much acid is just unpleasant and will need salt to counterbalance.

Heat--as in capsaicin, chili peppers--can produce much the same effect.

Echoing papin's information above; NA and K (sodium and potassium) exist in balance in the body. Too far in one direction and you have a heart attack (too much K), too much in the other and (if memory serves; I could be wrong) you essentially drown (or is it edema? I can't remember). If avoiding sodium is related to a health concern, please speak to your primary healthcare provider before adjusting your diet in this way.

First, I recall that salt has a unique taste and also functions to enhance other flavors and suppress bitterness. Potassium chloride is often marketed as one, but its bitter, metallic aftertaste makes it unpalatable for many, as the user experienced.

Next, I think about what can mimic salt's flavor-enhancing role. This is a well-known technique in low-sodium cooking: adding lemon juice or a splash of rice vinegar at the end of cooking can lift flavors similarly. However, too much acid can make a dish harsh, so it requires balance.

Then, I consider heat from chili peppers or hot sauces. Capsaicin triggers a sensation that draws attention and can compensate for reduced saltiness by adding a different kind of intensity. This fits well with Asian cuisines, where chili pastes or fresh peppers are common. Some of these may still contain sodium, but choosing low-sodium versions or using fresh chilies can help.

Finally, since the user mentioned blood pressure, I recall that sodium and potassium balance is physiologically important, and drastically altering sodium intake without medical guidance can be risky, especially if potassium intake is also being modified. I should include a disclaimer about consulting a healthcare provider, given the health context.

I'll structure the response by first stating clearly that there is no perfect substitute, then explaining how acids and heat can help reduce the need for salt, and ending with the health advisory.

Tips for a small kitchen

I enjoy cooking but have a seriously small kitchen. There is only about 3 ft of work surface and that has kettle and toaster on it. I have a fair amount of shelf space but still need to larder goods and plates in another room.

Do what professional chefs do: clean constantly.

Put all of your ingredients out in an organized place. Use them. Put them away. Clean the station.

If you can, prepare. Put stuff that is prepped back in the fridge until you need it.

Try to use the same few tools for the whole meal--cutlery, mixing bowls, cutting board. Quickly rinse and re-use rather than multiplying utensils.

Aim for dishes that can be cooked in stages in the same pot rather than needing multiple pots or saucepans.

Try out dishes with fewer ingredients. Great chefs can do wonders with 3, 4, or 5. Maybe you don't need more complicated?

Put non-essentials away. Move the kettle and toaster to a shelf until you're done. Use the sink as a repository for anything you're not using but might still need.

Use another room, too. A nearby table could become your staging area, a place to put ingredients that are prepped, finished, or waiting to be used (so your work area isn't cluttered with them).

Just some ideas.

I give it ten minutes after kneading, bash it down again, then another hour before baking. I've tried adding sugar as well but this hasn't made much impact.

A big factor besides the dough is the temperature at which you bake the bread.

If you are not baking it at some recipe specified temperature you are probably playing on the safe side and your breads won't raise much.

You have to heat the CO2 pockets quickly so that they expand before the dough hardens. The more temperature you can give it the better.

What are some key points to store coffee to preserve freshness?

What is the difference between sea salt and regular table salt?

I often sea sea salt sold in grinders to be used at the table, with comments about how it tastes better. What sort of taste differences would I notice using sea salt vs table salt, and what other differences might using one over the other impart?

I've also noticed people say that regular table salt is unhealthy, but that sea salt is somehow healthier for you.

I can say, as a salt snob, that sea salt is a far more flavorful product. I can't even use regular table salt anymore.

Sea salt is salt formed from evaporated sea water, is not iodized, and because it doesn't come from salt mines requires very little processing. Some people will say that because it's "natural", sea salt must be better for you. The mayo clinic seems to disagree: <http://www.mayoclinic.com/health/sea-salt/AN01142>
thinking:
The user is asking about sea salt versus table salt from multiple angles: the basic difference, taste difference, other practical differences, and the health perception. I need to address each, but the question has a personal curiosity angle so I can respond in an informal, opinionated but informed way.

First, I recall the fundamental difference: sea salt is produced by evaporating seawater, which leaves behind not just sodium chloride but also trace minerals like magnesium, calcium, and potassium. Table salt is typically mined from underground salt deposits and then heavily refined to remove those same minerals, resulting in almost pure sodium chloride. It's then often iodized and anti-caking agents are added. So right away, sea salt is less processed and retains its natural mineral content.

For taste, the trace minerals in sea salt can impart a more complex, subtle flavor note—some people describe table salt as harsh or metallic, partly due to the iodine or additives, while sea salt tastes "cleaner" or "saltier" but with more depth. Also, the larger, irregular crystals of sea salt (especially from grinders) dissolve differently on the tongue, giving a burst of flavor rather than a uniform saltiness. That’s the main sensory difference a salt snob would notice.

Other differences: table salt’s iodine is a public health addition to prevent deficiency, which sea salt lacks. Sea salt might also have a different texture in cooked dishes because it dissolves slower, and its mineral content can affect fermentation or brining if you’re using it in specific recipes. However, in most cooking, the difference is subtle.

On health: the claim that sea salt is healthier likely stems from the naturalistic fallacy—it's less refined and therefore perceived as better. But objectively, both are overwhelmingly sodium chloride, and the trace minerals in sea salt are present in amounts too small to offer any real nutritional benefit. The Mayo Clinic and other health authorities state that they are essentially equivalent nutritionally, and excess sodium from either is a health risk. So the health angle is a myth, and I’ll reference the Mayo Clinic link to back that up.

Since the answer is going to be personal and direct, I’ll lead with my own strong preference for sea salt’s flavor, then briefly explain the origin and processing difference, mention the iodine trade-off, and close by debunking the health claim with the citation. That covers all the user’s points without getting overly technical. I’ll keep the tone conversational but authoritative, as a knowledgeable enthusiast.

How should I prepare Risotto

I've been watching a lot of Hells Kitchen, and one of the signature dishes that Chef Ramsay has the chefs prepare is Risotto. This seems like a simple enough dish but often times the seasoned chefs on the show get it wrong. I'd like to try making this dish at home, so what is the technique I should use to ensure a tasty final result?

One of my favorite recipes is Giada De Laurentis' [Wild Mushroom with Peas](http://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/giada-de-laurentiis/mushroom-risotto-with-peas-recipe/index.html). It's rather simple, but amazingly delicious.

The most common flubs when making a risotto are overcooking or dumping in all the liquid at once. I always use the wooden spoon test to determine when the risotto is finished.

First, stir often!

Periodically drag your spoon down the center of the pan as to part the risotto. If the path the spoon makes closes *quickly* then it isn't finished yet. If the part stays open, then you've overcooked it. Ideally it slowly oozes back together.

You're looking for two important things in a perfect risotto:

- **Creamy**
  - The finished risotto should be creamy, not runny, and not gummy. The spoon test takes care of this.
- **Tender**
  - The rice grains should be tender, not crunchy, and not mushy. You should taste frequently as you approach the end of the cooking time. You want the grains slightly *al dente*. You should know that you have rice in your mouth and not just a good tasting mystery-paste.

The user is asking for the proper technique to make risotto after seeing it frequently botched on Hell's Kitchen. Despite seeming straightforward, risotto trips up many cooks because it demands attention to timing and texture. The core of the answer needs to address what goes wrong and how to get it right, so I need to recall the fundamental principles: using warm stock added gradually while stirring, cooking until the rice is just al dente, and achieving a creamy consistency without it being soupy or gluey.

I know that the two most common mistakes are dumping all the liquid in at once—which essentially boils the rice and prevents proper starch release—and overcooking until the grains turn to mush. The wooden spoon test is a classic, reliable indicator of doneness and proper consistency: drawing a path through the risotto lets you watch how the mixture behaves. If it flows back immediately, it needs more cooking; if it stays rigidly parted, it’s overdone. The ideal is a slow, undulating re-merge. This visual cue encapsulates both the liquid content and the starch development.

Texture is the ultimate quality check. You want it creamy (from the starch released during patient stirring) but not runny or gummy. The grains should be tender yet firm to the bite—al dente—so you feel individual rice kernels, not a homogeneous paste. Recommending a specific, well-tested recipe gives the user a concrete starting point, and Giada De Laurentiis’ wild mushroom with peas is a flavorful, approachable option. Does adding salt when soaking dry beans toughen or soften the skin of the bean?

I have heard opinions on both sides of this. The the latest [answer on this site, says salt softens bean skins](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/a/20719/6395) quoted Cooks Illustrated (I can't see the article, but I trust CI), while another [answer says salt hardens the beans' skins](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/a/6554/6395).

In case is varies by bean, I'm interested in:

- Kidney Beans
- Black Beans
- Small Red Beans

So which is it?
Inquiring Minds want to know.

Soften. Other things that typically are added with salt will tend to toughen the beans, but it isn't the fault of the salt. For decades, chefs have circulated the oral tradition that adding salt hardens beans, but it's a myth.

Several scientific studies verify that adding salt to the soaking water for dried beans will reduce the cooking times. The first and most cited article, originally published in 1977, can be found [here](http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2621.1977.tb14460.x/abstract). As mentioned in the first answer you cited, the fine folks at *Cooks Illustrated* found in 2008 that **3 TBSP per gallon of water produces soft skins while not over-salting the interior of the beans**.

Since you can't see the full article, here is the science according to CI:

> "Why does soaking dried beans in salted water make them cook up with
> softer skins? It has to do with how the sodium ions in salt interact
> with the cells of the bean skins. As the beans soak, the sodium ions
> replace some of the calcium and magnesium ions in the skins. Because
> sodium ions are weaker than mineral ions, they allow more water to
> penetrate into the skins, leading to a softer texture. During soaking,
> the sodium ions will only filter partway into the beans, so their
> greatest effect is on the cells in the outermost part of the beans."

Harold McGee's NY Times blog (August 9, 2008) also notes that adding salt early enough will allow complete penetration of the bean, which improves flavor.

On the other hand, things typically added with salt -- particularly sugar and calcium-rich products -- tend to toughen beans (and the salt gets the blame). This toughening effect is most notable in baked-bean recipes using things like ketchup, molasses, and BBQ sauce. You can bake these beans for days, yet the beans will stay whole and firm. The actual mechanism for this effect is not clear; one hypothesis currently circulating seems to be that these products stabilize the cell-cell "glue" (e.g., Shirley Corriher says so on Good Eats "Pantry Raid III - Cool Beans", transcript online [here](http://www.goodeatsfanpage.com/season3/Beans/BeansTranscript.htm)), but I could not find any peer-reviewed study specifically verifying that hypothesis.

The question is about a long-standing cooking myth: does adding salt to the soaking water make bean skins tough or soft? Conflicting advice exists, so I need to resolve it with reliable food-science knowledge. The user specifically mentions kidney, black, and small red beans, but the underlying chemistry should apply to all common dried beans.

First, I recall that this is a classic food-science myth. Many older cookbooks and oral traditions claim salt toughens beans, but more recent experimental work debunks that. I know that Cooks Illustrated ran controlled tests and found salt actually softens skins, and there's a 1977 study often cited. The key is understanding the ion exchange: bean skins contain calcium and magnesium ions that cross-link pectin, making cell walls firmer. When you soak in salted water, sodium ions—weaker in charge—replace some of those divalent cations, loosening the pectin structure so the skin hydrates more easily and becomes softer. That's the core mechanism.

I also need to address why the myth persists. Many recipes that add salt during soaking or cooking also include acidic ingredients (tomatoes, vinegar, molasses) or calcium-rich sweeteners like molasses. Those can indeed toughen beans because acid strengthens pectin, and calcium cross-links it. But the salt gets blamed. I recall Shirley Corriher and Alton Brown discussing this "glue" effect for sugary, calcium-heavy sauces in baked beans. So the explanation will separate the effect of salt from those other ingredients.

Why does the second bowl of popcorn pop better in the microwave? And how can I capitalize on that?

Picture this.

1. I make 1/4 cup of popcorn kernels in the microwave. No paper bag - just a glass bowl with a glass lid, where the lid has holes in it to allow steam to escape. After about 5 minutes, about 3/4 of the kernels have popped. If I go longer, the popped kernels start to burn, and even some of the unpopped kernels burn too. So I stop at 5 minutes, with the bowl about 80% full of popped popcorn.
2. I then empty the glass bowl of all the popcorn into another bowl, for eating. But before eating, I make another 1/4 cup of popcorn kernels in the microwave again. This time, at about 4 1/2 minutes, there are so many popped kernels that it lifts the glass lid off the top of the bowl, perfectly cooked. I empty it into my eating bowl...

I didn't use oil or anything, but I got perfect air-popped popcorn from just a microwave. Only thing is, it took two tries. Also, this happens ***every time.*** Part of the reason I make a second bowl at all is because the popcorns are just so much better than the first bowl's.

How can I get the first batch to cook just as well as the second one? I have tried "pre-heating" just the bowl in the microwave for about 30 seconds. It does help. But apparently this is actually very bad and dangerous for the components of the microwave.

I don't know what's happening. But if I had to guess, there are tiny water molecules in the microwave that are messing things up. Or, something about the bowl being warm helps the kernels pop.

Do you have a suggestion on how to make a perfect bowl of air-popped popcorn in one go?

I am the original question-asker reporting back...

I was able to make perfect popcorn by adding about 1 teaspoon of water to the bottom of the bowl. But please don't try this unless you have a glass lid with holes in it (see below).

There were concerns about the bowl, the microwave, and the lid. Ultimately, I believe it was the humidity under the lid from the previous batch that was creating the perfect environment for the kernels in the second try. I never mentioned that the lid with holes in it frequently had some condensation on it before I put it back on for a second batch, because I didn't think it would be relevant.

To test the humidity theory, I added about 2 teaspoons of water to the bottom of the bowl, then mixed up the popcorn kernels in it. After about 9-10 minutes (about twice as long as before), I had a bowl of perfectly cooked popcorn. It was incredible that just about every single kernel had the exact same color (brownish-orange) inside the center of the popcorn, especially after that length of time. The bowl was 101% filled with popped kernels, although I stopped it before it could lift the lid off. It's possible that by using less water, you could achieve the same result in less time.

Chemically, this was a bit like buttering popcorn to help it cook more evenly, except with water and a microwave instead of oil and a stove. It's a very unusual way to think of using water because in any other context, water has a very high specific heat - it is objectively a bad heat conductor. Never would you think of stationary water as a "heat conductor", except inside a microwave, as microwaves work mainly by heating the water molecules in food.

The reason why I think the lid must have holes in it for this to be effective is because you have to give a way for steam to escape. The kernels won't pop (and release steam) if there is already a saturation of steam inside the bowl. Also, without holes in the lid, the steam inside the bowl will become so incredibly hot, that you'll likely just wind up superheating the water or glass or something, potentially melting and breaking the glass especially if it's the more common soda-lime glass. The final popcorn will probably be wet, too, and it will take a lot longer to pop all the kernels. This popcorn was surprisingly dry!

I could not determine anything from microwaving the bowl with water in it. The bowl says Pyrex on it. The lid is borosilicate glass. The bowl has some paintings on it. It's still possible that this was a factor.

So in conclusion, I added a really small spoonful of water to my popcorn kernels, mixed it up, cooked it twice as long in glass with holes in it, and got perfectly popped popcorn, dry and evenly cooked.
thinking:
The user is struggling with inconsistent popcorn popping in the microwave: the first batch only partially pops and burns, while the second batch, made immediately after in the same bowl, pops perfectly. The key difference between batches is that the bowl and lid are warm for the second batch, and there’s often condensation on the lid from the first batch’s steam. I need to figure out why that matters and how to replicate the second batch’s conditions from the start.

Microwave popcorn pops because the kernels contain a small amount of natural moisture trapped inside the starchy endosperm. When heated, that water vaporizes, building pressure until the hull ruptures. Uneven popping and burning happen when some kernels heat too slowly or too fast—maybe because the initial microwave energy isn’t distributing well across the cold, dry kernels. The glass bowl itself doesn’t absorb microwaves well, so the kernels are heated directly by the microwave field. If the kernels are very dry on the outside, they might not couple with the microwaves as efficiently at first.

For the second batch, the bowl is already warm, and there’s residual steam and condensation inside from the first batch. That thin film of moisture on the lid and maybe on the kernels’ surfaces could act as a heat-transfer medium: water molecules absorb microwave energy very effectively, so even a tiny amount of added water can superheat locally, creating steam that rapidly surrounds and indirectly heats the kernels. This steamy microenvironment might help all kernels reach popping temperature more uniformly, preventing hot spots that burn some before others pop. The warm bowl also means less energy is wasted heating the bowl itself, but preheating it empty is risky because without a load to absorb microwaves, the magnetron can reflect energy back and get damaged.

The solution, then, is to introduce a controlled amount of water at the start. Adding a small spoonful of water (about a teaspoon) to the raw kernels and mixing it in mimics the residual humidity of the second batch. That water will heat quickly, turning to steam that envelops the kernels and likely penetrates their hulls slightly, hydrating the outer starch and ensuring even heating. The lid must have vent holes, otherwise steam pressure could build up dangerously and the popcorn would turn out wet. The cooking time will be longer because the water absorbs energy first, but the result should be near-total popping with minimal burning.

I’ll present this as a direct recommendation: add a teaspoon of water to the kernels in the bowl, stir, cover with the vented glass lid, and cook about twice as long as usual, monitoring until popping slows. I’ll explain the science of how moisture improves microwave coupling and even cooking, and caution about using the proper lid for safety.

Why not use alcohol ice?

I don't really drink alcohol so it's more of a theoretical question.
I know that some people don't like ice because it dilutes the drink, so they prefer to use metal or stone cubes instead.

However they have smaller thermal capacity and thermal conductivity than water ice.

So my question is - why not use ice made from the very drink you are trying to cool?

Granted, some cocktails may be ruined by freezing but something like whiskey or bourbon or gin should be fine, I think.
Sure, freezing alcohol requires much lower temperatures then water but the whole glass shouldn't be too cold; such ice won't dilute the drink and should have reasonable thermal capacity/conductivity.

Sure, it may require a specialized freezer (in a bar or a restaurant) but a simple dry ice box should also work.

Ethanol has a *much* lower freezing temperature than water: -114°C. This is considerably colder than dry ice and would require expensive specialised equipment to make and store. It would also be dangerous if it made contact with skin or was swallowed.

Freezing an alcoholic drink, which is mostly water, mostly freezes the water while mostly alcohol stays liquid, so it wouldn't be feasible to have a solid that was the same mixture as the drink itself.

Using frozen alcohol would be dangerously cold and would immediately melt anyway. What is commonly done if someone wants a very cold drink without ice is to store the ingredients and glassware in the freezer so that they start very cold (but still liquid).
thinking:
The user is asking why we can't freeze an alcoholic drink (like whiskey) into ice cubes to chill the drink without dilution, similar to using water ice but avoiding the watering-down effect. They've considered metal or stone cubes but note their thermal drawbacks, and they think freezing the drink itself might work if a cold enough freezer or dry ice is used. I need to address the scientific and practical reasons this isn't done.

First, I recall the freezing behavior of ethanol-water mixtures. Pure ethanol freezes at -114°C, far lower than water's 0°C. Alcoholic beverages are mostly water with some ethanol, so when chilled, the water component begins to freeze first, forming nearly pure water ice while the remaining liquid becomes more concentrated in ethanol. That means you can't get a solid cube with the same composition as the original drink; the "ice" would be mostly water ice, still diluting the drink when it melts, while leaving a boozy liquid core that might remain unfrozen. The user's assumption that freezing the whole drink avoids dilution is flawed because fractional freezing separates the mixture.

Next, consider the temperature requirements. Even if one aimed to freeze pure ethanol or a very high-proof spirit, reaching -114°C requires specialized cryogenic equipment, not a standard freezer or even a dry ice box (dry ice is -78.5°C). So it's impractical for bars or home use. The user’s dry ice suggestion wouldn't work for solidifying spirits.

Then there's the safety issue. A solid at -114°C is dangerously cold. Contact with skin or, worse, the mouth and throat if accidentally swallowed, would cause severe cold burns or frostbite immediately. The user thought the glass wouldn't get too cold, but the cube itself is the hazard, especially if it directly touches tissues. Also, placing such a frozen cube into a room-temperature drink would cause it to melt rapidly from the extreme temperature difference, potentially cracking or shattering, and it would hardly provide sustained cooling—it would just chill briefly and turn into liquid alcohol, throwing off the drink's balance.

The practical solution that already exists is simply to store the spirit and the glassware in a normal freezer. Since the ethanol content prevents the drink from freezing solid, it can be chilled well below 0°C and still poured as a liquid, achieving a very cold, undiluted drink. This covers what the user is observing people do instead.

I'll structure the response by first pointing out the freezing point mismatch and fractional freezing, then the equipment impracticality, then the safety dangers, and finally the existing alternative. That matches the key points in the final answer without paraphrasing directly.Ethanol has a much lower freezing point than water (−114°C vs 0°C). Alcoholic drinks are ethanol–water mixtures, and when you try to freeze them the water freezes out first as nearly pure ice, leaving a more concentrated liquid. You cannot obtain a solid cube with the same composition as the original drink; the “ice” would still be mostly water and would dilute the drink, while a boozy liquid core remains unfrozen.

Achieving −114°C requires specialized cryogenic equipment; a dry‑ice box (−78.5°C) is not cold enough. Even if you could make such cubes, they would be dangerously cold—direct contact with skin or accidental swallowing would cause severe frostbite almost instantly. Placing a solid at −114°C into a drink would also cause explosive melting and thermal shock, making it impractical and hazardous.

The common undiluted alternative is to chill the bottled spirits and the glassware in a freezer. The alcohol content keeps the drink liquid at freezer temperatures, so it can be served very cold without any ice.

Is there a trick for softening butter quickly?

I often don't realize a baking recipe requires softened butter until after I start adding in the other wet ingredients and it's too late to wait for butter to soften the normal way (with time). So, I will usually microwave the butter until it accidentally all melts or add in the butter when it's still too hard, which impacts the overall success of the recipe. What are some tricks for softening butter quickly?

**Use a grater**

If your butter is too stiff, try using a cheese grater on it. The mechanical action will warm the butter slightly and soften it, and the huge increase in surface area will allow the room's ambient warmth to soften the butter much faster. Spread the butter shavings in a single layer to maximize surface area, and they should soften in a few minutes. You'll be unlikely to over-soften the butter with this method, so you won't run a risk of winding up with melted butter instead of softened butter.

The user has a specific baking problem: they start a recipe, realize butter needs to be softened, and need a quick fix that won't melt the butter or leave it too hard. Their attempts so far—microwaving (which often accidentally melts it) or using cold butter—ruin the texture. So I need to focus on methods that rapidly bring cold butter to a pliable, spreadable state without overheating. Softened butter is ideally around 65–68°F, firm but yielding to pressure. Melting destroys its ability to trap air when creamed, leading to dense baked goods. Hard butter clumps unevenly.

Common quick-softening tricks include cutting into small cubes and letting them sit, using a rolling pin to pound the butter flat between parchment, or microwaving on very low power in 5-second increments. However, in the middle of a recipe with wet ingredients already added, you can’t really spread the butter out to warm on the counter for long, and the microwave is too risky for marginal temperature control. The rolling pin method works but requires some muscle and might still leave chunks if not careful.

The grater method stands out as ideal here. Cold butter straight from the fridge is firm enough to grate cleanly, and the mechanical action of grating adds a tiny bit of friction heat, starting the softening. More importantly, the thin shreds have massive surface area compared to a whole stick, allowing ambient heat in the kitchen to warm them through in a minute or two. You can spread the shreds on a plate or even the mixing bowl side and they’ll reach softness quickly—no risk of melting, because you’re not applying sustained heat. Once soft, they incorporate smoothly into the wet mixture, even if it's already partially mixed. This method is forgiving and doesn't require precise timing or equipment beyond a box grater. I’ll structure the answer to present this trick first, explaining the surface-area science and why it avoids the melting pitfall, and maybe note that other methods exist but the grater is most reliable in their specific scenario.

Why do my silicone spatulas melt in frying oil?

I have bought three silicone spatulas so far and all of them start "melting" when used to flip frying eggs.

I don't leave them in the pan or anything and, supposedly, silicone should be able to withstand much higher temperatures than frying oil.

But I've had the same happen with a "silicone basket"-like utensil (I don't know exactly what it was called) which, quite literally, melted and fell apart when I used it for the first time to fish french fries out of the frier.

I also see a lot of people having the same experience over the wire/internet.

Why is this happening and is there a way to confirm the utensils are real silicone and not something else?

EDIT:
  
After some digging I have discovered I have, in fact, bought a nylon spatula, instead of a silicone one.

I am going to copy @unlisted's comment for benefit of future readers:

> Though both obviously 'plasticky' nylon is hard & silicone is soft. If it will squish a bit, it's silicone. Nylon will bend but you could never describe it as 'squishy'. Of course, even if it passes that test it may still not be food-grade.

**If the products are melting and falling apart in hot oil at cooking temperatures I think you have experimentally confirmed that they are not food grade silicone.** Food-grade silicone should be completely functional in the range of frying temperatures.

In a guide to food-grade silicone:

> Temperature resistance is one of the principal attributes of food-grade silicone. This is particularly crucial in food processing where temperatures can vary from boiling hot to freezing cold. **Food grade silicone can generally function in temperatures varying between -60°C and +250°C** (special grades up to +300°C). [Source](https://barnwell.co.uk/why-use-food-grade-silicone/)

In a guide to safe deep-frying:

> If you have a food thermometer heat the oil to 160C for low, 180C for moderate and **190C for high**. [Source](https://www.bbcgoodfood.com/howto/guide/how-deep-fry-safely)

As for buying reliable products, my recommendation would be to buy branded products from reputable shops. With experience and common sense you can get a sense for what brands and products to trust.
thinking:
The user is describing a common problem: “silicone” spatulas melting in hot oil during frying. They later edited the question to reveal they discovered the spatula was actually nylon. So the core question is why this happened and how to confirm if utensils are real silicone.

First, I need to recall the properties of food-grade silicone. Silicone is known for its high heat resistance—typically stable from around -60°C to 250°C, with some grades going higher. Frying oil temperatures usually range from 160°C to 190°C, which is well within silicone’s tolerance. So genuine silicone should never melt or fall apart in a frying pan or deep fryer.

The fact that the utensils are melting means they cannot be real food-grade silicone. Nylon, by contrast, has a much lower melting point (around 220°C but can soften and deform at lower temperatures, especially in direct contact with hot oil). The user’s own observation—the spatula bending versus squishing—also distinguishes nylon (hard, bendable) from silicone (soft, squishy).

For the answer, I’ll structure it by first stating the experimental proof: melting confirms it’s not food-grade silicone. content:
Why doesn't Greek cuisine use a lot of spices, compared to neighbors?

According to what I know almost all countries in the Mediterranean which surround Greece use a lot of spices in their cuisine. Greece itself has been occupied by such countries for hundreds of years. There has always been trade and travel between Greece and the other countries. So how come spices aren't being used that much at all?

Compared to say, Turkey, or Italy, Greek food is not spicy at all. I am not saying this is a bad thing, or that it is bland - I just find it curious that over the millennia no significant use of spices has developed like it did in Italy, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey, Bulgaria. Out of those countries most use a lot of spices including capsicums, and the few ones that don't, still use a lot of spices (like say Syria).

It's known that even in antiquity spices were known in Greece and used for medical reasons. This makes it even more curious. Are there any historical reasons for that perhaps?

Thanks.

The question of "why not" is difficult to answer definitively, or really at all. We can't ask folks 2000 years ago why they didn't care about cumin. However, there are some historical impacts on Greek cuisine that bear on this, so let's explore them:

1. You mention Turkey, Syria, and Lebanon as Greek neighbors. But consider that Greece is also historically next to Austria, and currently next to Romania and Bulgaria, and is closer to Slovakia than it is to Lebanon. So if you look at Greece as being midway between Syria and Kosovo, the frequency of spice use also puts it midway.
2. Greek cuisine doesn't rely heavily on spices partly because it does rely heavily on herbs and alliums. Because of the climate, onions, garlic, leeks, parsley, dill, oregano, thyme, and others grow readily and plentifully all over the islands and peninsulas. So do citrus, also used for seasoning Greek dishes. Many Greek dishes will have onions, garlic, lemon, and as much as 2 cups of minced herbs in them. Given this, one can see why Greek cooks didn't feel the need to add two teaspoons of cumin and dried peppers as well. Italy, having a similar climate, largely takes a similar approach.
3. One place where Greek spice usage is on a parallel with Syria is [in sweets](https://www.thespruceeats.com/spices-used-in-greek-cooking-1705406). The palette of spices used for Greek pastries, cookies, and cakes is as great as -- and extremely similar to -- the ones used in the Middle East. This is undoubtedly because most places in the region got their sweet recipes from the Persian and Ottoman empires, so they're really the same recipes.
4. Greece, like other ancient regions, includes multiple cuisines. Some of these use more spices than others, particularly Thrace.

Note that above I'm using the term "spices" to refer to its accepted use, of "aromatic seeds, stems, and bark".
thinking:
I need to understand why Greek cuisine seems to lack the heavy spice use of its neighbors, despite shared history and trade. The question is curious about historical or practical reasons, noting that even in antiquity Greeks knew spices medicinally. So I’m essentially being asked to account for an absence, which is tricky because “why not” questions don’t have a single definitive answer. I’ll approach it by examining factors that might have made spice use less common in everyday Greek cooking compared to, say, Turkish or Syrian cuisine.

First, I recall the basics: “spices” in culinary terms usually mean dried aromatic seeds, bark, or roots—think cumin, cinnamon, pepper, cloves. That’s distinct from herbs (fresh leafy parts) and from capsicum-based heat. The user mentioned capsicums, but those are New World additions, so the real comparison is about these dry spices. Greek climate is dry and rocky, perfect for hardy herbs like oregano, thyme, dill, and for alliums like onions, garlic, leeks, plus citrus like lemon. These grow abundantly all over the islands and peninsulas, giving cooks ready access to big flavors without needing imported dried spices. This is very similar to Italy, which also leans on basil, oregano, rosemary, garlic, and lemon rather than loads of dried spices. So a practical explanation emerges: why reach for expensive, traded seeds when your garden overflows with potent seasonings?

I consider the historical angle. Ancient Greeks did use spices like coriander and cumin, but often medicinally or sparingly. During the Roman and Byzantine periods, spice trade flourished, but those spices remained luxury items, not daily staples for the common kitchen. The Ottoman occupation certainly brought complex spice blends to the region, but this influence may have been absorbed unevenly. I recall that in Greek cuisine, sweets—like baklava, melomakarona, kourabiedes—rely heavily on cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and allspice, a palette that closely mirrors Middle Eastern and Turkish pastries. That makes sense because many of those dessert traditions stem from the Persian and then Ottoman imperial kitchens, spreading similar recipes across the empire. So Greek cooking does use spices, but they’ve been channeled mainly into sweets and special occasions rather than everyday savory dishes.

The user’s comparison set—Turkey, Syria, Lebanon—represents spice-forward cuisines. But I should broaden the geographic lens. Greece isn’t only surrounded by those; it’s also close to the Balkans (Albania, North Macedonia, Bulgaria) and even historically linked to Central Europe via Austria. Many Balkan cuisines use fewer aromatic spices, often relying on paprika (which came later), dill, or parsley. If I imagine Greece positioned midway between the spice-heavy east and the sparer north, its spice usage looks like a middle ground. Moreover, Greek cuisine isn’t monolithic: the region of Thrace, for instance, uses more spices like allspice and cumin in savory pies and stews, likely due to its proximity to Turkey and Bulgaria. This internal variation shows that the “Greek cuisine” label covers a spectrum.

Any initial thought that Greece might simply be “bland” or that occupation should have automatically infused more spice ignores how culinary traditions develop from bottom-up availability and daily practice. Herbs and alliums are the backbone, making additional dried spices less necessary. I might have first assumed that Ottoman rule would uniformly spice-up Greek food, but that overlooks the strength of pre-existing local ingredient traditions and the possibility that such influence was class- or region-specific.

So I’ll structure the answer by first acknowledging the difficulty of proving a negative, then offering these points: recast the geographic neighbors to show Greece as a middle point; explain the herb-and-allium abundance as an alternative to spices, with Italy as a parallel; highlight that in sweets, spice use is indeed on par with the Middle East due to shared imperial recipes; and note that Greece contains many regional cuisines, some of which are more spice-heavy. Finally, I’ll clarify the definition of “spices” to avoid confusion with capsicums or herbs. The tone will be informative, addressing the historical and practical angles without overclaiming a single cause.

content:
How Can Cooked Meat Still Have Protein Value?

I've been taught 2 things that seem to contradict each other:

- Cooked meat has plenty of protein
- Heating proteins denatures them and damages/changes them

If this is the case, then cooked meat must have very little usable protein, *which is clearly not the case*.

**How does protein in a fully cooked food, e.g. chicken/pork/eggs survive the cooking process in a usable form?**

Note I'm not asking about burnt meat, browning or flavour reactions, or rare meat e.g. a medium/rare cooked steak.

Structural proteins in foods, i.e. albumin in eggs, myosin in muscle meats, gluten in wheat, are formed by amino acids in complex structures. Proteins are folded and clumped chains of peptides, and peptides are chains of amino acids. Your body uses stomach acid and proteases (enzymes) to break down proteins in digestion, but this requires time and energy (stomach churning, body heat).

The amino acids are what your body requires. They're used to build more complex proteins. Cooking gives a head start in un-clumping/unfolding proteins, and in some conditions into peptides and amino acids, that are easier for your body to digest making them more *'bioavailable'*.

Some of these amino acids can be produced by your body using nitrogen compounds from breaking down other amino acids and nutrients. The ones your body can't produce on its own have to be obtained in the proteins you eat. These are called 'essential amino acids'.

Different protein sources have different amino acid compositions, giving them different *'protein values'* in how complete the range of essential amino acids are available; i.e. collagen/gelatin is a common structural protein that provides great texture for sensory applications, but the protein value is 0 for regulatory labelling requirements in some countries since it is missing an essential amino acid.
thinking:
The apparent contradiction stems from a misunderstanding of what "denature" means in a nutritional context. Denaturation is the loss of a protein's three-dimensional folded structure—the unspooling of its native conformation due to heat—without breaking the peptide bonds that link amino acids together. What cooks often call "damage" is the destruction of that delicate shape, which is functionally critical for things like enzyme activity or the texture of meat, but not for the protein’s nutritional worth. The body’s goal in digestion is precisely to break those proteins down into individual amino acids and short peptides anyway, using stomach acid and proteases. A denatured, unfolded protein actually gives digestive enzymes easier access to the peptide backbone, increasing the speed and completeness of breakdown. So cooking, rather than destroying usable protein, typically enhances its bioavailability.

The key is that the amino acids themselves—including the nine essential ones humans must obtain from food—survive typical cooking temperatures largely intact. Only under severe conditions like charring or prolonged boiling do peptide bonds hydrolyze to any significant degree, and even then the individual amino acids remain, often still absorbable. The "protein value" of a food, as in the completeness of its essential amino acid profile, is a property of the primary sequence, which heat does not alter. For example, collagen is a protein with zero essential amino acid score because it lacks tryptophan; cooking it to gelatin changes texture and solubility but doesn’t fix that inherent amino acid gap. The question’s core confusion thus resolves by recognizing that the nutritional unit is the amino acid, not the folded protein structure, and cooking aids the very digestive dismantling that was going to happen anyway.

I’ll structure the response by first clarifying that denaturation is unfolding, not chemical destruction of amino acids. Then I’ll link that to digestion, explaining how cooking acts as a pre-digestion step that improves amino acid availability. Finally, I’ll address the concept of protein quality, showing that the essential amino acid content remains unchanged by cooking, and touch on the collagen example to illustrate that protein value is about composition, not cooking damage.

content:
Can meat spoil outside the fridge if it's baked into bread as a filling?

I made some meat buns tonight (that is, buns with cooked chicken stuffed inside them before being baked), and I'm wondering if I should bother keeping the buns inside the fridge, because that would mean having to reheat them later.

Will the chicken inside them even go bad if the bread's there to protect it? It seems to me that the bread will act basically like a tin can and keep the meat preserved as long as the bread is, since the meat inside was heated and all the bacteria that might have been on it was cooked to death.

Is this a wrong way of thinking? Should I just refrigerate them just to be safe?

There are two differences between your buns and a tin can.

First, your buns were heated to a core temperature of under 100°C. Yes, your oven was probably set way higher, but the water content in your filling prevents it from getting hotter than boiling water. Commercial canning is done in the vicinity of 120-130°C, which is possible because the cans are cooked under pressure. So unlike in a can, *most* pathogens were destroyed, but not necessarily *all of them*. For human consumption, that’s perfectly fine *as long as the remaining ones don’t get the time-temperature combo to regrow*.

Second, a bread dough may be dense (although the aim is usually something different), but by no means airtight. Interestingly, [wrapping meat in dense dough was used as preservation method in medieval times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huff_paste) - the “ancestor” of today’s pork pies and pastries. But while the hard flour crust (not intended to be eaten originally) did form a protective layer and *usually* extended the shelf life more or less, it was by no means food safe judged by modern standards - although some pies were stored for months. But your fluffy buns are truly not a protective layer. Which means you should refrigerate your buns, but also that you get to enjoy the whole dish.
thinking:
The user is asking whether meat-filled baked buns need refrigeration, drawing a parallel to canned goods where the container preserves the contents after heating. They believe the bread forms a protective seal and that the baking heat killed all bacteria, so the meat inside should remain safe as long as the bread is intact. This misunderstands both the nature of the baking process and the properties of bread as a barrier.

First, I need to address the temperature aspect. In baking, the internal temperature of a moist filling like chicken is limited by water evaporation; even if the oven is at 200°C, the filling itself cannot exceed about 100°C until most water is boiled off. This is sufficient to kill vegetative bacteria, but not necessarily heat-resistant spores such as those from *Clostridium* species. Commercial canning, by contrast, uses pressure to achieve temperatures around 120–130°C, which destroys spores and enables long-term shelf stability. So the user’s assumption that “all bacteria were cooked to death” is inaccurate—some spores may survive, and under favorable conditions (warmth, moisture, time) they can germinate and grow.

Second, the bread-as-tin-can analogy fails because bread is porous and not airtight. A sealed metal can prevents recontamination and blocks oxygen, which is crucial for preventing aerobic spoilage and some pathogen growth. Bread dough, even if dense, still allows air exchange, and standard fluffy buns are far from impermeable. The reference to historical huff paste in the final answer is useful to show that while dense dough could somewhat extend shelf life, it didn’t make food shelf-stable by modern safety standards, and certainly not at room temperature for extended periods.

Thus, the user’s intuition is partially correct that heating reduces bacteria, but the incomplete kill and lack of a hermetic seal mean the buns remain perishable. I’ll structure the response to first gently correct the analogy, then explain the two key scientific differences—core temperature limitations and lack of airtightness—and finally recommend refrigeration with a note that reheating is a small inconvenience for safety. I’ll avoid any alarmism but be clear about the food-safety reasoning.

Just make sure that the food in the steamer will take less time to steam than the food below takes to boil.

I also think about the practical examples from various cuisines: the Moroccan couscousière is a classic, where the stew in the bottom generates steam to cook the couscous above. No flavor issues arise from the steam of plain boiling vegetables, but flavored broths might impart subtle tastes. I’ll structure the answer around a clear yes, mention the necessary equipment like a steamer insert, give the couscousière as a cultural example, and caution about timing differences.

content:
How do I get better at tasting?

I think this question might be borderline off-topic. I am open to suggestions for making it fit the SA format better

Many drinks (coffee, whisk(e)y, wine) are more enjoyable once one can discern the different flavours in those drinks. I.e., once one moves beyond 'tastes like wine' to 'tastes like blueberries and honey'. The same is true for some foods (chocolate comes to mind, with descriptions similar to those used for wines. Also [olive oil](https://cooking.stackexchange.com/questions/655/proper-olive-oil-tasting-technique).). On top of that, it is a fun (and, for cooks, useful) skill to be able to taste a dish and mentally separate out the different ingredients that went into it.

Some people (so-called [supertasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supertaster)) are predisposed to have a sharp sense of taste. Assuming I am not a supertaster, how can I improve my tasting skills?

You get better through concentration and lack of distractions. Just as you shouldn't eat while watching TV. You'll miss all the flavors.

Sit back. Take small samples. Let it lay or slosh around in your mouth for a while--several seconds at least. Think about what you taste and feel.

Soon you will find those one-tone flavors have a background to them or a subtle second or third flavor coming out of nowhere.

After a while, you'll start noticing those underlying flavors every time you use that ingredient and notice it missing when you have a not-so-good variety.
thinking:
The user is asking how to improve tasting skills, noting that discerning specific flavors in drinks and foods makes them more enjoyable and is useful for cooks. The core of tasting is paying attention to sensory input, but most people eat and drink while distracted. To get better, one must create conditions for focused tasting. Distractions like TV or conversation dull perception because the brain can't fully process flavor signals. So the first step is to eliminate those.

Physically, taking small samples and letting them move around the mouth for several seconds exposes more of the food or drink to taste buds and olfactory receptors, which are essential for picking up volatile aroma compounds that create complex flavors. The act of consciously thinking about what's being tasted helps train the brain to separate and identify individual notes, much like learning to recognize subtleties in any skill through deliberate practice. Over time, this focused repetition builds a mental library of flavor references, making it easier to spot background notes or missing elements in lower-quality ingredients.

The answer should be straightforward and practical, mirroring the concise style of the final answer. I'll highlight concentration and lack of distractions first, then the technique of small sips and letting the sample linger, and end with the natural progression of noticing more depth and eventually relying on that expanded palate.

I think I can smell the food inside my microwave. Is that bad?

I figured it's not necessarily unsafe, since you only need a cage to block the microwaves from escaping, but I'm not familiar with the precise architecture of a microwave oven.

Microwave doors don't have an airtight seal; the window between the electronics and the cooking compartment is also not airtight, and the electronics are cooled by a fan. It would be surprising if some cooking smells didn't escape. In practice, every microwave I've ever had allows me to smell the cooking, from the very cheapest to some rather fancy ones with grill and convection.

This means that being able to smell the food cooking says nothing about the safety of the microwave, and you have no need to worry (unless there are other indications such as damage)

So from the cheapest to the fanciest models, cooking smells always escape during operation.
